stem_md: If  $x, y, z, t > 1$  then:   $$ \left(\log _{zxt}x\right)^2+\left(\log _{xyt}y\right)^2+\left(\log _{xyz}z\right)^2+\left(\log _{yzt}t\right)^2>\frac{1}{4} $$
solution_md:
Denote  $\ln x=a>0;\ln y=b>0;\ln z=c>0;\ln t=d>0$ . $\log _{zxt}x=\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln zxt}=\dfrac{a}{a+c+d}$ ; $\log _{xyt}y=\dfrac{b}{a+b+d}$ ; $\log_{xyz}z=\dfrac{c}{a+b+c}$ ; $\log _{yzt}t=\dfrac{d}{b+c+d}$ . $a+b+c+d=S;a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=S_1;ab+ac+ad+bc+bd+cd=S_2$ . $S^2=S_1+2S_2>S_1$ .

Using these relations and the Titu's lemma, results: $\left(\log _{zxt}x\right)^2+\left(\log _{xyt}y\right)^2+\left(\log _{xyz}z\right)^2+\left(\log _{yzt}t\right)^2=$  $\left(\dfrac{a}{a+c+d}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{b}{a+b+d}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{c}{a+b+c}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{d}{b+c+d}\right)^2\ge$  $\ge\dfrac{(a+b+c+d)^2}{(a+c+d)^2+(a+b+d)^2+(a+b+c)^2+(b+c+d)^2}=$  $=\dfrac{S^2}{2S^2+S_1}>\dfrac{S^2}{3S^2}=\dfrac{1}{3}>\dfrac{1}{4}$ .

stem_md: Let  $\alpha > 0$  be a real number. Compute the limit of the sequence  $\{x_n\}_{n\geq 1}$  defined by   $$ x_n=\begin{cases} \sum \limits_{k=1}^n \sinh \left(\frac{k}{n^2}\right),& \text{when}\ n>\frac{1}{\alpha} 0,& \text{when}\ n\leq \frac{1}{\alpha}\end{cases} $$
solution_md:
$\sinh x=x+\frac 16 x^3+.....$  by taylor series.
that means  $\sinh (\frac{k}{n^2})=\frac{k}{n^2}+\frac{1}{3!}\frac{k^3}{n^6}+....$ But nothing that the terms of the sum, are of the form  $\frac{k^m}{n^{2m}}=\frac{1}{n^{m-1}}\times \frac 1n(\frac{k}{n})^m$  which sums up to riemann sums multiplied by some vanishing terms, except in m=1. The threshold is unrelevant because of the archimedian property. so  $x_n \to \int_0^1 xdx=\frac 12$ Regards
Claudio

Let  $a$ ,  $b$  and  $c$  be complex numbers such that  $abc = 1$ . Find the value of the cubic root of 

\begin{tabular}{|ccc|} $b + n^3c$  &   $n(c - b)$  &  $n^2(b - c)$  $n^2(c - a)$  &  $c + n^3a$  &  $n(a - c)$  $n(b - a)$   &  $n^2(a - b)$  &  $a + n^3b$ \end{tabular}
solution_md: $D=\left|\begin{array}{lll} b + n^3c & n(c - b) & n^2(b - c)  n^2(c - a) & c + n^3a & n(a - c)  n(b - a) & n^2(a - b) & a + n^3b  \end{array}\right|$  $D\stackrel{C_{3}+nC_{2}}{=}\left|\begin{array}{lll} b + n^3c & n(c - b) & 0  n^2(c - a) & c + n^3a & na +n^{4}a  n(b - a) & n^2(a - b) & a + n^3a  \end{array}\right|$  $D=a(n^{3}+1)\left|\begin{array}{lll} b + n^3c & n(c - b) & 0  n^2(c - a) & c + n^3a & n  n(b - a) & n^2(a - b) & 1  \end{array}\right|$  $D\stackrel{R_{2}-nR_{3}}{=}a(n^{3}+1)\left|\begin{array}{lll} b + n^3c & n(c - b) & 0  n^2c - n^{2}b & c + n^3b & 0  n(b - a) & n^2(a - b) & 1  \end{array}\right|$  $D=a(n^{3}+1)\left|\begin{array}{ll} b + n^3c & n(c - b)  n^2c - n^{2}b & c + n^3b \end{array}\right|$  $D=abc(n^{3}+1)^{3}$ .

stem_md: If  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c > 0$ ;  $ab + bc + ca = 3$  then:   $$ 4\left(\tan^{-1} 2\right)\left(\tan^{-1}\left(\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)\right) \leq \pi \tan^{-1}\left(1 + \sqrt[3]{abc}\right) $$
solution_md:
<u>Lemma 1</u>: let  $g(x)=(1+x^2)\cdot \arctan x$ . Then  $g(x)$  is increasing for  $x>0$ *Proof*:  $g'(x)=1+2x\cdot \arctan x >0$  for  $x>0$   $_{\blacksquare}$ <u>Lemma 2</u>: let  $\displaystyle f(x)=\frac{\arctan(x+1)}{\arctan x}$  for  $x>0$ . Then  $f(x)$  is decreasing

*Proof*:  $\displaystyle f'(x)=\frac{\displaystyle \frac{\arctan x}{1+(x+1)^2}-\frac{\arctan(x+1)}{1+x^2}}{\arctan^2 x}=\frac{(1+x^2)\arctan x-(1+(x+1)^2)\arctan(x+1)}{(1+x^2)(1+(x+1)^2)\arctan^2 x}=\frac{g(x)-g(x+1)}{(1+x^2)(1+(x+1)^2)\arctan^2 x}<0$  by Lemma 1  $_{\blacksquare}$ By AM-GM we have that  $\frac{ab+bc+ca}{3}\geq \sqrt[3]{a^2b^2c^2}$ , thus  $1\geq \left(\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)^2$  and finally  $\sqrt[3]{abc}\leq 1$ The given inequality is equivalent to the following:  $\frac{\arctan\left(1+\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)}{\arctan\left(\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)}\geq \frac{4}{\pi}\arctan(2)$ , that is  $f\left(\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)\geq \frac{4}{\pi}\arctan(2)$ By Lemma 2, since  $f(x)$  is decreasing and  $\sqrt[3]{abc}\leq 1$ , we obtain  $f\left(\sqrt[3]{abc}\right)\geq f(1)=\frac{\arctan(2)}{\arctan(1)}=\frac{4}{\pi}\arctan(2)$  as required

stem_md: It is possible to partition the set  $\{100, 101,\cdots , 1000\}$  into two subsets so that for any two distinct elements  $x$  and  $y$  belonging to the same subset  $ \sqrt[3]{x + y}$  is irrational?
solution_md:
The answer is no. $\lfloor\sqrt[3]{x+y}\rfloor\le\lfloor\sqrt[3]{1000+999}\rfloor=12$ .
We will find  $3$  numbers  $a,b,c\in\{100,101,\dots,1000\}$  such that: $a+b=m^3;a+c=n^3;b+c=p^3;m,n,p\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $m,n,p\le12$ .
We choose: $a+b=11^3=1331; a+c=9^3=729; b+c=10^3=1000$ .
Results: $a=530;b=801;c=199$ .

Assume exists the sets  $A,B$  such that  $A\cup B=\{100,101,\dots,1000\};A\cap B=\phi$  and $\forall x_1,y_1\in A, x_1\ne y_1; x_2,y_2\in B, x_2\ne y_2$  results  $\sqrt[3]{x_1+y_1}\notin\mathbb{Q},\sqrt[3]{x_2+y_2}\notin\mathbb{Q}$ .
WLOG, we can consider  $530\in A$ . Results  $199\in B, 801\in B$  (since  $\sqrt[3]{530+199}\in\mathbb{Q}$  and  $\sqrt[3]{530+801}\in\mathbb{Q})$ .
But in this case,  $\sqrt[3]{199+801}\in\mathbb{Q}$ , contradiction.

Hence, the requested partition is not possible.

stem_md: Let  $\{c_k\}_{k\geq1}$  be a sequence with  $0 \leq c_k \leq 1$ ,  $c_1 \neq 0$ ,  $\alpha > 1$ . Let  $C_n = c_1 + \cdots + c_n$ . Prove   $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty}\frac{C_1^{\alpha}+\cdots+C_n^{\alpha}}{\left(C_1+\cdots +C_n\right)^{\alpha}}=0 $$
solution_md:
Nice! The construction can actually be easily adapted to give arbitrary high values:
Choose any integer  $\alpha \ge 2$  (think of  $\alpha=2$  for the construction above) and a real number  $1 \le \beta <\alpha$  (think of  $\beta=\frac{3}{2}$ ).
Any integer can be written as  $n=c \cdot \alpha^k$  with  $1 \le c \le \alpha$ . Then define  $c_n=0$  for  $c \le \beta$  and  $c_n=1$  for  $c>\beta$ .
Then it's easy to check that  $C_{\alpha^n} \asymp \frac{\alpha-\beta}{\alpha+1} \cdot \alpha^n$  and
\[b_{k+1} \sim \frac{b_k}{\alpha^2}+\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha^2}+\frac{(\alpha-1)(\alpha-\beta)}{\alpha^2}\]
so that the limit of  $b_n$  will be  $\frac{\alpha-\beta+2}{2(\alpha+1)}$  and hence
\[\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{C_n}{M_n} \ge \frac{2(\alpha+1)}{\alpha-\beta+2}.\]
On choosing  $\beta=1$  we get the sequence  $C_n=n$  with  $L=2$ .
But for any  $\beta>1$ , the RHS will be larger than  $2$ .
In particular, choosing  $\beta$  very close to  $\alpha$ , we get an arbitrarily high value of the RHS.
(We could have just chosen  $\alpha$  large and  $\beta=\alpha-1$  from the beginning, but this would not have simplified the computations significantly.)**Edit** Needless to say: By comining these constructions for different  $\alpha \to \infty$ , we can easily construct a sequence where the limsup is in fact  $\infty$ .

By Stolz-Cesàro, it suffices to prove that
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{C_n^{\alpha}}{(C_1+\dots+C_n)^{\alpha}-(C_1+\dots+C_{n-1})^{\alpha}}=0.\]
By the mean value theorem, the denominator is  $\ge \alpha \cdot C_n \cdot (C_1+\dots+C_{n-1})^{\alpha-1}$  so it suffices to show that
\[\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{C_n^{\alpha-1}}{(C_1+\dots+C_{n-1})^{\alpha-1}} \to 0.\]
But since  $\alpha>1$ , this is equivalent to
\[\frac{C_n}{C_1+\dots+C_{n-1}} \to 0.\]
This is now easy to see directly, but for fun we can apply Stolz-Cesàro again to reduce the problem to showing that
\[\frac{C_n-C_{n-1}}{C_{n-1}} \to 0.\]
Or equivalently  $\frac{C_n}{C_{n-1}} \to 1$ .
So in fact this is all we need to know about our sequence (and of course this is obvious since  $C_i \to \infty$  and  $C_i \le C_{i+1}+1$ ).

In fact, it's not hard to show using the Stolz-Cèsaro argument that we have \[u(n) \sim \frac{L^{\alpha}}{1+(L-1)^{\alpha}} \cdot n^{1-\alpha}\] where \[L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_{n-1}},\] if that limit exists. In my opinion, the next question to think about would be whether we always have

As expected, the answer is <u>**no**</u>.
The following counterexample should work: Let  $c_1=c_4=1$ ,  $c_2=c_3=0$  and for  $n \geq 2$  define  $c_{2^n+k} = 0$  for  $1 \leq k \leq 2^{n-1}$ ,  $c_{2^n+k}=1$  for  $2^{n-1}+1 \leq k \leq 2^n$ . That is, starting at  $2^n+1$  we have a block of  $2^{n-1}$  zeroes, followed by  $2^{n-1}$     $1$ 's.
Then clearly  $C_{2^n}=2^{n-1}$  for  $n \geq 2$ . Let  $M_n := \frac{C_1+\cdots+C_n}{n}$  be the average of the first  $n$  values. Then  $M_4=\frac{5}{4}$  and for  $n \geq 2$  we have the recursion  $$ M_{2^{n+1}} = \frac{1}{2} M_{2^n}+\frac{1}{2^{n+1}}(2^n \cdot 2^{n-1}+(1+2+ \cdots +2^{n-1}))=\frac{1}{2}M_{2^n}+\frac{5}{8} 2^{n-1}+\frac{1}{8}. $$  If we denote  $b_n := \frac{M_{2^n}}{C_{2^n}}$ , we obtain the recursion  $b_{n+1}=\frac{1}{4} b_n+\frac{5}{16}+\frac{1}{2^{n+3}}$ .  From this it is not hard to see that  $\lim_{n \to \infty} b_n = \frac{5}{12}$  and thus  $\limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{C_n}{M_n} \geq \frac{12}{5}>2$ .
Now an interesting question would be to find a good upper bound for this limit, or show that it can be arbitrarily large.

More qualitatively speaking, this is what the constructions do:
You stay constant ( $c_i=0$ ) for quite some time, then go steeply up ( $c_i=1$ ) for a short time.
If you make the first segment sufficiently long compared to the second one (this corresponds to choosing  $\beta$  sufficiently large against  $\alpha$ ), you can make  $C_n$  (which will be the length of your steep part) decently large without changing  $M_n$  too much (since here the "weight" of the zero part will still be dominating).
Now, the construction with the intervals between consecutive powers of  $\alpha$  is just iterating this construction in intervals whose size grows sufficiently quickly to make you basically ignore the part from the previous intervals.

Well, the problem is not quite done. We only answered the question whether  $L$  (in a suitable sense) has to exist (it does not have to).
But this does not answer the question what happens with  $u(n)$  in these cases.
I did not do the computations, but somehow the  $u(n)$  has "another averaging out" compared to  $L$  so it might possibly still have a nice asymptotic behaviour in the examples constructed above.
(Btw, I just noticed that I somewhat mis-used the letter  $\alpha$ . Of course my use of  $\alpha$  in #17 is completely independent of the number  $\alpha$  in the original problem. Sorry for that.)

One natural point to start would be the following:
We have established that
\[\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_{n-1}}\]
does not have to be bounded as  $n \to \infty$ . How large can it be?
That is, how quickly can it grow? Well, clearly it is (asymptotically) less than  $n$  (and always at least  $1$ ).
Can it grow as quick as a power of  $n$ ? Or can we show that
\[\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_{n-1}} \le n^{\varepsilon}\]
as  $n \to \infty$ , for any given  $\varepsilon>0$ ? (Or, for starters, at least some  $\varepsilon<1$ ?)
Morally, the Stolz-Cèsaro argument should us then give something like  $u(n) \ll n^{1-\alpha+\varepsilon}$  although I didn't check it rigorously yet.

On another note, it might be interesting to consider the continuous analogue of the whole problem:
That is, for a nice monotonic positive function (say continuously differentiable) with  $f'(x) \le 1$  (Lipschitz with Lipschitz constant  $1$  should also be enough) study the behaviour of
\[u(T)=\frac{\int_0^T f(t)^{\alpha} dt}{\left(\int_0^T f(t) dt\right)^{\alpha}}.\]
The same arguments (with the discrete Stolz-Cesàro replaced by the continuous L'Hospital) should then give that always  $u(T) \to 0$  and that in fact  $u(T) \sim T^{1-\alpha}$  in certain well-behaved cases.
There should be no substantial difference between the continuous and the discrete version, but usually some technical difficulties (such as considering what the sequence is doing at certain "boundary indices") disappear in the continuous case which might make it easier to work in this setting.

I have now found a way to prove at least something in the direction suggested in #21.
For convenience, let us work with  $\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_n}$ , asymptotically this does not make a difference.
Recall that this is trivially bounded by  $1$  from below and (essentially) by  $n$  from above.
We are looking for a better upper bound.
Indeed, we clearly have  $\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_n} \le \frac{nC_n}{nC_1} \le \frac{C_n}{C_1}$  which is good if  $C_n$  is not too big.
On the other hand, if  $C_n$  is big we can exploit that  $C_{n-k} \ge C_n-k$ .
Applying this naively on the denominator, we would get an upper bound  $\frac{nC_n}{nC_n-\frac{n^2}{2}}$  which is only good if  $C_n$  is decently larger than  $\frac{n}{2}$ . But we can do much better by being slightly more clever:
Just forget the first  $n-k$  terms and estimate
\[C_1+\dots+C_n \ge C_{n-k+1}+C_{n-k+2}+\dots+C_n \ge kC_n-\frac{k^2}{2}.\]
Now the good thing is that we still have  $k$  at our disposal, so of course we just choose  $k$  to maximize the RHS which will happen at  $k\approx C_n$ . Then the bound is roughly  $\frac{C_n^2}{2}$  so that we get
\[\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_n} \le \frac{2n}{C_n}.\]
Combining the two bounds of  $\frac{2n}{C_n}$  and  $\frac{C_n}{C_1}$  we immediately get an upper bound of  $\sqrt{\frac{2n}{C_1}}$ .
So (up to constant factors) we can now bound the growth by  $\sqrt{n}$  (instead of the trivial  $n$ ).
Again, the question is: Can we do (much) better? I do not at all expect my argument to be optimal in this direction...

At a second thought, I think you can actually turn this argument into a construction:
You choose some rapidly growing sequence  $a_n$  being your "interval lengths".
Then you stay constant until  $a_n-\sqrt{a_n}$  and then go steeply up until  $a_n$ .
If you choose  $a_n$  sufficiently large against  $a_{n-1}$ , this will mean that  $C_{a_n} \sim \sqrt{a_n}$ .
On the other hand, the numbers  $C_i$  will be  $C_{a_{n-1}} \sim \sqrt{a_{n-1}}$  most of the time and only the steep part gives you another  $\frac{a_n}{2}$ . So the total sum will be approximately
\[a_n\sqrt{a_{n-1}}+\frac{a_n}{2},\]
leaving you with a quotient of
\[\frac{a_nC_{a_n}}{C_1+\dots+C_{a_n}} \approx \frac{a_n\sqrt{a_n}}{a_n\sqrt{a_{n-1}}+\frac{a_n}{2}} \approx \frac{\sqrt{a_n}}{\sqrt{a_{n-1}}}.\]
Again, if we choose  $a_n$  sufficiently large against  $a_{n-1}$ , this will mean that  $\frac{nC_n}{C_1+\dots+C_n}$  can come essentially as close to  $\sqrt{n}$  as we like.

Now the next logical step would be to compute the original sequence  $u(n)$  in this example or at least try to heuristically see whether something interesting happens here.

If I did not mess up the computation, in my example we should have
\[u(a_n) \sim \frac{1}{(\alpha+1)a_{n-1}^{\frac{\alpha}{2}}}\cdot a_n^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2}}.\]
So again, thinking of  $a_{n-1}$  as being arbitrarily small against  $a_n$ ,  $u(n)$  will come to  $n^{\frac{1-\alpha}{2}}$  infinitely often as close as we like.
And so indeed, this seems to be our first example of a sequence where we do not have  $u_n \ll n^{1-\alpha}$ .

If you change  $x^\alpha$  on  $\phi(x)$  a convex function non-negative on [0;+oo[
does this give a more general result ?

If you change $x^\alpha$ on $\phi(x)$ a convex function non-negative on [0;+oo[ does this give a more general result ?
Well, I think it will be hard to get a result for general $\phi$ . For instance, $\phi(x)=x$ is convex, but then $u(n)=1$ for all $n$ . Of course, as soon as you assume some nice conditions on $\phi$ , you will be able to show that $u(n) \to 0$ . But I think it will be very hard to extract asymptotic information on $u(n)$ in general, given how hard it already is for $x^{\alpha}$ (general convex functions can be much more nasty). On the other hand, of course a similar analysis should work for many concrete functions such as $x^{\alpha}\log(1+x)$ .

stem_md: Let  $f$  be a continuously differentiable function on  $[0, 1]$  and  $m \in \mathbb{N}$ . Let  $A = f(1)$  and let  $B=\int \limits_{0}^1 x^{-\frac{1}{m}}f(x)dx$ . Calculate   $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty} n\left(\int \limits_{0}^1 f(x)dx-\sum \limits_{k=1}^n \left(\frac{k^m}{n^m}-\frac{(k-1)^m}{n^m}\right)f\left(\frac{(k-1)^m}{n^m}\right)\right) $$  in terms of  $A$  and  $B$ .
solution_md:
In the case of  $m=1$ , we have  $\frac{f(1)-f(0)}{2}$ .

Let  $g(x)=mx^{m-1}f(x^m)$  ( $m\geq2, m\in\mathbb{N}$ ).
Now we have $\frac{g(1)-g(0)}{2}=\frac{mf(1)}{2}=\frac{m}{2}A, \int_{0}^{1}g(x)\,dx=\int_{0}^{1}f(x)\,dx$ .
And using the substitution  $x^{\frac{1}{m}}\rightarrow x$ , we have $B=m\int_{0}^{1}x^{m-2}f(x^m)\,dx$ .

By the binomial theorem, we can denote $k^m-(k-1)^m={}_{m} C_{1}(k-1)^{m-1}+ {}_{m} C_{2}(k-1)^{m-2}+\cdots+1$ .

Therefore, by the taylor theorem, $\lim_{n\to\infty}n\left(\int_{0}^{1}g(x)\,dx-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}g\left(\frac{k-1}{n}\right)-\frac{{}_{m} C_{2}}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n}\left(\frac{k-1}{n}\right)^{m-2}f\left(\left(\frac{k-1}{n}\right)^{m}\right)\right)$  $=\frac{g(1)-g(0)}{2}-{}_{m} C_{2}\int_{0}^{1}x^{m-2}f(x^m)\,dx=\frac{m}{2}A-\frac{m-1}{2}B.$

stem_md: If  $b$ ,  $c$  are the legs, and  $a$  is the hypotenuse of a right triangle, prove that  $$ \left(a+b+c\right)\left(\frac{1}{a}+\frac{1}{b}+\frac{1}{c}\right)\geq 5+3\sqrt{2} $$
solution_md:
The following general statement is true:
**In any triangle $ABC$ satisfying $\max\{A, B, C\}\ge \phi\ge 90^{\circ}$ the following inequality holds: $$ \boxed{\left(a + b + c \right)\left(\frac 1a + \frac 1b + \frac 1c\right) \ge 5 + \frac {3 - 2\cos \phi}{\sin\frac \phi 2}}\, . $$**
**Proof.** Assume without loss of generality that $a\ge b\ge c.$ Then it's easy to prove that the function $f:\left[\sqrt{bc}, \infty\right)\to\mathbb{R}$ given by $$ f(a) = (a + b + c)\left(\frac 1a + \frac 1b + \frac 1c\right) $$ is increasing. Indeed, $f^{\prime}(a)\ge 0$ reduces to $a^2\ge bc,$ which is clearly true. By the law of cosines we have that $a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos A,$ which together with the fact that $A\ge \phi\ge 90^{\circ}$ allows us to write the following inequality: $$ a^2 \ge b^2 + c^2 -2bc\cos\phi. $$ In other words, $a\ge \sqrt{b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos\phi}$ and since $f$ is an increasing function we immediately get that: $$ f(a)\ge f\left(\sqrt{b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos\phi}\right). $$ Therefore, it is enough to prove that the following inequality holds: $$ f\left(\sqrt{b^2 + c^2 - 2bc\cos\phi}\right) \ge 5 + \frac {3 - 2\cos \phi}{\sin\frac \phi 2}. $$ For simplicity, consider $x\ge 1$ such that $b = x\cdot c$ and let $k = \cos\phi.$ This means that the conclusion reduces to proving that: $$ \begin{array}{c}\displaystyle \left(\sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx} + x +1\right)\left(\frac 1{\sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx}} + \frac 1x + 1\right)\ge 5 + \frac {3 - 2k}{\sqrt{\frac {1 - k}2}}.\end{array} $$ Expanding the left-hand side of the previous inequality and grouping conveniently yields: $$ \begin{array}{c}\displaystyle \frac {x + 1}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx}} + \left(\frac 1x + 1\right)\sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx} + \left(x + \frac 1x\right) + 3\ge 5 + \frac {3 - 2k}{\sqrt{\frac {1 - k}2}}.\end{array} $$ But $x + \frac 1x\ge 2$ for all positive real numbers $x,$ so it suffices to show that: $$ \begin{array}{c} \displaystyle \frac {x + 1}{\sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx}} + \left(\frac 1x + 1\right) \sqrt{x^2 + 1 - 2kx} \ge \frac {3 - 2k}{\sqrt{\frac {1 - k}2}} \end{array}. $$ From here it's just a matter of squaring both sides of this inequality and performing some tedious computations, the last step of which being: $$ \begin{array}{c} \displaystyle (x - 1)^2\cdot \frac {E(x, k)}{x^2 \Big(x^2 + 1 - 2kx\Big) \Big(1 - k\Big)} \ge 0\end{array}, $$ where $$ \begin{array}{c} E(x, k) = \Big(1 - k\Big) \Big(x^4 + 1\Big) + \Big(6 - 10 k + 4 k^2\Big) \Big(x^3 + x\Big) + \Big(1 - 15 k + 16 k^2 - 4 k^3\Big) x^2 \end{array}. $$ All terms are clearly nonnegative as $k \le 0$ and this completes the proof.

stem_md: If  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c > 0$ , prove that  $$ \frac{a}{b+c}+\frac{b}{c+a}+\frac{c}{a+b}\geq \frac{a+b}{a+b+2c}+\frac{b+c}{2a+b+c}+\frac{c+a}{a+2b+c} $$
solution_md:
Let  $f(x)=\frac x{1-x}-\frac{1-x}{1+x}=\frac{3x-1}{1-x^2}$ . Replace  $(a,b,c)$  by  $\left(\frac a{a+b+c},\frac b{a+b+c},\frac c{a+b+c}\right)$ , then it suffices to show that inequality for  $a+b+c=1$ .
That is:  $$ \sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac a{1-a}\ge\sum_{\text{cyc}}\frac{1-a}{1+a} $$  or  $$ f(a)+f(b)+f(c)\ge0. $$  Using the tangent-line trick, we have the inequality:  $$ f(x)\ge\frac{27x-9}8\Leftrightarrow(3x-1)^2(3x+1)\ge0, $$  true for  $x>0$ . By this:  $$ f(a)+f(b)+f(c)\ge\frac{27a-9}8+\frac{27b-9}8+\frac{27c-9}8=0, $$  and we're done.

stem_md: Find all continuous functions  $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  such that  $$ f(-x)+\int \limits_0^xtf(x-t)dt=x,\ \forall\ x\in \mathbb{R} $$
solution_md:
The equation has the unique solution  $f(x)=-\sinh x.$  First, since   $$ f(-x)=x-\int_0^xtf(x-t) \ dt \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (1) $$  and  $f$  is continuous,  $f$  is differentiable. Now changing  $t$  to  $x-t$  in the integral on the RHS of  $(1)$  gives  $$ f(-x)=x-\int_0^x(x-t)f(t) \ dt=x-x\int_0^xf(t)+\int_0^xtf(t) \ dt $$  and thus differentiating gives  $$ -f'(-x)=1-\int_0^xf(t) \ dt. \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (2) $$  So, again since  $f$  is continuous,  $\int_0^xf(t) \ dt$  is differentiable and hence, by  $(2),$   $f'$  is differentiable too and  $$ f''(-x)=-f(x). \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (3) $$  Differentiating  $(3)$  twice gives   $$ f^{(4)}(-x)=-f''(x). \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (4) $$   
Now in  $(4)$  change  $x$  to  $-x$  and then use  $(3)$  to get  $f^{(4)}(x)=f(x),$  which is a linear differential equation with the general solution   $$ f(x)=c_1e^x+c_2e^{-x}+c_3\cos x + c_4\sin x. \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (5) $$  It follows from  $(3),(5)$  that  $c_1=-c_2, \ c_4=0$  and then, since  $f(0)=0,$  by  $(1),$  we get  $c_3=0.$  Also, since  $f'(0)=-1,$  by  $(2),$  we must have  $c_1=-\frac{1}{2}$  and thus  $f(x)=-\frac{1}{2}(e^x-e^{-x})=-\sinh x.$  Finally, see that  $f(x)=-\sinh x$  satisfies  $(1).$

[*] Prove that   $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty} \left(n+\frac{1}{4}-\zeta(3)-\zeta(5)-\cdots -\zeta(2n+1)\right)=0 $$  [*] Calculate   $$ \sum \limits_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(n+\frac{1}{4}-\zeta(3)-\zeta(5)-\cdots -\zeta(2n+1)\right) $$  [/list]
solution_md:
[list=1] [*] Prove that $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty} \left(n+\frac{1}{4}-\zeta(3)-\zeta(5)-\cdots -\zeta(2n+1)\right)=0 $$ [*] Calculate $$ \sum \limits_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(n+\frac{1}{4}-\zeta(3)-\zeta(5)-\cdots -\zeta(2n+1)\right) $$ [/list]
For 1. we have $\sum _{k=2}^{\infty } (\zeta (k)-1)=\sum _{k=2}^{\infty } \sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^k}=\sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \sum _{k=2}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^k}=\sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n (n-1)}=1$ and $\sum _{k=1}^{\infty } (\zeta (2 k)-1)=\sum _{k=1}^{\infty } \sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^{2 k}}=\sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \sum _{k=1}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^{2 k}}=\sum _{n=2}^{\infty } \frac{1}{n^2-1}=\frac{3}{4}$ Substracting we have $\sum _{k=1}^{\infty } (\zeta (2 k+1)-1) = \frac{1}{4}$ which is the first limit.

stem_md:
Let  $u$ ,  $v$ ,  $w$  complex numbers such that:  $u + v + w = 1$ ,  $u^2 + v^2 + w^2 = 3$ ,  $uvw = 1$ . Prove that
[list=1]
[*]  $u$ ,  $v$ ,  $w$  are distinct numbers two by two
[*] If  $S(k)= u^k + v^k + w^k$ , then  $S(k)$  is an odd natural number
[*] The expression  $$ \frac{u^{2n+1} - v^{2n+1}}{u-v}+\frac{v^{2n+1}-w^{2n+1}}{v-w}+\frac{w^{2n+1}-u^{2n+1}}{w-u} $$  is an integer number.
[/list]
solution_md:
$\textbf{u,v,w are pairwise distinct}$ .
Assume  $u=v$ . $u+v+w=1\Longrightarrow w=1-2u$ . $u^2+v^2+w^2=3\Longrightarrow w^2=3-2u^2$ .
Results: $(1-2u)^2=3-2u^2\Longrightarrow 6u^2-4u-2=0\Longrightarrow u\in\left\{1,-\dfrac{1}{3}\right\}$ .
For  $u=1$  results  $w=-1$ , but  $uvw=u^2w=-1\ne1$ .
For  $u=-\dfrac{1}{3}$  results  $w=\dfrac{5}{3}$ , but  $uvw=\dfrac{5}{27}\ne 1$ .
Hence the assumption is false.
Results:  $u,v,w$  are pairwise distinct. $\textbf{S(k)}\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $\textbf{S(k) is an odd number}, \forall k\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$ . $u+v+w=1$ ; $uv+uw+vw=\dfrac{(u+v+w)^2-(u^2+v^2+w^2)}{2}=-1$ ; $uvw=1$ .
Results applying the Vieta's relations: $u,v,w$  are the solutions of the equation $x^3-x^2-x-1=0$ . $u^3-u^2-u-1=0\Longrightarrow u^3=u^2+u+1\Longrightarrow u^{k+1}=u^{k}+u^{k-1}+u^{k-2}, \forall k\in\mathbb{N},n\ge2$ .
Similarly,  $v^{k+1}=v^{k}+v^{k-1}+v^{k-2}, w^{k+1}=w^{k}+w^{k-1}+w^{k-2}$ .
Results:  $S(k+1)=S(k)+S(k-1)+S(k-2)$ .
By induction,  $S(k)\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $S(k)$  is an odd number.
Step 1: for  $k\in\{0,1,2\}$ : $S(0)=3$ ; $S(1)=1;S(2)=3$ .
Step 2: for  $k\ge 2$ :
Assume  $S(k-2),S(k-1),S(k)\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $S(k-2),S(k-1),S(k)$  are odd numbers.
Results:  $S(k+1)=S(k)+S(k-1)+S(k-2)\in\mathbb{N}$  and  $S(k+1)$  is an odd number. $\textbf{E(n)}=u^nv^n+u^nw^n+v^nw^n\in\mathbb{Z},\;\forall n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}$  and  $E(n)$  is an odd number.
Proof by induction.
Step 1: for  $n\in\{0,1,2\}$ : $E(0)=3\in\mathbb{Z}$ ; $E(1)=-1\in\mathbb{Z}$ ; $E(2)=[E(1)]^2-2uvw\cdot (u+v+w)=-1\in\mathbb{Z}$ .
Step 2: for  $n\ge2$ :
Assume  $E(n),E(n-1),E(n-2)\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $E(n),E(n-1),E(n-2)$  are odd numbers. $E(n+1)=(uv+uw+vw)E(n)-(u^{n+1}v^nw+u^nv^{n+1}w+u^{n+1}w^nv+u^nw^{n+1}v+v^{n+1}w^nu+v^nw^{n+1}u)=$  $=-E(n)-uvw[u^{n-1}v^{n-1}(u+v)+u^{n-1}w^{n-1}(u+w)+v^{n-1}w^{n-1}(v+w)]=$  $=-E(n)-[u^{n-1}v^{n-1}(1-w)+u^{n-1}w^{n-1}(1-v)+v^{n-1}w^{n-1}(1-u)]=$  $=-E(n)-E(n-1)+uvw\cdot E(n-2)=-E(n)-E(n-1)+E(n-2)\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $E(n+1)$  is an odd number. $\textbf{S(k)}\in\mathbb{Z}$  and  $\textbf{S(k) is an odd number}, \forall k\in\mathbb{Z}$ .
The property is true for  $k\in\mathbb{N}$ .
For  $k=0: S(0)=3$ ;
For  $k=-n,\;n\in\mathbb{N}$ : $S(-n)=\dfrac{1}{u^n}+\dfrac{1}{v^n}+\dfrac{1}{w^n}=\dfrac{u^nv^n+u^nw^n+v^nw^n}{(uvw)^n}=E(n)$ . $\textbf{F(n)}\in\mathbb{Z}$ , where $F(n)=\dfrac{u^{2n+1} - v^{2n+1}}{u-v}+\dfrac{v^{2n+1}-w^{2n+1}}{v-w}+\dfrac{w^{2n+1}-u^{2n+1}}{w-u}$  $\dfrac{u^{2n+1} - v^{2n+1}}{u-v}=u^{2n}+u^{2n-1}v+u^{2n-2}v^2+\dots+u^2v^{2n-2}+uv^{2n-1}+v^{2n}$  and the similar relations.
Results: $F(n)=2(u^{2n}+v^{2n}+w^{2n})+(u^nv^n+u^nw^n+v^nw^n)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(u^{2n-k}v^k+u^kv^{2n-k}+u^{2n-k}w^k+u^kw^{2n-k}+v^{2n-k}w^k+v^kw^{2n-k})=$  $=2S(2n)+E(n)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}[u^kv^k(u^{2n-2k}+v^{2n-2k})+u^kw^k(u^{2n-2k}+w^{2n-2k})+v^kw^k(v^{2n-2k}+w^{2n-2k})]=$  $=2S(2n)+E(n)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}[u^kv^k(S(2n-2k)-w^{2n-2k})+u^kw^k(S(2n-2k)-v^{2n-2k})+v^kw^k(S(2n-2k)-u^{2n-2k})]=$  $=2S(2n)+E(n)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S(2n-2k)E(k)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(uvw)^k(w^{2n-3k}+v^{2n-3k}+u^{2n-3k})=$  $=2S(2n)+E(n)+\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S(2n-2k)E(k)-\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}S(2n-3k)\in\mathbb{Z}$ .

stem_md: Let  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  be the sides of an acute triangle  $\triangle ABC$  , then for any  $x, y, z \geq 0$ , such that  $xy+yz+zx=1$  holds inequality:  $$ a^2x + b^2y + c^2z \geq 4F $$   where  $F$  is the area of the triangle  $\triangle ABC$
solution_md:
The inequality holds for any triangle, not necessarily acute.

Consider the triangle  $ABC$  with  $a=BC,b=AC,c=AB$ .
Using the sine theorem, results: $F=\dfrac{bc\sin A}{2}=\dfrac{a^2}{2}\cdot\dfrac{b}{a}\cdot\dfrac{c}{a}\cdot\sin A=$  $=\dfrac{a^2}{2}\cdot\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A}\cdot\dfrac{\sin C}{\sin A}\cdot\sin A=\dfrac{a^2\sin B\cdot\sin C}{2\sin A}\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow a^2=2F\cdot\dfrac{\sin A}{\sin B\cdot\sin C}$ .
Similarly,  $b^2=2F\cdot\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A\cdot\sin C},c^2=2F\cdot\dfrac{\sin C}{\sin A\cdot\sin B}$ .

The inequality becomes: $a^2x+b^2y+c^2z\ge 4F\Longleftrightarrow 2F\cdot\left(\dfrac{x\sin A}{\sin B\cdot\sin C}+\dfrac{y\sin B}{\sin A\cdot\sin C}+\dfrac{z\sin C}{\sin A\cdot\sin B}\right)\ge 4F\Longleftrightarrow$  $\Longleftrightarrow x\sin^2 A+y\sin^2 B+z\sin^2 C\ge 2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C\quad(1)$ .
Denote  $E=x\sin^2 A+y\sin^2 B+z\sin^2 C$ .

Consider  $A,B,C,z$  fixed. $\textbf{Case 1: }z=0$ .
Results:  $xy=1\Longrightarrow x>0,y=\dfrac{1}{x}$ .
Using AM-GM: $E=x\sin^2A+\dfrac{\sin^2B}{x}\ge2\sin A\cdot\sin B\ge2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C$ .
The equality holds for: $\sin C=1\Longrightarrow C=90^\circ$  and $x\sin^2A=\dfrac{\sin^2B}{x}\Longrightarrow x=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A}=\dfrac{\cos A}{\sin A}=\cot A$ . $\textbf{Case 2: }z>0$ .
We determine the values of  $x,y$  which minimize the expression $xy+xz+yz=1\Longrightarrow x=\dfrac{1-yz}{y+z}$ .
The expression  $E$  becomes: $E(y)=\dfrac{1-yz}{y+z}\sin^2A+y\sin^2B+z\sin^2C$ .
The derivative of  $E(y)$  is $E'(y)=\dfrac{(y+z)^2\sin^2B-(z^2+1)\sin^2A}{(y+z)^2}$ . $E'(y)=0$  has the solutions  $y_1=-\dfrac{\sin A}{\sin B}\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}-z<0; y_2=\dfrac{\sin A}{\sin B}\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}-z>y_1$ . $0\le yz\le 1\Longrightarrow 0\le y\le \dfrac{1}{z}$ .
Results: 
a) if  $y_2\le0$ , the minimum of the expression  $E(y)$  occurs for  $y=0$ ;
b) if  $0<y_2\le\dfrac{1}{z}$ , the minimum of the expression  $E(y)$  occurs for  $y=y_2$ ;
c) if  $y_2\ge \dfrac{1}{z}$ ,the minimum of the expression  $E(y)$  occurs for  $y=\dfrac{1}{z}$ . $\textbf{Case 2.1: }y_2\le0$ .
For  $y=0$  results  $x=\dfrac{1}{z}$ . $\min{E(y)}=E(0)=\dfrac{\sin^2A}{z}+z\sin^2C\ge 2\sin A\cdot\sin C\ge 2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C$ , hence the inequality  $(1)$  is true.
The equality holds for: $\sin B=1\Longrightarrow B=90^\circ$  and $z\sin^2C=\dfrac{\sin^2A}{z}\Longrightarrow z=\dfrac{\sin A}{\sin C}=\dfrac{\cos C}{\sin C}=\cot C$ . $\textbf{Case 2.2: }0<y_2<\dfrac{1}{z}$ . $\min{E(y)}=E(y_2)$ .
The corresponding  $x$  is  $x_2=\dfrac{1-y_2z}{y_2+z}=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A}\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}-z$ . $ E(y_2)\ge2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C\Longleftrightarrow$  $\Longleftrightarrow 2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}\ge z(\sin^2A+\sin^2B-\sin^2C)+2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C\quad(2)$ .
Using  $\sin^2A=\dfrac{1-\cos2A}{2}$  and the similar relations and  $\cos{(A+B)}=-\cos C$  results: $\sin^2A+\sin^2B-\sin^2C=2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\cos C$ .
The inequality  $(2)$  becomes: $2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}\ge 2z\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\cos C+2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C\Longleftrightarrow$  $\Longleftrightarrow \sqrt{z^2+1}\ge z\cos C+\sin C\Longleftrightarrow$  $\Longleftrightarrow z^2+1\ge z^2\cos^2C+2z\sin C\cdot\cos C+\sin^2C\Longleftrightarrow$  $\Longleftrightarrow (z\sin C-\cos C)^2\ge0$ , true.
The equality holds for: $z\sin C-\cos C=0\Longrightarrow z=\cot C$ ; $x=x_2=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A}\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}-z=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin A}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sin C}-\dfrac{\cos C}{\sin C}=$  $=\dfrac{\sin(A+C)-\sin A\cdot\cos C}{\sin A\cdot\sin C}=\cot A$ ; $y=y_2=\dfrac{\sin A}{\sin B}\cdot\sqrt{z^2+1}-z=\cot B$ . $\textbf{Case 2.3: }y_2\ge\dfrac{1}{z}$ .
For  $y=\dfrac{1}{z}$  results  $x=0$ . $\min{E(y)}=E\left(\dfrac{1}{z}\right)=\dfrac{\sin^2B}{z}+z\sin^2C\ge2\sin B\cdot\sin C\ge2\sin A\cdot\sin B\cdot\sin C$ .
The equality holds for: $\sin A=1\Longleftrightarrow A=90^\circ$  and $z\sin^2C=\dfrac{\sin^2B}{z}\Longrightarrow z=\dfrac{\sin B}{\sin C}=\dfrac{\cos C}{\sin C}=\cot C$ .  $\textbf{Final conclusion:}$ If  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c$  are the sides of a triangle  $\triangle ABC$  , then for any  $x, y, z \geq 0$ , such that  $xy+yz+zx=1$  holds the inequality:  $$ a^2x + b^2y + c^2z \geq 4F $$  where  $F$  is the area of the triangle  $\triangle ABC$ .
The equality occurs for the cumulative conditions: $\begin{cases}\max\{A,B,C\}\le90^\circ ;(x,y,z)=(\cot A,\cot B,\cot C).\end{cases}$

stem_md: For  $p$ ,  $q$ ,  $l$  strictly positive real numbers, consider the following problem: for  $y \geq 0$  fixed, determine the values  $x \geq 0$  such that  $x^p - lx^q \leq y$ . Denote by  $S(y)$  the set of solutions of this problem. Prove that if one has  $p < q$ ,  $\epsilon \in (0, l^\frac{1}{p-q})$ ,  $0 \leq x \leq \epsilon$  and  $x \in S(y)$ , then   $$ x\leq ky^{\delta},\ \text{where}\ k=\epsilon\left(\epsilon^p-l\epsilon^q\right)^{-\frac{1}{p}}\ \text{and}\ \delta=\frac{1}{p} $$

stem_md: Consider the sequence of polynomials  $P_0(x) = 2$ ,  $P_1(x) = x$  and  $P_n(x) = xP_{n-1}(x) - P_{n-2}(x)$  for  $n \geq 2$ . Let  $x_n$  be the greatest zero of  $P_n$  in the the interval  $|x| \leq 2$ . Show that   $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty}n^2\left(4-2\pi +n^2\int \limits_{x_n}^2P_n(x)dx\right)=2\pi - 4-\frac{\pi^3}{12} $$
solution_md: Let  $\{T_n(x)\}$  be the sequence of [Chebyshev polynomials ](https://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Chebyshev_polynomials) of the first kind. See that  $P_n(x)$  and  $2T_n(x/2)$  satisfy the same recurrence relation with the same initial conditions. Thus  $P_n(x)=2T_n(x/2)$  and so, for  $x \in [-2,2],$  if we put  $x=2\cos \theta,$  then we get   $$ P_n(x)=2T_n(x/2)=2T_n(\cos \theta)=2\cos(n\theta). $$  It's now clear that  $x_n=2\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2n}\right)$  and hence for  $n \ge 2$  we have  $$ \int_{x_n}^2P_n(x) \ dx=4\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2n}}\sin \theta \cos(n\theta) \ d\theta=\frac{4(n\sin(\frac{\pi}{2n})-1)}{n^2-1}. $$  The rest of the solution is straightforward.

\begin{align*}

stem_md: Let  $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  a periodic and continue function with period  $T$  and  $F : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$  antiderivative of  $f$ . Then   $$ \int \limits_0^T \left[F(nx)-F(x)-f(x)\frac{(n-1)T}{2}\right]dx=0 $$
solution_md: I guess  $n$  is supposed to be a positive integer. So  $F(x)=\int_0^xf(t) \ dt$  and hence  $$ \int_0^T(F(nx)-F(x)) \ dx=\int_0^T\left(\int_0^{nx}f(t) \ dt-\int_0^xf(t) \ dt\right)dx=\int_0^T\int_x^{nx}f(t) \ dt \ dx $$    $$ =\int_0^T \int_{\frac{t}{n}}^tf(t) \ dx \ dt + \int_T^{nT}\int_{\frac{t}{n}}^T f(t) \ dx \ dt=\int_0^T\left(1-\frac{1}{n}\right)tf(t) \ dt + \int_T^{nT}\left(T-\frac{t}{n}\right)f(t) \ dt $$    $$ =\int_0^T tf(t) \ dt-\frac{1}{n}\int_0^{nT}tf(t) \ dt + T \int_T^{nT}f(t) \ dt. \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (1) $$  Now   $$ \int_T^{nT}f(t) \ dt = \sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\int_{kT}^{(k+1)T}f(t) \ dt=\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}\int_0^T f(t) \ dt = (n-1)\int_0^T f(t) \ dt \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (2) $$  and   $$ \int_0^{nT}tf(t) \ dt = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\int_{kT}^{(k+1)T}tf(t) \ dt=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\int_0^T(kT+t)f(t) \ dt=\frac{n(n-1)}{2}T\int_0^Tf(t) \ dt+n \int_0^T tf(t) \ dt. \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (3) $$  Put  $(2),(3)$  in  $(1)$  to get the result.

stem_md: Compute   $$ \lim \limits_{n \to \infty}\frac{1}{n}\sum \limits_{k=1}^n\frac{\sqrt[n+k+1]{n+1}-\sqrt[n+k]{n}}{\sqrt[n+k]{n+1}-\sqrt[n+k]{n}} $$
solution_md:
Let's denote  $a_n=\frac{\sqrt[n+k+1]{n+1}-\sqrt[n+k]{n}}{\sqrt[n+k]{n+1}-\sqrt[n+k]{n}}$ After straightforward manipulations we get  $$ a_n=\frac{e^{-\frac{\ln n}{(n+k)(n+k+1)}}e^{\frac{\ln(1+\frac1n)}{n+k+1}}-1}{e^{\frac{\ln(1+\frac1n)}{n+k}}-1}=\frac{\bigg(\Big(1-\frac{\ln n}{(n+k)(n+k+1)}+O(\frac{\ln^2n}{n^4})\Big)\Big(1+\frac1{n(n+k+1)}+O(\frac1{n^3})\Big)-1\bigg)}{1+\frac1{n(n+k)}+O(\frac1{n^3})-1} $$    $$ =1-\frac{n\ln n}{n+k}+O\left(\frac{\ln n}n\right) $$  Therefore,  $$ S_n=\sum_{k=1}^na_n=n\,-\,n\ln n\ln 2\,+\,O(\ln n),\,\,\text{and}\,\, \frac{S_n}{n}=1\,-\,\ln 2\ln n\,+\,O\left(\frac{\ln n}n\right)\,\to -\infty\,\,\text{at}\,\,n\to\infty $$  The numeric evaluation confirms the result.
Maybe we intended to consider the limit  $\frac{S_n}{n\ln n}$  instead? In that case we get a finite number:  $\,-\,\ln 2$ .

stem_md: In the  $[ABCD]$  tetrahedron having all the faces acute angled triangles, is denoted by  $r_X$ ,  $R_X$  the radius lengths of the circle inscribed and circumscribed respectively on the face opposite to the  $X \in \{A,B,C,D\}$  peak, and with  $R$  the length of the radius of the sphere circumscribed to the tetrahedron. Show that inequality occurs  $$ 8R^2 \geq (r_A + R_A)^2 + (r_B + R_B)^2 + (r_C + R_C)^2 + (r_D + R_D)^2 $$
solution_md: By   $$ \left(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB}+\overrightarrow{OC}+\overrightarrow{OD}\right)^2\geq0 $$  we get  $\sum{AB}^2\leq16R^2.$ By Walker's inequality we get  $$ 4\left(r_X+R_X\right)^2\leq a_X^2+b_X^2+c_X^2. $$  See also [url]https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6t243f6h2399104_inequality_in_tetrahedron

stem_md: In the any  $[ABCD]$  tetrahedron we denote with  $\alpha$ ,  $\beta$ ,  $\gamma$  the measures, in radians, of the angles of the three pairs of opposite edges and with  $r$ ,  $R$  the lengths of the rays of the sphere inscribed and respectively circumscribed the tetrahedron. Demonstrate  inequality  $$ \left(\frac{3r}{R}\right)^3\leq \sin \frac{\alpha +\beta +\gamma}{3} $$  (A refinement of inequality  $R \geq 3r$ ).
solution_md:
Let  $V=[ABCD]$  and  $BC=a, CA=b, AB=c, DA=d, DB=e, DC=f$ . We'll use the inequality  $$ V\ge 8\sqrt{3}r^3 $$  which can be found for example in the book "Recent Advances in Geometric Inequalities" by D.S. Mitrinovic, J.E. Pecaric and V. Volenec (XVIII.2.40). Also we'll use the inequality  $$ 16R^2\ge a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2+f^2 $$  which follows from the formula  $LHS-RHS=g^2$  where  $g$  is the distance between the circumcenter and the centroid of  $ABCD$ .
By these inequalities we get  $$ \left(\frac{3r}{R}\right)^3\le \frac{72\sqrt3 V}{\sqrt{(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2+f^2)^3}}.\quad\quad (1) $$  On the other hand, using Jensen's inequality we get  $$ \sin \frac{\alpha +\beta +\gamma}{3}\ge \frac{\sin{\alpha}+\sin\beta+\sin\gamma}{3}=\frac{2V}{adh_a}+\frac{2V}{beh_b}+\frac{2V}{cfh_c}
\ge \frac{4V}{(a^2+d^2)m_a}+\frac{4V}{(b^2+e^2)m_b}+\frac{4V}{(c^2+f^2)m_c}= $$    $$ = \frac{8V}{(a^2+d^2)\sqrt{-a^2+b^2+c^2-d^2+e^2+f^2}}+\frac{8V}{(b^2+e^2)\sqrt{a^2-b^2+c^2+d^2-e^2+f^2}}+\frac{8V}{(c^2+f^2)\sqrt{a^2+b^2-c^2+d^2+e^2-f^2}}\quad (2) $$  where  $h_a, h_b, h_c$  are the distances between the pairs of edges  $BC$  and  $AD$ ,  $CA$  and  $BD$ ,  $AB$  and  $CD$  respectively,  $m_a, m_b, m_c$  are the lengths of the segments joining the midpoints of the same pairs of edges respectively and we also used the formulas for  $m_a$  and for  $V$  in terms of  $h_a$  (we assumed that  $\alpha$  is the angle between  $BC$  and  $DA$  etc.).
Now by  $(1)$  and  $(2)$  it suffices to prove that  $$ \frac{9\sqrt3}{\sqrt{(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2+e^2+f^2)^3}}\le \sum_{(a, d)\to (b, e)\to (c, f)}\frac{1}{(a^2+d^2)\sqrt{-a^2+b^2+c^2-d^2+e^2+f^2}}. $$  Denote  $A=\sqrt{-a^2+b^2+c^2-d^2+e^2+f^2}$  and so on. Then we need to show that  $$ \frac{9\sqrt3}{\sqrt{(A^2+B^2+C^2)^3}}\le \frac{2}{A(B^2+C^2)}+\frac{2}{B(C^2+A^2)}+\frac{2}{C(A^2+B^2)}. $$  Note that  $F(A, B, C)\ge F\left(A, \sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}\right)$  where  $$ F(A, B, C):=\frac{2}{A(B^2+C^2)}+\frac{2}{B(C^2+A^2)}+\frac{2}{C(A^2+B^2)}-\frac{9\sqrt3}{\sqrt{(A^2+B^2+C^2)^3}}. $$  Indeed,  $$ F(A, B, C)\ge F\left(A, \sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}, \sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}\right)\iff $$    $$ \frac{1}{B(C^2+A^2)}+\frac{1}{C(A^2+B^2)}\ge \frac{2}{\sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}\left(A^2+\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}\right)}\iff $$    $$ \frac{(A^2+BC)(B+C)}{BC(A^2+B^2)(A^2+C^2)}\ge \frac{2}{\sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}\left(A^2+\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}\right)}\iff $$    $$ A^4\left((B+C)\sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}-2BC\right)+A^2\left(\frac{(B+C)^3}{2}\sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}-2BC(B^2+C^2)\right)+\left(BC(B+C)\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}\sqrt{\frac{B^2+C^2}{2}}-2B^3C^3\right)\ge 0 $$  which is true because the expressions in the brackets are nonnegative.
Thus it suffices to prove that  $F(A, 1, 1)\ge 0$  which is equivalent to  $$ \sqrt{(A^2+2)^3}\cdot \frac{A^2+4A+1}{A(A^2+1)}\ge 9\sqrt3\iff $$    $$ (A^6+6A^4+12A^2+8)(A^4+16A^2+1+8A^3+8A+2A^2)\ge 243(A^6+2A^4+A^2)\iff $$    $$ A^{10}+8A^9+24A^8+56A^7-122A^6+144A^5-256A^4+160A^3+156A^2+64A+8\ge 0\iff $$    $$ (A-1)^2(A^8+10A^7+43A^6+132A^5+99A^4+210A^3+65A^2+80A+8)\ge 0 $$  which is clearly true. Hence the inequality  $F(A, B, C)\ge 0$  is established and the desired inequality follows.

stem_md: If  $a$ ,  $b$ ,  $c \geq 1$ ;  $y \geq x \geq 1$ ;  $p$ ,  $q$ ,  $r > 0$  then  $$ \left(\frac{1+y\left(a^pb^qc^r\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q+r}}}{1+x\left(a^pb^qc^r\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q+r}}}\right)^{\frac{p+q+r}{\left(a^pb^qc^r\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q+r}}}}\left(\frac{1+xa}{1+ya}\right)^{\frac{p}{a}}\left(\frac{1+xb}{1+yb}\right)^{\frac{q}{b}}\left(\frac{1+xc}{1+yc}\right)^{\frac{r}{c}} $$     $$ \geq \prod \limits_{cyc}\left(\frac{1+y\left(a^pb^q\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q}}}{1+x\left(a^pb^q\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q}}}\right)^{\frac{p+q}{\left(a^pb^q\right)^{\frac{1}{p+q}}}} $$
solution_md:
Let  $f(y,z)\coloneqq\frac{1}{e^z}\log(1+ye^z)$ ,  $g(z)\coloneqq f(y,z)-f(x,z)$ ,  $A\coloneqq\log a$  and so on.
It is equivalent to showing that
\[(p+q+r)g\left(\frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\right)+\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}pg(A)-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(p+q)g\left(\frac{pA+qB}{p+q}\right)\geq 0\]
and it suffices to show
\[(p+q+r)f\left(x,\frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\right)+\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}pf(x,A)-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(p+q)f\left(x,\frac{pA+qB}{p+q}\right)\geq 0\]
is increasing for  $x\geq 1$  in  $x$ .
Let  $F(z)\coloneqq\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x,z)=\frac{1}{1+xe^z}$ . Then, it is equivalent to
\[(p+q+r)F\left(\frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\right)+\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}pF(A)-\sum_{\mathrm{cyc}}(p+q)F\left(\frac{pA+qB}{p+q}\right)\geq 0\]
where  $A,B,C\geq 0$  and  $p,q,r>0$ , with  $x\geq 1$ .

Noticing that  $F^{\prime\prime}(z)=\frac{xe^z(xe^z-1)}{(1+xe^z)^3}\geq 0$  for  $z\geq 0$ , we can apply Jensen's inequality to  $F$ .
WLOG, we can assume  $A\leq B\leq \frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\leq C$  and we get
\[A\leq \frac{pA+qB}{p+q}\leq B\leq \frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\leq \left\{\frac{pA+rC}{p+r},\frac{qB+rC}{q+r}\right\}\leq C.\]
By Jensen,
\[pf(A)+qf(B)\geq(p+q)f\left(\frac{pA+qB}{p+q}\right),\]
\[(p+q+r)f\left(\frac{pA+qB+rC}{p+q+r}\right)+rf(C)\geq(p+r)f\left(\frac{pA+rC}{p+r}\right)+(q+r)f\left(\frac{qB+rC}{q+r}\right)\]
which completes the proof.

P.S. (2025/04/02 18:55 UTC) I didn't know that the inequality I used is known as the weighted Popoviciu inequality :)

stem_md: In  $\mathbb{R}^3$ , let there be a cube  $Q$  and a sequence of other cubes, all of which are homothetic to  $Q$  with coefficients of homothety that are each smaller than  $1$ . Prove that if this sequence of homothetic cubes completely fills  $Q$ , the sum of their coefficients of homothety is not less than  $4$ .
solution_md:
I don't know about the rest of you, but I found this to be a really cool problem. 

Without loss of generality, we can let  $Q$  be the unit cube. If you visualize the scenario, a given homothetic cube with coefficient of homothety equal to  $a_i$  can cover at most a length of  $3a_i$  of the side-length  $Q$ . Since the sum of all side-lengths in  $Q$  is  $12$ , this means that   $$ \sum _{i \ cubes} 3 a_i \geq 12 \implies \sum _{i \ cubes} a_ i \geq 4, $$   
as desired.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/MIPT/2019 MIPT Undergraduate Contest/2237540.json

A given cube of side length  $a_i$  can only cover at most  $3a_i^2$  of the surface of the big cube so we must have
\[\sum_i a_i^2 \ge 2.\]
The claim then follows from Cauchy-Schwarz since
\[\left(\sum_i a_i\right)\left(\sum_i a_i^3\right) \ge \left(\sum_i a_i^2\right)^2\]
and  $\sum_i a_i^3=1$ .

In fact, using Hölder instead of Cauchy-Schwarz the second solution shows that

for all  $p \le 2$ . The first solution would only show this for  $p \le 1$ .

stem_md: Does there exist a strictly increasing function  $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$  that takes on only irrational values?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Yes.</details>
<details><summary>Hint</summary>Use a Liouville-type construction.</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>It clearly suffices to construct such a function  $f:[0,1) \to [0,1)$ .
It is tempting to just take the map  $g:[0,1) \to [0,1)$  defined by
\[x=\frac{a_1}{10}+\frac{a_2}{10^2}+\frac{a_3}{10^3}+\dots \mapsto \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{a_k}{10^{k!}}\]
i.e. applying a Liouville-type construction to the decimal digits of  $x$ .
By construction this is strictly increasing and takes irrational values -- unless the decimal expansion of  $x$  is finite.
One way to get around this issue is to instead choose  $(b_1,b_2,b_3,\dots)=(a_1,1,a_2,1,a_3,1,\dots)$  and apply Liouville's construction to this sequence i.e. we map
\[x=\frac{a_1}{10}+\frac{a_2}{10^2}+\frac{a_3}{10^3}+\dots \mapsto \frac{a_1}{10^{1!}}+\frac{1}{10^{2!}}+\frac{a_2}{10^{3!}}+\frac{1}{10^{4!}}+\dots.\]
This function  $f$  eventually works (one has to take a little care about ambiguous representations like  $0.09999999$  but we can just decide that in this case we choose either one (e.g. the larger one). 
Of course one could also do the same with binary expansion instead of decimal.</details>

stem_md: Prove the inequality   $$ \sum _{k = 1} ^n (x_k - x_{k-1})^2 \geq 4 \sin ^2 \frac{\pi}{2n} \cdot \sum ^n _{k = 0} x_k ^2 $$  for any sequence of real numbers  $x_0, x_1, ..., x_n$  for which  $x_0 = x_n = 0.$
solution_md:
Interesting! I had not considered a DFT solution to this. I wanted to rely on properties of quadratic forms instead. 

The problem is equivalent to finding the minimal eigenvalue of the quadratic form  $Q$  on the LHS of the inequality. Notice that   $$  Q(x_0, x_1, \dots , x_n) + Q(x_0 , -x_1, \dots, (-1)^n x_n) = 4(x_0^2 + x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n ^2) $$  Since this quadratic form clearly has non-negative eigenvalues, this implies that they are between  $0$  and  $4$ . We can consider  $Q$  to be a matrix with  $2$  on its main diagonal and  $-1$  on the two neighboring (minor? could someone give the right word?) diagonals. Then we get the following equation for eigenvalues  $\lambda$ :   $$ x_{k+1} - (2- \lambda) x_k + x_{k-1} = 0, $$  which, given the earlier observation about the range for eigenvalues, can be transformed as   $$ x_{k+1} - 2 \cos \phi x_k + x_{k-1} = 0. $$  This recurrence relation can be solved to obtain the explicit form   $$ x_k = a e^{ik \phi} + b e^{-ik \phi} $$  with the boundary conditions of  $a + b = ae^{in \phi} + b e^{-in \phi} = 0.$  This implies that  $\phi = \frac{\pi \ell}{n},$  and   $$ \lambda = 2 \left( 1 - \cos \frac{\pi \ell}{n} \right) = 4 \sin ^2 \frac{\pi \ell}{n}, \ x_k = \sin \frac{\pi \ell}{n} k. $$  Observe that the eigenvector obtained from this formula is the zero vector for  $\ell$  that is a multiple of  $n$ . For  $\ell = 1, \dots n-1,$  we get  $n-1$  distinct eigenvectors! Out of all of these vectors, the minimal eigenvector is obtained to be   $$ \lambda _{min} = 4 \sin ^2 \frac{\pi}{2n}, $$  from which the problem's desired conclusion follows.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/MIPT/2019 MIPT Undergraduate Contest/2237548.json

candidates:
I have surely seen a similar problem before.  :ewpu: 
The obvious reformulation is that
\[\sum_k x_kx_{k-1} \le \cos \frac{\pi}{n} \cdot \sum_k x_k^2.\]
This is already much less scary but still non-trivial.
The trick is to use <details><summary>Hint</summary>the discrete Fourier transform.</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>The discrete Fourier Transform will allow us to transform the nasty cyclic sum on the LHS into something nice:
Write  $y_k=\sum_i x_i \omega^{ki}$  where  $\omega$  is a  $n$ -th root of unity.
Then an easy computation using orthogonality shows that  $nx_k=\sum_j y_j\omega^{-kj}$  (Fourier Inversion).
Hence the condition simply is that  $\sum_j y_j=0$ .
Now, how do both sides of the inequality transform?
We have
\[n\sum_k x_k^2=\sum_j \vert y_j\vert^2\]
and
\[n\sum_k x_kx_{k-1}=\sum_j \omega^j \vert y_j\vert^2=\sum_j \cos \frac{2\pi j}{n} \vert y_j\vert^2.\]
(Note that the whole sum is real by assumption.)
Hence we are left to show that
\[\sum_k \cos \frac{2\pi k}{n} \vert y_k\vert^2 \le \cos \frac{\pi}{n} \cdot \sum_k \vert y_k\vert^2.\]
Note that  $y_i=\overline{y_{n-i}}$  so that we may assume w.l.o.g. that all the  $y_i$  are real.
Hence we need to prove the above inequality for real numbers  $y_i$  with  $\sum_i y_i=0$ . More generally, using the identity
\[\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{1}{\cos \frac{\pi}{n}-\cos \frac{2k\pi}{n}}=0\]
it suffices to show that
\[\frac{y_1^2}{a_1}+\dots+\frac{y_{n-1}^2}{a_{n-1}} \ge \frac{(y_1+\dots+y_{n-1})^2}{a_1+\dots+a_{n-1}}\]
whenever the  $a_i$  are positive numbers. But this is immediate by Cauchy-Schwarz.
(Indeed, the equality case will be exactly the choice  $y_k=\frac{1}{\cos \frac{\pi}{n}-\cos \frac{2k\pi}{n}}$ , up to scalar multiples of course, which can then be translated to give the  $x_i$ .)</details>

stem_md: Petya and Vasya are playing the following game. Petya chooses a non-negative random value  $\xi$  with expectation  $\mathbb{E} [\xi ] = 1$ , after which Vasya chooses his own value  $\eta$  with expectation  $\mathbb{E} [\eta ] = 1$  without reference to the value of  $\xi$ . For which maximal value  $p$  can Petya choose a value  $\xi$  in such a way that for any choice of Vasya's  $\eta$ , the inequality  $\mathbb{P}[\eta \geq \xi ] \leq p$  holds?
solution_md:
No, here's why. 

Vasya can choose  $\eta$ , which is distributed just as  $\xi$ , meaning  $\xi \geq n$  is satisfied with probability no smaller than  $1/2$ . So  $p$  cannot be smaller than  $1/2$ . Now let's prove that the value of  $x$ , which is normally distributed on  $[0,2]$ , the value of  $p = 1/2$  works for Petya. The random variable Vasya chooses is given by the function   $$ F(x) = \mathbb{P} (\eta \geq x), $$  which is defined on  $[0, \infty)$  and decreases from  $1$  to  $0$  in the limit. Then the probability that we're interested in can be written as   $$ \mathbb{P} (\eta \geq \xi) = \frac{1}{2} \int _0 ^2 F(x) dx \leq \frac{1}{2} \int ^\infty _0  F(x) dx = - \frac{1}{2} \int _0 ^\infty x dF(x) = \frac{1}{2} \mathbb{E}[\eta] = \frac{1}{2}.  $$

stem_md:
$F$ * is the multiplicative group of the field  $F$ . $F$ * is of finitely generated.
Is it true that  $F$ * is cyclic?
Additional question: (wasn’t at the olympiad) $K$ * is the multiplicative group of the field  $K$ . $L \subseteq $  $K$ * is a finitely generated subgroup.
Is it true that  $L$  is cyclic?
solution_md:
$F^*$ is finitely generated. Is it true that $F^*$ is cyclic?
Yes. If the characteristic of $F$ is zero, then $F^*$ contains $\mathbb{Q}^*,$ which is not finitely generated. Thus $F^*$ is not finitely generated in this case because every subgroup of a finitely generated abelian group is finitely generated; see [here](https://ysharifi.wordpress.com/2022/03/12/every-subgroup-of-an-abelian-group-generated-by-n-elements-can-be-generated-by-at-most-n-elements/) for a proof. Suppose now that the characteristic of $F$ is $p > 0,$ and let $\{x_1, \cdots ,x_n\}$ be a set of generators of $F^*.$ Suppose that $x_i$ is not algebraic over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for some $i.$ Then $\mathbb{Z}_p(x_i)$ is isomorphic to the field of rational functions $\mathbb{Z}_p(x)$ and it's easy to see that the multiplicative group of any field of rational functions is not finitely generated. So $\mathbb{Z}_p(x_1)^*,$ which is a subgroup of $F^*,$ is not finitely generated hence $F^*$ is not finitely generated. Therefore $x_i$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ for all $i$ and so $F^*$ is finite hence cyclic.
$L \subseteq $ $K^*$ is a finitely generated subgroup. Is it true that $L$ is cyclic?
No. For example, the subgroup of $\mathbb{Q}^*$ generated by $2,3$ is not cyclic.

stem_md: $A,B \in M_{2\times 2}(C)$ Prove that: $Tr(AAABBABAABBB)=tr(BBBAABABBAAA)$
solution_md:
We know $A^2=(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I$ holds for all $2\times 2$ matrices $A$ . Let $t_A,d_A,t_B,d_B$ be the trace and determinant of $A$ and $B$ , respectively. We have \begin{align*}\operatorname{tr}(AAABBABAABBB)=~~&\operatorname{tr}\bigg(((t_A^2+d_A)A+t_Ad_AI)(t_BB+d_BI)AB(t_AA+d_AI)((t_B^2+d_B)B+t_Bd_BI)\bigg)=~~&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)(t_B^2+d_B)t_At_BABABAB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)t_At_B^2d_BABABA+(t_B^2+d_B)t_A^2t_Bd_ABABAB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)(t_B^2+d_B)t_Bd_AABABB+(t_A^2+d_A)(t_B^2+d_B)t_Ad_BAABAB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)(t_B^2+d_B)d_Ad_BAABB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg(((t_A^2+d_A)t_B^2d_Ad_B+(t_B^2+d_B)t_A^2d_Ad_B)ABAB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)t_At_Bd_B^2AABA+(t_B^2+d_B)t_At_Bd_A^2BABB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg(t_A^2t_B^2d_Ad_BBABA\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg((t_A^2+d_A)d_At_Bd_B^2AAB+(t_B^2+d_B)t_Ad_Bd_A^2ABB\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg(t_At_B^2d_A^2d_BBAB+t_A^2t_Bd_Ad_B^2ABA\bigg)+&\operatorname{tr}\bigg(t_At_Bd_A^2d_B^2AB\bigg)\end{align*} which is arranged such that each line is symmetric in $A$ and $B$ . Hence $\operatorname{tr}(AAABBABAABBB)$ is symmetric in $A$ and $B$ , which is exactly the result.

candidates: No. Suppose you were given such a function f. Notice that f can't be locally monotonic anywhere (else it would have derivatives somewhere there) and for x_0 we must have either that for some \epsilon>0 that for all x\in(x_0,x_0+epsilon) that f(x_0)<f(x) or that for some \epsilon>0 that for all x\in(x_0,x_0+epsilon) that f(x_0)>f(x) because else by the continuity of f we would have f(x)=f(x_0) arbitrary close to the right of x_0 which contradicts the limit. So now we can construct a sequence (x_{r_k}) and (x_{l_k}) (r and l for right and left) which has either of these two properties (where depending if l or r we choose the interval on the right or left) (if we couldn't construct those we would have found an interval where f is monotonic) with the addition that we choose them closely so that they converge (the next point in the sequence will be taken in that interval). Now look at the limit point x_\infty and see that f has neither of those properties at x_\infty which is a contradiction.

stem_md:
Let  $f:[1,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$  be a continuous function. Assume that for every  $a>0$ , the equation  $f(x)=ax$  has at least one solution in the interval  $[1,\infty)$ .
(a) Prove that for every  $a>0$ , the equation  $f(x)=ax$  has infinitely many solutions.
(b) Give an example of a strictly increasing continuous function  $f$  with these properties.
solution_md:
(a) Assume that for some  $a>0$  there are only finitely many solutions. Then in particular there exists  $M \geq 1$  such that  $\frac{f(x)}{x} \not= a$  for all  $x \geq M$ . By continuity, we either have  $\forall \, x \geq M \colon \frac{f(x)}{x}  < a$  or  $\forall \, x \geq M \colon \frac{f(x)}{x}  > a$ . 
Consider the first case. Again by continuity, there exists  $c < \infty$  such that  $\frac{f(x)}{x}  < c$  for all  $x \in [1, M]$ . But then we have  $\frac{f(x)}{x}  < \max \{a, c\}$  for all  $x \in [1, \infty)$ , and hence the function  $\frac{f(x)}{x} $  cannot be surjective, a contradiction.
The second case is analogous.
(b) Clearly, it is sufficient if  $\liminf_{x \to \infty} \frac{f(x)}{x}  = 0$  and  $\limsup_{x \to \infty} \frac{f(x)}{x} = \infty$ .
Consider the continuous, piecewise linear function  $f$  with  $f(1)=1$  and such that for all  $n \in \mathbb{N}$  we have  $f(2^{4^n} ) = 2^{2 \cdot 4^{n-1} } + 1$  and  $f(2^{4^n} + 1 ) = 2^{2 \cdot 4^n }$ . Clearly,  $f$  is increasing and satisfies   $$  \limsup_{x \to \infty} \frac{f(x)}{x}  \geq \limsup_{n \to \infty} \frac{2^{2 \cdot 4^n}}{2^{4^n} + 1} = \infty $$  and  $$ \liminf_{x \to \infty} \frac{f(x)}{x}  \leq \liminf_{n \to \infty} \frac{2^{2 \cdot 4^{n-1}} + 1 }{2^{4^n}} = 0. $$  Maybe it is possible to find a simpler example which can be described by a single formula...

stem_md: Let  $P_0,P_1,P_2,\ldots$  be a sequence of convex polygons such that, for each  $k\ge0$ , the vertices of  $P_{k+1}$  are the midpoints of all sides of  $P_k$ . Prove that there exists a unique point lying inside all these polygons.
solution_md: It is a well known topological result that the intersection of a nested family of compact sets in a  $T_2$  space is nonempty (it can be easily proven by noting that for every  $k \ge 0$ ,  $P_k$  is closed in the Euclidean plane, so assuming that  $\underset{k \in \mathbb{N}}{\cap} P_k = \emptyset$ , we can complement the finite subcover of  $P_{k}^c$ , the existence of which is guaranteed by the compactness of  $P_0$ , giving us a finite set of  $P_k$ 's with an empty intersection, which is not possible), so  $\underset{k \in \mathbb{N}}{\cap} P_k \neq \emptyset$ . Assume that there exist  $M, N \in \underset{k \in \mathbb{N}}{\cap} P_k$  with  $M \neq N$ , and let  $d := |M - N|$ . Let the vertices of  $P_k$  be denoted by  $A^{(P_k)}_1, ..., A^{(P_k)}_n$ , where  $A^{(P_{k + 1})}_i$  is the midpoint of  $A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}$  (the indices are taken modulo  $n$ ). Note that since the polygons are convex,  $cos \angle A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}A^{(P_k)}_{i + 2} \ge 0$ , implying  $$ \sum {A^{(P_{k + 1})}_iA^{(P_{k+1})}_{i+1}}^2 = \frac{1}{4} \sum {A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+2}}^2 = \frac{1}{4} \sum ({A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}}^2 + {A^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}A^{(P_k)}_{i+2}}^2 - 2A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}\cdot A^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}A^{(P_k)}_{i+2}cos \angle A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}A^{(P_k)}_{i + 2}) \le \frac{1}{4} \sum ({A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}}^2 + {A^{(P_k)}_{i + 1}A^{(P_k)}_{i+2}}^2) = \frac{1}{2} {A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}}^2, $$  which means  ${A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}}^2 \overset{k \rightarrow \infty}{\longrightarrow} 0$ . By choosing a large enough  $k$  (for example a  $k$  such that  ${A^{(P_k)}_iA^{(P_k)}_{i+1}}^2 < \frac{d^2}{2}$  should suffice on account of the triangle inequality, Cauchy-Schwarz, and the convexity of  $P_k$ ) we get that  $M$  and  $N$  cannot simultaneously be in  $P_k$ , which contradicts our initial assumption. Therefore,  $\underset{k \in \mathbb{N}}{\cap} P_k$  contains one element.

stem_md: Let  $\mathcal M_n(\mathbb R)$  denote the set of all real  $n\times n$  matrices. Find all surjective functions  $f:\mathcal M_n(\mathbb R)\to\{0,1,\ldots,n\}$  which satisfy  $$ f(XY)\le\min\{f(X),f(Y)\} $$  for all  $X,Y\in\mathcal M_n(\mathbb R)$ .
solution_md:
We will prove that the only such function is  $f(X) = \text{rank}(X)$ Note that  $P(X,I_n)$  yields  $f(X) \leqslant f(I_n).$ Let  $X \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$  and  $Y = X^{-1}.$ Since  $P(X, Y)$  gives  $f(I_n) \leqslant f(X)$  it means that  $f(X) = f(I_n)$  for all  $X \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ Now, take  $X \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$  and  $Y \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ . $f(Y) \geqslant f(XY) \geqslant f(X^{-1} \cdot XY) = f(Y) \Rightarrow f(Y) = f(XY)$  $f(Y) \geqslant f(YX) \geqslant f(YX \cdot X^{-1}) = f(Y) \Rightarrow f(Y) = f(YX)$ So, we get that  $f(Y)=f(XY)=f(YX)$  for any  $X \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$  and  $Y \in M_n(\mathbb{R}) $   $(\dagger)$ For  $k \in \{0,1,2,\dots ,n\}$  let  $J_k$  be the rank  $k$  canonical matrix.

Take  $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$  with  $\text{rank}(A) = k$ .

We know there exist matrices  $P,Q \in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$  such that  $A=Q^{-1}J_kP$ Due to  $(\dagger)$  we get that  $f(A) = f(Q\cdot Q^{-1}J_kP\cdot P^{-1})=f(J_k)$  for any  $A \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$  with rank  $k$ .

Therefore, the set of values  $T = \{f(J_0), f(J_1), \dots ,f(J_n) \}$  uniquely determines  $f$ .

Note that  $f(J_k) = f(J_k J_{k+1}) \leqslant f(J_{k+1})$  for all  $0\leqslant k \leqslant n-1$ Since  $f$  is surjective it means that  $f(J_k) = k$  for all  $0\leqslant k \leqslant n$ We conclude that  $f(X) = \text{rank}(X)$  for all  $X \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer and  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be a continuous function such that  $$ \int^1_0x^kf(x)dx=1 $$  for every  $k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ . Prove that  $$ \int^1_0f(x)^2dx\ge n^2. $$
solution_md:
Two proofs: **First proof:** Same as before until last claim. For the last claim, let   $$  g(x) = \frac{a_1}{x+1} +\dots + \frac{a_n}{x+n} - 1, $$   
and notice that the problem conditions give  $g(k) = 0$  for  $k = 1,\dots,n-1.$  Putting in a common denominator, we may write   $$  g(x) = \frac{Q(x)}{(x+1)\cdots(x+n)}. $$   
If  $g(k)=0,$  we must have  $Q(k) = 0.$  Since  $\text{deg}(Q) = n-1,$  and since  $\lim_{x \to \infty} g(x) = -1,$  we have   $$ Q(x) = - x(x-1)\cdots(x-(n-1)). $$   
Now, note that  $a_1 + \cdots + a_n = \lim_{x \to \infty} x(g(x)+1),$  which equals the coefficient of order  $n-1$  of  $Q(x) + (x+1)\cdots(x+n), $  which is easily seen to be  $n^2.$  **Second proof.** Let  $\{P_k\}_k$  denote the sequence of [Legendre Polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_polynomials). By letting  $Q_n = \sqrt{2n+1} P_n,$  then  $Q_n$  form an *orthonormal basis* of  $L^2([0,1]).$ By the recursive definition of the Legendre polynomials, it is not hard to see that  $P_i(1) = 1,$  which implies that, for  $k\le n-1,$    $$  \int_{0}^1 P_k(x) f(x) \, dx = 1. $$   
 Hence,   $$  \int_{0}^1 |f(x)|^2 \, dx = \sum_{j\ge 0} |\langle Q_j, f \rangle|^2 \ge \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (2j+1) |\langle P_j, f \rangle|^2 =  \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} (2j+1) = n^2. $$

candidates: A quick observation , there exists some  $p(x)=a_1+a_2x+\dots+a_nx^{n-1}$  such that   $$ \int_0^1x^kp(x)dx=1 \ \forall \ k=0,1,\dots,n-1 $$   Therefore for all  $k\in\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$    $$ \int_0^1x^k(f(x)-p(x))dx=0 $$   Adding those  $k$ -equations by multiplying with  $a_i$     $$ \int_0^1p(x)(f(x)-p(x))dx=0 $$   Hence   $$ 0\leq\int_0^1(f(x)-p(x))^2dx=\int_0^1f(x)(f(x)-p(x))dx=\int_0^1f(x)^2dx \ - \ \sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_{k+1}\int_0^1x^kf(x)dx $$     $$ \implies\int_0^1f(x)^2dx\geq\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}a_{k+1}\int_0^1x^kf(x)dx=a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n $$     $$ \implies\int_0^1f(x)^2dx\geq a_1+a_2+\dots+a_n $$   Now it only remains to prove that  $a_1+\dots+a_n=n^2$  , which I leave as an exercise .

stem_md:
Let  $f_0:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be a continuous function. Define the sequence of functions  $f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  by  $$ f_n(x)=\int^x_0f_{n-1}(t)dt $$  for all integers  $n\ge1$ .

a) Prove that the series  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)$  is convergent for every  $x\in[0,1]$ .
b) Find an explicit formula for the sum of the series  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x),x\in[0,1]$ .
solution_md: $(a)$  We prove stronger than that . Clearly  $f_0$  is bounded , hence there is  $M>0$  such that  $|f_0(x)|\leq M$  for all  $x\in[0,1]$  . Again by FTC   $$ f_n'(x)=f_{n-1}(x) \ \forall \ x\in[0,1] $$   So by induction it follows easily that   $$ |f_n(x)|\leq\frac{Mx^n}{n!} \ \forall \ x\in[0,1] $$     $$ \implies\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f_n(x)|\leq\frac{M}{n!} $$   Since  $\sum_n\frac{1}{n!}$  is convergent ,  $\sum_nf_n$  is **uniformly convergent** on  $[0,1]$  . $(b)$  Denote  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)=F(x)$  . As previously we have   $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(x) $$   Since the RHS is u.c. from  $(a)$  , so is LHS , and hence term by term differentiation is allowed . It follows that   $$ F'(x)=f_0(x)+F(x) $$     $$ \implies F(x)=e^x\int_0^xe^{-t}f_0(t)dt $$     $$ \implies\boxed{\color{blue}\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)=e^x\int_0^xe^{-t}f_0(t)dt \ \ , \ \ x\in[0,1]} $$  <u>**N.B.**</u> : As a side note , this (iterated) uniform convergence criteria gave birth to theory of linear integral equations as iterated kernels and resolvent kernels that arises in solutions of those equations .

**a)** Note that  $A^2 - (\text{tr} A)A + (\det A)I = 0$ . $(A+tI)^2 = A^2 + 2t A + t^2 I = (\text{tr} A + 2t)A + (-\det A + t^2) I$ For sufficiently large  $t$ ,  $b = \text{tr} A + 2t > 0$  and  $c = -\det A + t^2 > 0$ . Then,
\[A = \frac{1}{b}(A+tI)^2 + \frac{c}{b}(-I) = \bigg( \sqrt{\frac{1}{b}} (A+tI) \bigg)^2 + \left( \sqrt{\frac{c}{b}} \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1  -1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} \right)^2\]**b)** If such  $B,C\in\mathcal{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$  exist, then
\[\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1  1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = B^2 + C^2 = B^2 - iBC + iCB - (iC)^2 = (B+iC)(B-iC).\]
Thus
\[-1 = \det \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1  1 & 0 \end{pmatrix} = \det(B+iC) \det(B-iC) = |\det(B+iC) |^2 \geq 0\]
gives contradiction!

stem_md:
Inside a square consider circles such that the sum of their circumferences is twice the perimeter of the square.

a) Find the minimum number of circles having this property.
b) Prove that there exist infinitely many lines which intersect at least 3 of these circles.
solution_md:
For  $a)$  the diameter of each circle is at most the side length of the square, which quickly yields that we have at least 3 circles.

For  $b)$  just project the circles onto one of the sides of the square. Each circle corresponds to a segment with length equal to its diameter.
It quickly follows that there exists an interval in which at least 3 segments are overlapping. Any line perpendicular on that segment intersects the 3 circles corresponding to those 3 segments.

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\rightarrow R$  be a continuous function and n be an integer number,n>0.Prove that  $\int_0^1f(x)dx \le (n+1)*\int_0^1 x^n*f(x)dx $
solution_md:
For a given integer $n\ge 1$ , let $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ be a non-decreasing function. Prove that $$ \int_0^1f(x)dx\le(n+1)\int_0^1x^nf(x)dx. $$ Find all non-decreasing continuous functions for which equality holds.
Proof: (Trivial by Chebyshev's inequality, but we will keep it simpler) We know ∀ \( x \in [0, 1] \), the inequality \[ x \geq x^{n+1} \] holds. **claim:** \( x - x^{n+1} \) is increasing on \( [0, 1) \). Define \( h(x) = x - x^{n+1} \). derivative of \( h(x) \): \[ h'(x) = 1 - (n+1)x^n \quad \text{for} \quad x \in [0, 1). \] We need to show that \( h'(x) \geq 0 \) for all \( x \in [0, 1) \). equality holds when \( x = \frac{1}{(n+1)^{1/n}} \), and for \( x \in [0, 1) \), we have \[ 1 - (n+1)x^n \geq 0. \] Thus, \[ 1 \geq (n+1)x^n. \] This implies \[ f(x) \geq (n+1) f(x) x^n \] and integrating both sides from 0 to 1: \[ \int_0^1 f(x) \, dx \geq (n+1) \int_0^1 f(x) x^n \, dx. \] The inequality returns equality when \( f(x) = c \), where \( c \in \mathbb{R} \) is any constant function. \(\boxed{\text{Q.E.D.}}\)

stem_md: Let  $A=(a_{ij})$  be a real  $n\times n$  matrix such that  $A^n\ne0$  and  $a_{ij}a_{ji}\le0$  for all  $i,j$ . Prove that there exist two nonreal numbers among eigenvalues of  $A$ .
solution_md:
Let  $\lambda_1, \cdots , \lambda_n$  be the eigenvalues of  $A$  counting multiplicity. Since  $A^n \neq 0$ , there is at least one nonzero eigenvalue.

Since  $a_{ii}^2 \leq 0 \implies a_{ii} = 0$  for all  $1\leq i\leq n$ , we have  $\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i = \text{tr}(A) = 0$ .

Let the characteristic polynomial be  $\text{det} (t I - A) = t^n + c_{n-2} t^{n-2} + \cdots$ . Then
\[c_{n-2} = \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n} \lambda_i \lambda_j ,\]
and
\[c_{n-2} = \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n} \left| \begin{array}{cc} 0 & a_{ij}  a_{ji} & 0 \end{array} \right| =  \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n} -a_{ij} a_{ji} \geq 0.\]
Therefore
\[\sum_{1\leq i\leq n} \lambda_i^2 =\left( \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i \right)^2 - 2 \sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n} \lambda_i \lambda_j = - 2c_{n-2} \leq 0.\]
Hence, there is at least one non real among  $\lambda_i$ 's. Since the coefficients of characteristic polynomials are real numbers, the non real eigenvalues are paired by conjugates. So proof is done.

stem_md: a) Prove that if  $k$  is an even positive integer and  $A$  is a real symmetric  $n\times n$  matrix such that  $\operatorname{tr}(A^k)^{k+1}=\operatorname{tr}(A^{k+1})^k$ , then  $$ A^n=\operatorname{tr}(A)A^{n-1}. $$  b) Does the assertion from a) also hold for odd positive integers  $k$ ?
solution_md:
a) Prove that if $k$ is an even positive integer and $A$ is a real symmetric $n\times n$ matrix such that $\operatorname{tr}(A^k)^{k+1}=\operatorname{tr}(A^{k+1})^k$ , then $$ A^n=\operatorname{tr}(A)A^{n-1}. $$
That's basically a fairly simple result of the following inequality. Claim 1. If $x_1, \cdots , x_m, \ m \ge 2,$ are positive real numbers and $0 < p < 1,$ then $$ (x_1+ \cdots + x_m)^p < x_1^p+ \cdots + x_m^p. $$ Proof. Using induction over $m,$ it is clear that we only need to prove the claim for $m=2.$ To do that, consider the function $$ f(t):=(1+t)^p-1-t^p, \ \ \ t \ge 0, $$ and see that $f'(t) < 0$ for $t > 0.$ So, since $f(0)=0,$ we have $f(t) < 0$ for all $t > 0,$ and hence $f(x_1/x_2) < 0,$ which proves our inequality for $m=2.$ Claim 2. If $y_1, \cdots , y_m, \ m \ge 2,$ are non-zero real numbers and $k > 0$ is an even integer, then $$ (y_1^{k+1}+ \cdots +y_m^{k+1})^k < (y_1^k+\cdots + y_m^k)^{k+1}. $$ Proof. We may assume that $y_i > 0$ for all $i$ because if the inequality is true for $|y_i|,$ then since $k$ is even, we'll have $$ (y_1^{k+1}+ \cdots + y_m^{k+1})^k=|y_1^{k+1}+ \cdots + y_m^{k+1}|^k \le (|y_1|^{k+1}+ \cdots +|y_m|^{k+1})^k < (|y_1|^k+ \cdots + |y_m|^k)^{k+1}=(y_1^k+ \cdots + y_m^k)^{k+1}. $$ Now use Claim 1 with $x_i:=y_i^{k+1}, \ 1 \le i \le m,$ and $p:=\frac{k}{k+1},$ to finish the proof.**Back to your problem**; we consider two cases. Case 1: $A$ has at most one non-zero eigenvalue. In this case $A^n=\text{tr}(A)A^{n-1},$ by Cayley-Hamilton. Case 2: $A$ has more than one non-zero eigenvalue. In this case, let $\lambda_1, \cdots, \lambda_m, \ m \ge 2,$ be the non-zero eigenvalues of $A,$ which are all real numbers because $A$ is real symmetric. We're given that $\text{tr}(A^k)^{k+1}=\text{tr}(A^{k+1})^k$ and so $$ (\lambda_1^k+ \cdots + \lambda_m^k)^{k+1}=(\lambda_1^{k+1}+ \cdots + \lambda_m^{k+1})^k, $$ which is impossible by Claim 2. So this case can never happen and the proof is complete.
b) Does the assertion from a) also hold for odd positive integers $k$ ?
Not necessarily. For example, for $k=1,$ consider any diagonal matrix $A \in M_3(\mathbb{R})$ with diagonal entries $a,b,c$ such that $abc \ne 0$ and $ab+ac+bc=0.$

stem_md: a) Compute  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}n\int^1_0\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^ndx. $$  b) Let  $k\ge1$  be an integer. Compute  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}n^{k+1}\int^1_0\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^nx^kdx. $$
solution_md:
The following is a well-known and useful result that I'm going to use (I've given a proof of it [here](https://ysharificalc.wordpress.com/2017/10/18/limit-of-integrals-6/)). Fact. If $f: [0,1] \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous, then $\lim_{n\to\infty} n\int_0^1t^nf(t) \ dt=f(1).$
a) Compute $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}n\int^1_0\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^ndx. $$
The answer is $\frac{1}{2}.$ To see that, let $t:=\frac{1-x}{1+x}.$ Then $x=\frac{1-t}{1+t}$ and $$ n\int_0^1\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^ndx=2n\int_0^1\frac{t^n}{(1+t)^2} \ dt $$ and so using the above Fact with $f(t):=\frac{2}{(1+t)^2}$ we get $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}n\int_0^1\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^ndx=f(1)=\frac{1}{2}. $$
b) Let $k\ge1$ be an integer. Compute $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}n^{k+1}\int^1_0\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^nx^kdx. $$
The answer is $\frac{k!}{2^{k+1}}.$ To see that, again make the substitution $x=\frac{1-t}{1+t}$ to get $$ I_k(n):=n^{k+1}\int^1_0\left(\frac{1-x}{1+x}\right)^nx^kdx=2n^{k+1}\int_0^1\frac{t^n(1-t)^k}{(1+t)^{k+2}} \ dt=\frac{n^{k+1}}{2^{k+1}}\int_0^1t^n(1-t)^k\left(1-\frac{1-t}{2}\right)^{-k-2}dt. $$ So using the binomial series for $\left(1-\frac{1-t}{2}\right)^{-k-2}$ we get $$ I_k(n)=\frac{n^{k+1}}{2^{k+1}}\int_0^1t^n\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^{m+k}dt. $$ Now use integration by parts with $t^ndt=dv$ and $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{1}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^{m+k}=u$ to get $$ I_k(n)=\frac{n^{k+1}}{2^{k+1}(n+1)}\int_0^1t^{n+1}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{m+k}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^{m+k-1}dt. $$ Do integration by parts again this time with $t^{n+1}dt=dv$ and $\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{m+k}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^{m+k-1}=u$ to get $$ I_k(n)=\frac{n^{k+1}}{2^{k+1}(n+1)(n+2)}\int_0^1t^{n+2}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(m+k)(m+k-1)}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^{m+k-2}dt. $$ Repeating integration by parts $k$ times, we will eventually get $$ I_k(n)=\frac{n^{k+1}}{2^{k+1}(n+1)(n+2) \cdots (n+k)}\int_0^1t^{n+k}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(m+k)(m+k-1) \cdots (m+1)}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^m dt. $$ Hence $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}I_k(n)=\frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\lim_{n\to\infty}n\int_0^1t^{n+k}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(m+k)(m+k-1) \cdots (m+1)}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^m dt $$ $$ =\frac{1}{2^{k+1}}\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+k)\int_0^1t^{n+k}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(m+k)(m+k-1) \cdots (m+1)}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^m dt $$ and so using the above Fact with $f(t):=\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}\frac{(m+k)(m+k-1) \cdots (m+1)}{2^m}\binom{m+k-1}{m}(1-t)^m,$ we get $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}I_k(n)=\frac{1}{2^{k+1}}f(1)=\frac{k!}{2^{k+1}}. $$ Remark. For $k=0,$ the answers in a), b) are the same and so we have $\lim_{n\to\infty}I_k(n)=\frac{k!}{2^{k+1}}$ for all integers $k \ge 0.$

stem_md: Find all continuous functions  $f:[1,8]\to\mathbb R$ , such that  $$ \int^2_1f(t^3)^2dt+2\int^2_1f(t^3)dt=\frac23\int^8_1f(t)dt-\int^2_1(t^2-1)^2dt. $$
solution_md:
Using the substitution  $t=u^3$  and then returning to the variable  $t$ : $\int^8_1f(t)dt=3\int^2_1u^2f(u^3)du=3\int^2_1t^2f(t^3)dt$ . $\int^2_1f^2(t^3)dt+2\int^2_1f(t^3)dt=\dfrac23\int^8_1f(t)dt-\int^2_1(t^2-1)^2dt\Longleftrightarrow$  $\int^2_1f^2(t^3)dt+2\int^2_1f(t^3)dt-2\int^2_1t^2f(t^3)dt+\int^2_1(t^2-1)^2dt=0\Longleftrightarrow$  $\int^2_1[f^2(t^3)-2(t^2-1)f(t^3)+(t^2-1)^2]dt=0\Longleftrightarrow$  $\int^2_1[f(t^3)-(t^2-1)]^2dt=0$ . $f(t)$  is continuous for  $t\in[1,8]\Longrightarrow f(t^3)$  is continuous for  $t\in[1,2]$ . $\begin{cases}\int^2_1[f(t^3)-(t^2-1)]^2dt=0f(t^3)\text{ is continuous}\end{cases}\Longrightarrow f(t^3)-(t^2-1)=0,\;\forall t\in[1,2]$ .

Results: $f(t^3)=t^2-1,\;\forall t\in[1,2]\Longrightarrow f(t)=t^{\frac{2}{3}}-1,\;\forall t\in[1,8]$ .

solution_md:
Interpret $M,N$ as operators, and let $v\in \text{ker}M$ , and $Nv=w\Rightarrow Nw=N^2v=0$ . Then $v=(MN+NM)v=Mw$ , so the matrices of $M$ and $N$ w.r.t. basis $\{v,w\}$ are the required ones. Note that we didn't use the nilpotence of $M$ . Indeed, we only need to assume one of the matrices is nilpotent, and the other one will follow from the conditions.

stem_md: Find the maximum value of  $$ \int^1_0|f'(x)|^2|f(x)|\frac1{\sqrt x}dx $$  over all continuously differentiable functions  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  with  $f(0)=0$  and  $$ \int^1_0|f'(x)|^2dx\le1. $$
solution_md:
By the cauchy - schwarz inequality, we can denote
\[0\leq x\leq1,\,\,\,\vert f(x)\vert=\bigg\vert\int_{0}^{x}f’(t)\,dt\bigg\vert\leq\int_{0}^{x}\vert f’(t)\vert\,dt\leq\left(\int_{0}^{x}\left\{f’(t)\right\}^2\,dt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(\int_{0}^{x}1^2\,dt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\]

Thus, we have
\[0\leq x\leq1,\,\,\,\frac{\vert f(x)\vert}{\sqrt{x}}\leq\left(\int_{0}^{x}\left\{f’(t)\right\}^2\,dt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\Rightarrow \frac{\vert f(x)\vert\left\{f’(x)\right\}^2}{\sqrt{x}}\leq \left\{f’(x)\right\}^2\left(\int_{0}^{x}\left\{f’(t)\right\}^2\,dt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\]

And let the function  $g(x)=\int_{0}^{x}\left\{f’(t)\right\}^2\,dt$ , we have
\[\left\{f’(x)\right\}^2\left(\int_{0}^{x}\left\{f’(t)\right\}^2\,dt\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}=g’(x)\left\{g(x)\right\}^{\frac{1}{2}}\]
Therefore, we can deduce
\[\int_{0}^{1}\frac{\vert f(x)\vert\left\{f’(x)\right\}^2}{\sqrt{x}}\,dx\leq\int_{0}^{1}g’(x)\left\{g(x)\right\} ^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dx=\left[\frac{2}{3}\left\{g(x)\right\} ^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{2}{3}\left\{g(1)\right\}^{\frac{3}{2}}\leq\frac{2}{3}\] by the fact that  $g(1)\leq1$

stem_md: Let  $A\in M_2(\mathbb Q)$  such that there is  $n\in\mathbb N,n\ne0$ , with  $A^n=-I_2$ . Prove that either  $A^2=-I_2$  or  $A^3=-I_2$ .
solution_md:
The minimal polynomial  $m$  of  $A$  has degree  $1$  or  $2$  and divides  $x^n+1=\dfrac{x^{2n}-1}{x^n-1}$ .
Let  $P_d$  be the  $d^{th}$  cyclotomic polynomial; recall that  $P_d$  is irreducible. Since  $x^n+1=\dfrac{\Pi_{d|2n}P_d}{\Pi_{d|n}P_d}$ , $x^n+1$  is a product of cyclotomic polynomials and  $m$  too.
The values of  $d$  that we consider satisfy   $degree(P_d)=\phi(d)\leq 2$ ; then  $d\in\{1,2,3,4,6\}$  and  $P_d=x\pm 1,x^2\pm x+1$  or  $x^2+1$ .
Note that  $x^3+1=(x+1)(x^2-x+1)$ .
EDIT. 
Since  $A$  is semisimple,  $m$  has simple complex  roots.
 If  $x-1$  divides  $m$  then  $A^n$  admits  $1$  as eigenvalue, that is contradictory.
If  $m=\chi_A=x^2+x+1$  then  $spectrum(A)=\{j,j^2\}$  (where  $j=e^{2i\pi/3}$ )  $spectrum(A^2)=\{j^2,j\}$ . Thus  $A^3=I,A^4=A,A^5=A^2,\cdots$  -a periodic sequence- that is impossible because  $-I$  is not reached. 
  $\square$

stem_md:
Let  $A\in M_n(\mathbb{C}) $  and  $a\in \mathbb{C} $  such that  $A-A^*=2aI_n $ , where  $A^*=(\overline{A})^T $  and  $I_n$  is identity matrix.  
(i)  Show that  $|\det A|\ge |a|^n $ . 
 
(ii) Show that if  $|\det A|=|a|^n $   then  $A=aI_n$ .
solution_md:
i) Firstly  $A-A^*$  is a skew-hermitian matrix; then  $a=i\beta$  where  $\beta\in \mathbb{R}$ . Note that  $AA^*=A^*A$  and  $A$  is a normal matrix; thus  $A,A^*$  are simultaneously diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis; finally, we may assume that  $A=diag((\alpha_k+i\beta)_k),A^*=diag((\alpha_k-i\beta)_k)$ .
Therefore  $|\det(A)|=\Pi_k|\alpha_k+i\beta|=\Pi_k\sqrt{\alpha_k^2+\beta^2}\geq |\beta|^n$ . (where  $\alpha_k\in \mathbb{R}$ )
ii)  The equality stands iff for every  $k$ ,  $\alpha_k=0$ , that is, iff  $A=i\beta I_n$ .
In fact the previous reasoning for ii) works only if  $\beta\not=0$ . If  $\beta=0$ , then  $A$  is hermitian and  $\det(A)=0$ ; in this case,  $A$  is orthogonally similar to  $diag(0,\alpha_2,\cdots,\alpha_n)$  where the  $(\alpha_k)_{k\geq 2}$  are real.

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a nonzero natural number and  $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$  be a function such that  $f(2014)=1-f(2013)$ . Let  $x_1,x_2,x_3,\ldots,x_n$  be real numbers not equal to each other. If  $$ \begin{vmatrix}1+f(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)f(x_1)&1+f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)f(x_1)&f(x_2)&1+f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdotsf(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&1+f(x_n)\end{vmatrix}=0, $$  prove that  $f$  is not continuous.
solution_md:
Write the given matrix as  $M$ . Observe that :  $~ M = \mathbf{Id}_n + H = I + H~$  , where  $I = \mathbf{Id}_n$  is the identity matrix of order  $n$  , and   $$ H = \begin{bmatrix}f(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)f(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)f(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdotsf(x_1)&f(x_2)&f(x_3)&\cdots&f(x_n)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 1 1 \vdots 1\end{bmatrix} \cdot\begin{bmatrix}f(x_1) f(x_2) f(x_3) \vdots f(x_n)\end{bmatrix}^T = \mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}^T $$   Thus, by the [Matrix - Determinant Lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_determinant_lemma), we have :   $$ 0 = \det(M) = \det\big(I + H\big) = \big(1 ~+~ \mathbf{v}^T I^{-1}\mathbf{u}\big)~\cdot~\det(I) = 1 ~+~ \mathbf{v}^T\mathbf{u} = 1 ~+~ \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k) $$   Now, on the contrary to the stament which are supposed to prove, *let us assume that*  $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ *is continuous*. Since  $0 \not\in \text{Range}(f)$ , and  $f$  is assumed to be continuous, thus  $f(x)$  must have the same sign for all  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ . Otherwise, without loss of generality, if there exists two unequal numbers  $p$  and  $q$  with  $p < q$  such that  $f$  has different signs at  $p$  and  $q$ , then by [Intermediate Value Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intermediate_value_theorem), there will exist some  $c \in (p,q)$  satisfying  $f(c) = 0$  which leads us to a contradiction as it is given that  $0 \not\in \text{Range}(f)$ .

Now, we have already found out that   $$ 1 + \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^n f(x_k) = (-1) ~<~ 0 $$   which implies that  $f(x_k) < 0$  for all  $k = 1, 2, \cdots, n$ . But, we have been supplied with the information that  $f(2013) + f(2014) = 1 > 0$  which leads us to the conclusion that  $f(2013) > 0$  and  $f(2014) > 0$ . This contradicts the fact that  $f$  has the same sign at all  $x \in \mathbb{R}$ .

Thus,  $f$  is **not** continuous.  $~\blacksquare$
