Problem 1.
Let  $f$  be a continuous and decreasing real valued function, defined on  $[0, \pi/2]$ . Prove the inequalities  $$ \int_{\frac{\pi}{2}-1}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(x)dx\le\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}f(x)\cos xdx\le\int_{0}^{1}f(x)dx $$  when do equalities hold?

Problem 2.
a) Prove that for every matrix  $X\in M_2(\mathbb{C})$  there exists a matrix  $Y\in M_2(\mathbb{C})$  such that  $Y^3=X^2$ .

b) Prove that there exists a matrix  $A\in M_3(\mathbb{C})$  such that  $Z^3\neq A^2$  for all  $Z\in M_3(\mathbb{C})$

Problem 3.
Let  $A_1, A_2, ... , A_k$  be idempotent matrices ( $A_i^2=A_i$ ) in  $ M_n(\mathbb{R})$ . Prove that  $$ \sum_{i=1}^kN(A_i)\ge rank(I - \prod_{i=1}^kA_i) $$   where  $N(A_i)=n-rank(A_i)$  and $M_n(\mathbb{R})$  is the set of square  $n\times n$  matrices with real entries.

Problem 4. 
Let  $n \ge 1$  be an integer and let   $$ I_n=\int_0^{\infty}\frac{\arctan x}{(1+x^2)^n} dx. $$  Prove that
a)  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{I_n}{n}=\frac{\pi ^2}{6}$ b) $\int_0^{\infty}\arctan\cdot \ln(1+\frac{1}{x^2})dx=\frac{\pi ^2}{6}$

I've put some hints, which practically solve problems 2 and 3 right away, in the following blog post: https://mathproblems123.wordpress.com/2016/03/05/seemous-2016-problems/

A solution to problem 4 can be found here: https://mathproblems123.wordpress.com/2016/03/06/seemous-2016-problem-4-solution/

Let $A_1, A_2, \ldots , A_k$ be idempotent matrices in $M_n(\mathbb{R}){}$ . Prove that \[\sum_{i=1}^k\left(n-\text{rk}(A_i)\right)\geqslant\text{rk}\left(I_n - \prod_{i=1}^kA_i\right).\]
Fix an index $i{}$ and note that because $A_i$ is idempotent, then $A_i(I_n-A_i)X_i=O_n$ for any matrix $X_i$ . Hence, by Sylvester \[n-\text{rk}(A_i)\geqslant\text{rk}((I_n-A_i)X_i)-\text{rk}(O_n)=\text{rk}((I_n-A_i)X_i).\]for any matrix $X_i$ . By summing and using the supra-additivity of the rank we may infer \[\sum_{i=1}^k\left(n-\text{rk}(A_i)\right)\geqslant\sum_{i=1}^k\text{rk}((I_n-A_i)X_i)\geqslant\text{rk}\left(\sum_{i=1}^k(I_n-A_i)X_i\right).\]By letting $X_1=I_n$ and $X_i=A_1A_2\cdots A_{i-1}$ for $i\geqslant 2$ the conclusion immediately follows.

stem_md:
Consider  $0<a<T$ ,  $D=\mathbb{R}\backslash \{  kT+a\mid k\in \mathbb{Z}\}$ , and let  $f:D\to \mathbb{R}$  a  $T-$ periodic and differentiable function which satisfies  $f' > 1$  on  $(0, a)$  and  $$ f(0)=0,\lim_{\substack{x\to ax<a}}f(x)=+\infty \text{ and }\lim_{\substack{x\to a x<a}}\frac{f'(x)}{f^2(x)}=1. $$  

- Prove that for every  $n\in \mathbb{N}^*$ , the equation  $f(x)=x$  has a unique solution in the interval  $(nT, nT+a)$  , denoted  $x_n$ .[/*]
- Let  $y_n=nT+a-x_n$  and  $z_n=\int_0^{y_n}f(x)\text{d}x$ . Prove that  $\lim_{n\to \infty}{y_n}=0$  and study the convergence of the series  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{y_n}$  and  $\sum_{n=1}^{n}{z_n}$ .
solution_md:
I have doubts about the proof of paragraph  $\textbf{d) }$  and please correct/complete it with supplementary observations.  $\textbf{a) }x_n\textbf{ is unique}$ .
Let be the function  $g_n:(nT, nT+a)\to\mathbb{R}, g_n(x)=f(x)-x$ , where  $n\in \mathbb{N}^*$ .
Denote  $t=x-nT\in(0,a)$ . $g_n(x)=f(x)-x=f(t+nT)-(t+nT)=f(t)-(t+nT)$ . $g_n'(x)=f'(t)-1>0,\forall t\in(0,a)\Longrightarrow g_n(x)$  is strictly increasing  $\quad(1)$ . $g_n$  is differentiable, hence continuous and we can apply the intermediate value theorem: $\begin{cases}\lim_{x\searrow nT}g_n(x)=f(nT)-nT=f(0)-nT=-nT<0; \lim_{x\nearrow nT+a}g_n(x)=\lim_{x\nearrow nT+a}f(x)-(nT+a)=\lim_{t\nearrow a}f(t)-(nT+a)=+\infty.\end{cases}\quad(2)$ From  $(2)$  results:  $\exists x_n\in(nT, nT+a)$  such that  $g_n(x_n)=0\Longleftrightarrow f(x_n)=x_n$ .
Using  $(1)$  results:  $x_n$  is unique. $\textbf{b) }\lim_{n\to \infty}{y_n}=0$ .
The sequence  $(y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$  is strictly descending.  $\quad(1)$ For  $n\in\mathbb{N}: x_{n}\in(nT,nT+a), x_n+T\in((n+1)T,(n+1)T+a)$ . $g_{n+1}(x_n+T)=f(x_n)-(x_n+T)=f(x_n)-x_n-T=-T<0=g_{n+1}(x_{n+1})\Longrightarrow $  $x_n+T<x_{n+1}\Longrightarrow nT+a-x_n>(n+1)T+a-x_{n+1}\Longrightarrow y_n>y_{n+1}$ .
The sequence  $(y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$  is bounded:  $0<y_n<a.\quad(2)$ From  $(1)$  and  $(2)$ :  $(y_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$  is convergent and exists $y=\lim_{n\to \infty}{y_n}\ge0$ . $f'(x)>1>0,\forall x\in(0,a)\Longrightarrow$  the function  $f(x)$  is strictly increasing on  $[0,a)$ .
Let be  $\varepsilon\in(0,a)$  and  $N_{\varepsilon}=\left\lceil\dfrac{f(a-\varepsilon)}{T}\right\rceil$ .
Using  $x_n-nT\in(0,a),a-\varepsilon\in(0,a)$ , results for all  $n\in\mathbb{N}, n>N_{\varepsilon}$ : $f(x_n)=x_n>nT>N_{\varepsilon}T\ge f(a-\varepsilon)\Longrightarrow f(x_n-nT)>f(a-\varepsilon)\Longrightarrow$  $\Longrightarrow f(a-y_n)>f(a-\varepsilon)\Longrightarrow a-y_n>a-\varepsilon\Longrightarrow y_n<\varepsilon$ .
Hence,  $\forall \varepsilon\in(0,a), \exists N_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{N}$  such that  $\forall n\in\mathbb{N}, n>N_{\varepsilon}$  results  $0<y_n<\varepsilon$ .
Using the definition of the limit, results: $\lim_{n\to \infty}{y_n}=0$ . $\textbf{c) The series }\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{y_n}$ .
Consider the  $T-$ periodic function $h:\cup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}(kT,kT+a]\to\mathbb{R}$ , $h(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{1}{f(x)},\text{ for }x\in(kT,kT+a);0,\text{ for }x=kT+a.\end{cases}$ The function  $h(x)$  is continuous on  $(kT,kT+a]$  and differentiable on  $(kT,kT+a)$ . $\dfrac{f'(x)}{f^2(x)}=-\left(\dfrac{1}{f(x)}\right)^{'}=-h'(x)$ .
Using this relation we can find an approximation for  $f(x_n)=f(nT+a-y_n), n\in\mathbb{N}$ . $\lim_{\substack{x\to nT+a x<nT+a}}\dfrac{f'(x)}{f^2(x)}=1\Longrightarrow \lim_{\substack{x\to nT+a x<nT+a}}h'(x)=-1$ .
Using the mean value theorem: $h(nT+a)-h(nT+a-y_n)=y_n\cdot h'(c_n)$ , where  $c_n\in(nT+a-y_n,nT+a),\lim_{n\to\infty}y_n=0, \lim_{n\to\infty}h'(c_n)=-1$ .
Results: $\lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{y_n}{h(nT+a-y_n)}=1\Longrightarrow y_n=\dfrac{1}{f(nT+a-y_n)}\cdot d_n$ , where  $\lim_{n\to\infty}d_n=1$ . $\lim_{n\to\infty}d_n=1\Longrightarrow \forall\varepsilon>0,\exists N_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{N}$  such that  $d_n\in(1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon), \forall n\in\mathbb{N}, n>N_{\varepsilon}$ . $f(nT+a-y_n)=f(x_n)=x_n\in(nT,nT+a)$ .
Results for  $\varepsilon\in(0,1),n>N_{\varepsilon}$ : $\dfrac{1}{(n+1)T}\cdot(1-\varepsilon)<y_n<\dfrac{1}{nT}\cdot(1+\varepsilon)$ . $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{y_n}>\sum_{n=N_{\varepsilon}}^{\infty}{y_n}>\sum_{n=N_{\varepsilon}}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{(n+1)T}\cdot(1-\varepsilon)=\dfrac{1-\varepsilon}{T}\cdot\sum_{n=N_{\varepsilon+1}}^{\infty}\dfrac{1}{n}=\infty$ ,
hence the series  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{y_n}$  is divergent. $\textbf{d) The series }\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{z_n}$ .
Let be  $\delta$  a real number with the property  $0<\delta<a$  and  $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ .
Using the previous paragraph, exists  $N_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbb{N}$  such that  $y_n<\min\left\{\delta,\dfrac{1+\varepsilon}{nT}\right\},\forall n\in\mathbb{N}, n>N_{\varepsilon}$ . $f(x)$  is a differentiable function means: $\forall x_0\in(-T+a,a), \lim_{h\to0}\dfrac{f(x_0+h)-f(x_0)}{h}=f'(x_0)$  exists and is finite.
Results:  $\exists M>0$  such that  $1\le f'(x)\le M,\forall x\in[0,\delta]\Longrightarrow 0\le f(x)\le Mx,\forall x\in[0,\delta]$ . $z_n=\int_0^{y_n}f(x)\text{d}x\le \int_0^{y_n}Mx dx= \dfrac{My_n^2}{2}<\dfrac{M(1+\varepsilon)^2}{2T^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{n^2}$ . $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{z_n}=\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\varepsilon}}{z_n}+\sum_{n=N_{\varepsilon}+1}^{\infty}{z_n}$ .
Denote  $S_1=\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\varepsilon}}{z_n}$ , finite and $S_2=\sum_{n=N_{\varepsilon}+1}^{\infty}{z_n}\le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{M(1+\varepsilon)^2}{2T^2}\cdot\dfrac{1}{n^2}=\dfrac{M(1+\varepsilon)^2}{2T^2}\cdot\dfrac{\pi^2}{6}$ . $0\le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}{z_n}\le S_1+S_2$ , finite, hence the series is convergent.

stem_md: Let  $n$  be a positive integer,  $k\in \mathbb{C}$  and  $A\in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$  such that  $\text{Tr } A\neq 0$  and   $$ \text{rank } A +\text{rank } ((\text{Tr } A) \cdot I_n - kA) =n. $$  Find  $\text{rank } A$ .
solution_md:
Weird problem.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>$\text{rank}\ A=k$ .</details>
<details><summary>Solution</summary>We show that  $k\neq 0$ . If  $k=0$ , then  $\text{rank}\ ( (\text{Tr}\ A)\cdot I-kA)=n$ , so  $\text{rank}\ A=0$  which implies  $\text{Tr}\ A=0$  which is impossible, hence  $k\neq 0$ .

Let  $\lambda=\frac{\text{Tr}\ A}{k}\neq 0$ . It holds that  $\text{rank}\ ( (\text{Tr}\ A)\cdot I-kA)=\text{rank}\ (\lambda I-A)$ .
We have that 
\[
\text{rank}(\lambda I-A)=n-\dim \ker(\lambda I-A)
\]
therefore
 \begin{align}\text{rank}\ A=\dim \ker(\lambda I-A)
\end{align} Now, every vector in  $X:=\ker(\lambda I-A)$  is an eigenvector with eigenvalue  $\lambda$ , hence  $X\leq \text{Im}\  A$ , which together with  $(1)$  implies that  $X=\text{Im}\ A$ . We have that  $\mathbb{C}^n=X\oplus \ker A$ . There is a basis of eigenvectors, hence  $A$  is diagonalizable and the number of nonzero entries in diagonal is equal to  $\dim X=\text{rank}\ A$ .
Summing elements on the diagonal we have 
\[
\text{Tr}\ A=\sum_{i=1}^{\text{rank}\ A}\lambda=\text{rank}\ A\cdot \lambda=\text{rank}\ A\cdot \frac{\text{Tr}\ A}{k}
\]
which implies that  $\text{rank}\ A=k$ .</details>

stem_md:
Let  $k>1$  be a real number. Calculate:
(a)  $L=\lim_{n\to \infty} \int_0^1\left( \frac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\text{d} x.$ (b)  $\lim_{n\to \infty} n\left\lbrack L- \int_0^1\left( \frac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\text{d} x\right\rbrack.$
solution_md:
(a) For  $x\in(0,1]$ , fixed: $\lim_{n\to \infty}\sqrt[n]{x}=1$ ; $\lim_{n\to \infty}n(\sqrt[n]{x}-1)=\ln{x}$ . $\lim_{n\to \infty}\left( \dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n=\lim_{n\to \infty}\left(1+ \dfrac{1-\sqrt[n]{x}}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n=e^{l_x}$ , where $l_x=\lim_{n\to \infty}n\cdot\dfrac{1-\sqrt[n]{x}}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}=-\dfrac{\ln{x}}{k}=\ln{\left(x^{-\frac{1}{k}}\right)}$ .
Results: $\lim_{n\to \infty}\left( \dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n=x^{-\frac{1}{k}}$ . $L=\lim_{n\to \infty} \int_0^1\left( \dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\text{d} x=\int_0^1x^{-\frac{1}{k}}\text{d} x=\dfrac{k}{k-1}$ .


(b)  $M=\lim_{n\to \infty} n\left\lbrack L- \int_0^1\left( \dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\text{d} x\right\rbrack=\lim_{n\to \infty} \int_0^1n\left\lbrack x^{-\frac{1}{k}}- \left(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\right\rbrack\text{d} x$ .

For  $x=a\in(0,1]$ , fixed and with the notation  $y=\dfrac{1}{n}\to0$ : $m_a=\lim_{n\to \infty} n\left[x^{-\frac{1}{k}}- \left(\dfrac{k}{\sqrt[n]{x}+k-1}\right)^n\right]=\lim_{y\searrow0}\dfrac{1}{y}\cdot\left[a^{-\frac{1}{k}}- \left(\dfrac{k}{a^y+k-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{y}}\right]=(\text{l'Hospital})$  $=\lim_{y\searrow0}\left(\dfrac{k}{a^y+k-1}\right)^{\frac{1}{y}}\cdot\dfrac{\ln\dfrac{k}{a^y+k-1}+\dfrac{y\cdot a^y\cdot\ln{a}}{a^y+k-1}}{y^2}=(\text{l'Hospital})$  $=a^{-\frac{1}{k}}\cdot\lim_{y\searrow0}\dfrac{(k-1)y\cdot a^y\cdot\ln^2{a}}{2y\cdot k^2}=a^{-\frac{1}{k}}\cdot\dfrac{(k-1)\ln^2{a}}{2k^2}$ .

Results (using the notation  $x$  instead  $a$ ): $M=\dfrac{k-1}{2k^2}\int_0^1x^{-\frac{1}{k}}\ln^2{x}\text{d}x=(\text{integration by parts})$  $\dfrac{k-1}{2k^2}\cdot\left[x^{1-\frac{1}{k}}\left(\dfrac{k}{k-1}\ln^2{x}-\dfrac{2k^2}{(k-1)^2}\ln{x}+\dfrac{2k^3}{(k-1)^3}\right)\right]_0^1$ .
Using  $\lim_{x\searrow0}x^{1-\frac{1}{k}}\cdot\ln^2{x}=\lim_{x\searrow0}x^{1-\frac{1}{k}}\cdot\ln{x}=0$ ,
results: $M=\dfrac{k-1}{2k^2}\cdot\dfrac{2k^3}{(k-1)^3}=\dfrac{k}{(k-1)^2}$ .

stem_md:
Consider  $A\in \mathcal{M}_{2020}(\mathbb{C})$  such that  $$ (1)\begin{cases}
A+A^{\times} =I_{2020}, 
A\cdot A^{\times}  =I_{2020},
\end{cases} $$  where  $A^{\times}$  is the adjugate matrix of  $A$ , i.e., the matrix whose elements are  $a_{ij}=(-1)^{i+j}d_{ji}$ , where  $d_{ji}$  is the determinant obtained from  $A$ , eliminating the line  $j$  and the column  $i$ .
Find the maximum number of matrices verifying  $(1)$  such that any two of them are not similar.
solution_md:
We have  $\det A=1$  and  $A+A^{-1}=I$ , or  $A^2-A+I=0$ .
So,  $A$  is diagonalizable with possible eigenvalues  $\lambda=\frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}2$  and  $\bar\lambda=\frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}2$ .
If the multiplicities are  $h,k$ , then $\det A=\lambda^{h-k}$  and since  $\lambda$  has order 6, we have  $h\equiv k(mod6)$ .
But  $h+k=2020$ , so  $h\equiv 1010\equiv 2(mod3)$ .
Thus,  $h=2+3s$ ,  $k=2018-3s$  with  $s=0,1,...,672$ .
We have 673 different similitude classes.

stem_md:
Let  $f: [0, 1] \to \mathbb{R}$  be a continuous strictly increasing function such that
\[ \lim_{x \to 0^+} \frac{f(x)}{x}=1. \]
(a) Prove that the sequence  $(x_n)_{n \ge 1}$  defined by
\[ x_n=f \left(\frac{1}{1} \right)+f \left(\frac{1}{2} \right)+\cdots+f \left(\frac{1}{n} \right)-\int_1^n f \left(\frac{1}{x} \right) \mathrm dx \]
is convergent.
(b) Find the limit of the sequence  $(y_n)_{n \ge 1}$  defined by
\[ y_n=f \left(\frac{1}{n+1} \right)+f \left(\frac{1}{n+2} \right)+\cdots+f \left(\frac{1}{2021n} \right). \]
solution_md:
1) we can take the ideas related to Euler-Mascheroni constant.

note that if  $f$  is continuos strictly increasing,  $f(1/x)$  is strictly decreasing, and for the condition above, we conclude that  $f(1/x)\sim 1/x$  when  $x$  is large.

Using Riemann sum is easy to show that  $\int_1^n f(1/x)dx<\sum_{k=1}^n f(1/k)-f(1/n)$ , that means  $f(1/n)<x_n$ . Also, as  $f(x)/x \to 0$  when  $x \to 0^+$  this implies that  $f(0)=0$  (this is because  $f$  is a continuous function and for given  $\epsilon>0$ , for  $x$  sufficiently small  $f(x)\leq (1+\epsilon)x$ ), hence  $0<f(1/n)<x_n$  due to monotony. Also, as  $f(1)$  is well defined, again by Riemman sums,  $\int_1^n f(1/x)dx>\sum_{k=1}^n f(1/k)-f(1)$ , so  $x_n<f(1)$ , being the sequence bounded.

only rest to prove that if is monotonic. 

note that  $x_{n+1}=\sum_{k=1}^n f(1/k)+f(1/(n+1))-\int_1^n f(1/n)dx-\int_{n}^{n+1} f(1/x)dx=x_n+f(1/(n+1))-\int_{n}^{n+1}f(1/x)dx$ But  $f(1/(n+1))<f(1/x)<f(1/n)$  in  $x \in [n,n+1]$  so  $f(1/(n+1))<\int_{n}^{n+1}f(1/x)dx<f(1/n)$ , implying  $f(1/n+1)-\int_{n}^{n+1}f(1/x)dx<0$ , so  $x_{n+1}<x_n$  and hence the sequence is strictly decreasing. 

Due to the monotonic sequence theorem, being bounded and strictly decreasing, means that  $x_n$  is a convergent sequence (a very functional one)
Note that if  $f(x)=x$ , leads to the sequence that converges to the Euler-Mascheroni constant  $\gamma=0.57721yadahyadahyadah...$ 2). Write  $y_n$  as: $y_n=\sum_{k=1}^{2021n} f(1/k)-\sum_{k=1}^n f(1/k)=x_{2021n}-x_n+\int_1^{2021 n}f(1/x)dx-\int_1^nf(1/x)dx=x_{2021n}-x_n+\int_n^{2021 n}f(1/x)dx $ note that  $\int_n^{2021 n}f(1/x)dx=\int_1^{2021} nf(1/nu)du$ By noting that  $f(1/x)\sim 1/x$  for  $x$  sufficiently large, this means that  $nf(1/nu)\sim 1/u$  when  $n$  is sufficiently large. in fact, for each  $\epsilon>0$  we have that  $(1-\epsilon)/u<nf(1/nu)<(1+\epsilon)/u$ , that means, for n sufficiently large: $(1-\epsilon)\ln 2021<\int_1^{2021} nf(1/nu)du<(1+\epsilon) \ln 2021$ Tending  $n \to \infty$  (implying that the liminf and limsup are bounded by  $(1\pm epsilon)\ln 2021$ , and then  $\epsilon \to 0$  we conclude that  $\lim_{n \to \infty}\int_1^{2021} nf(1/nu)du=\ln 2021$ So, by using a):  $\lim_{n \to \infty} y_n=\lim_{n \to \infty} x_{2021n}-x_n+\lim_{n \to \infty}\lim_{n \to \infty}\int_1^{2021} nf(1/nu)du=0+\ln 2021=\ln 2021$ Regards
Claudio.

stem_md: Let  $n \ge 2$  be a positive integer and let  $A \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$  be a matrix such that  $A^2=-I_n$ . If  $B \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$  and  $AB = BA$ , prove that  $\det B \ge 0$ .
solution_md:
Since  $A$  is real and admits only the eigenvalues  $\pm i$ ,  $n$  is even.
Suppose that  $B$  has a real eigenvalue  $b$ ; then  $Z=\ker((B-bI_n)^n)$  is an  $A$ -invariant real subspace.
Since  $A_{|Z}$  is real and admits only the eigenvalues  $\pm i$ ,  $dim(Z)$  is even, that is, the multiplicity of  $b$  is even. Done.  $\square$

Since the complex roots come in pairs in  $p_A(x)$ ,  $n=2k$  must be even and   $$ A\sim \text{diag}[iI_k,-iI_k]\sim\begin{pmatrix} O_k & I_k -I_k & O_k\end{pmatrix}=T. $$   We can let  $P\in GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ , and  $C\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$  such that  $A=PTP^{-1}$  and  $B=PCP^{-1}$ . As a block matrix,  $C=\begin{pmatrix} X & Y Z & W\end{pmatrix}$  with  $X,Y,Z,W\in\mathcal{M}_k(\mathbb{R})$ . The comutativity condition translates to  $CT=TC$ , which is equivalent to   $$ \begin{pmatrix} O_k & I_k -I_k & O_k\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} X & Y Z & W\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix} X & Y Z & W\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} O_k & I_k -I_k & O_k\end{pmatrix}\iff X=W\text{ and }Y=-Z. $$   But now   $$ \det(B) = \begin{vmatrix} X & Y -Y & X\end{vmatrix} = \det(X^2+Y^2)=\det(X+iY)\det(X-iY)=|\det(X+iY)|^2\geq 0. $$

Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer and let $A \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$ be a matrix such that $A^2=-I_n$ . If $B \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$ and $AB = BA$ , prove that $\det B \ge 0$ .
Let $p(x) = x^2 + 1$ . Then $p(A) = 0$ . Now, note that the characteristic polynomial of $A$ is a polynomial $f(x) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ and therefore minimal polynomial $m(x)$ must divide $\gcd(f(x), p(x)) \in \mathbb{R}[x]$ and this implies $m(x) = x^2 + 1$ as well. This implies that minimal polynomial of $A$ is $p(x) = x^2 + 1$ and hence $A$ is diagonalizable. Therefore, $A = XDX^{-1}$ where \[ D = \begin{pmatrix} i I_m &0 0 &-I_m \end{pmatrix} \] Now, the main idea is we want to find a matrix $E \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ that is similar to $D$ , as $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ will be one of the core hypothesis given here. Indeed, we could check that the matrix \[ E = \begin{pmatrix} 0 &I_m -I_m &0 \end{pmatrix} \] is similar to $D$ , as $E^2 + I = 0$ . Therefore, $A$ and $E$ are similar, and hence there exists $X \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ such that $A = XEX^{-1}$ . Now, write $B = XFX^{-1}$ for some $F \in M_n(\mathbb{R})$ . Then hypothesis implies $EF = FE$ . It suffices to prove that $\det(F) \ge 0$ and we will be done since $\det(B) = \det(F) \ge 0$ . Now, write $F = \begin{pmatrix} P &Q R &S \end{pmatrix}$ , where $P,Q,R,S \in \mathcal{M}_{m}(\mathbb{R})$ We then have \[ \begin{pmatrix} R &S -P &-Q \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 &I_m -I_m &0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} P &Q R &S \end{pmatrix} = EF = FE = \begin{pmatrix} P &Q R &S \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} 0 &I_m -I_m &0 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} -Q &P -S &R \end{pmatrix} \] Thus, we conclude that $P = S$ and $Q = -R$ . To finish this, it suffices to prove that if $P,Q \in \mathcal{M}_m(\mathbb{R})$ , then \[ \det \begin{pmatrix} P &Q -Q &P \end{pmatrix} = \det \begin{pmatrix} P - iQ &Q + iP -Q &P \end{pmatrix} = \det \begin{pmatrix} P - iQ &0 -Q &P + iQ \end{pmatrix} = \det(P - iQ)\det(P + iQ) = |\det(P + iQ)|^2 \ge 0 \]**Motivational Remark.** The motivation of taking the matrix $E$ is basically a trial-and-error process: I instead just continue with matrix $D$ , and somehow I got $DL = LD$ , where $L \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$ by doing a similar trick, but it's easy to construct a counterexample so. Therefore, I realized that the hypothesis $\mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{R})$ hasn't been used anywhere and therefore it would be best to preserve this condition by choosing a similar matrix to $D$ that is still nice to work with.

stem_md:
Let  $A \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$  be a matrix such that  $(AA^*)^2=A^*A$ , where  $A^*=(\bar{A})^t$  denotes the Hermitian transpose (i.e., the conjugate transpose) of  $A$ .
(a) Prove that  $AA^*=A^*A$ .
(b) Show that the non-zero eigenvalues of  $A$  have modulus one.
solution_md:
Let $A \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$ be a matrix such that $(AA^{\ast})^2=A^{\ast}A$ , where $A^{\ast}=(\overline{A})^t$ denotes the Hermitian transpose (i.e., the conjugate transpose) of $A$ . (a) Prove that $AA^{\ast}=A^{\ast}A$ . (b) Show that the non-zero eigenvalues of $A$ have modulus one.
This is a really nice practice for Special Matrices.**Claim 01.** For any matrix $X$ , $XX^{\ast}$ is a Hermitian matrix, and all of its eigenvalues are non-negative real numbers. *Proof.* Indeed, it is Hermitian since $(XX^{\ast})^{\ast} = (X^{\ast})^{\ast} X^{\ast} = XX^{\ast}$ . Now, let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $XX^{\ast}$ , then for some nonzero $v$ , we have \[ \lambda ||v||^2 = \langle \lambda v, v \rangle = \langle XX^{\ast}v, v \rangle = \langle X^{\ast} v, X^{\ast} v \rangle \ge 0 \implies \lambda \ge 0 \] -----------------**Claim 02.** Hermitian matrices are unitarily diagonalizable. *Proof.* Let $A$ be a Hermitian matrix and $L_A$ be its corresponding linear operator. As $L_A$ is Hermitian, there exists an orthonormal basis $\beta$ of $\mathbb{C}^n$ consisting of eigenvectors of $L_A$ . Thus, $[L_A]_{\beta}$ is diagonal. This implies $A = Q^{-1}[L_A]_{\beta}Q$ for some unitary matrix $Q$ , and thus, $A = Q^{\ast} [L_A]_{\beta} Q$ , as desired. ----------- Now, take any $\lambda \in \sigma(AA^{\ast})$ . By our claim, $\lambda \ge 0$ . Furthermore, we have \[ \lambda \in \sigma(AA^{\ast}) \stackrel{\text{Spectral Theorem}}{\implies} \lambda^2 \in \sigma((AA^{\ast})^2) = \sigma(A^{\ast}A) = \sigma(AA^{\ast}) \] Therefore, this implies that $\lambda \in \sigma(AA^{\ast}) \implies \lambda^{2^{n}} \in \sigma(AA^{\ast})$ for any $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . This implies $\lambda \ge 0$ is a root of $x^{2^{n}} - x$ for some $n \in \mathbb{N}$ . Thus, we have $\lambda \in \{ 0, 1 \}$ . Now, as $AA^{\ast}$ is Hermitian and any eigenvalues of $AA^{\ast}$ has to be either $0$ or $1$ , by our second claim, there exists unitary matrix $U$ such that \[ AA^{\ast} = U^{\ast} \begin{pmatrix} I_{k \times k} &O_{k \times n - k} O_{n - k \times k} &O_{n - k \times n - k} \end{pmatrix} U \] Therefore, we have \[ A^{\ast} A \stackrel{\text{Hypothesis}}{=} (AA^{\ast})^2 = U^{\ast} \begin{pmatrix} I_{k \times k} &O_{k \times n - k} O_{n - k \times k} &O_{n - k \times n - k} \end{pmatrix}^2 U = U^{\ast} \begin{pmatrix} I_{k \times k} &O_{k \times n - k} O_{n - k \times k} &O_{n - k \times n - k} \end{pmatrix} U = AA^{\ast} \] Now, as $A^{\ast} A = A A^{\ast}$ , then $A$ is normal, i.e. there exists a diagonal matrix $D$ and unitary matrix $V$ such that $A = V^{\ast} D V$ . We then have $A^{\ast} = (V^{\ast} DV)^{\ast} = V^{\ast} D^{\ast} V$ . From the problem's hypothesis we have \[ V^{\ast}(DD^{\ast})^2 V = (AA^{\ast})^2 = A^{\ast} A = V^{\ast}D^{\ast}D V \implies (DD^{\ast})^2 = D^{\ast} D\] Now, let $\alpha$ be any non-zero eigenvalue of $A$ . Then the condition above gives us $|\alpha|^4 = |\alpha|^2 \implies |\alpha| = 1$ , as desired.

For  $p \in \mathbb{R}$ , let  $(a_n)_{n \ge 1}$  be the sequence defined by
\[ a_n=\frac{1}{n^p} \int_0^n |\sin( \pi x)|^x \mathrm dx. \]
Determine all possible values of  $p$  for which the series  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$  converges.
solution_md:
I've shown [here](https://ysharificalc.wordpress.com/2021/07/24/limit-of-integrals-19/) (Example 3) that   $$ \int_0^n |\sin(\pi x)|^xdx \sim 2\sqrt{\frac{2n}{\pi}}, \ \ \ \ \ \ n \to \infty. $$   
So, by the limit comparison test,  $\sum a_n$  converges if and only if  $\sum \frac{1}{n^{p-\frac{1}{2}}}$  converges, which converges if and only if  $p-\frac{1}{2} > 1.$  So the answer is all the real numbers  $p > \frac{3}{2}.$

stem_md:
Let  $A, B \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$  be such that  $AB^2A = AB$ . Prove that:
a)  $(AB)^2 = AB.$ b)  $(AB - BA)^3 = O_n.$
solution_md:
$\bullet$  Since (*)  $(AB)(BA-I)=0$ ,  $AB,BA-I$  are simultaneously triangularizable (ST), then  $AB,BA$  too; 
we may assume that they are triangular. 
 Let  $(u_i)),(v_i)$  be their diagonals.
For every  $i$ ,  $u_i(v_i-1)=0$ , that is,  $u_i=0$  or  $v_i=1$ .

Since  $spectrum(AB)=spectrum(BA)$ , for every  $i$ ,  $u_i=v_i\in \{0,1\}$ . $\bullet$  (*) implies that  $BA-I=(I-(AB)^+(AB))W$ , where  $X^+$  is the Moore-Penrose inverse of  $X$  
and  the matrix  $W$  is arbitrary. 

Note that  $P=I-(AB)^+(AB)$  is the symmetric orthogonal projector onto  $\ker(AB)$ . 
Then, up to a change of orthonormal basis, we may assume that  $P=diag(I_{n-r},0_r)$  and we put  $W=\begin{pmatrix}U_{n-r}&VC&D_r\end{pmatrix}$ . Then  $BA-I=\begin{pmatrix}U&V0&0\end{pmatrix}$  and  $BA=\begin{pmatrix}U+I&V0&I\end{pmatrix}$ .
 Note that  $rank(P)=n-r=n-rank(AB)$  and  $rank(AB)=r$ . $\bullet$  Note that the eigenvalue  $1$  of  $BA$  has multiplicity at least  $r$ ,
 and that of  $AB$  too. Then for  $AB$ , -and consequently for  $BA$ - the multiplicity of  $1$  is  $r$  and that of  $0$  is  $n-r$ .

Moreover:  $0$  is a semi-simple eigenvalue of  $AB$ , $U+I=N$  is nilpotent and, therefore,  $U$  is invertible. If  $[x,y]^T\in\ker(BA-I)$ , then  $Ux+Vy=0$ ,  $x=-U^{-1}Vy$  and  $dim(\ker(BA-I))=r$ ; finally,  $1$  is a  semi-simple eigenvalue of  $BA$  -and also of  $AB$ -. $\bullet$  Thus  $AB$  is diagonalizable and  $(AB)^2=AB$ ; beware,  $0$  is not necessarily a semi-simple eigenvalue of  $BA$ .

Up to a change of basis, we may assume that  $AB=diag(0_{n-r},I_r)$ . We find again  $P=diag(I_{n-r},0_r)$  
and the above value of  $BA=\begin{pmatrix}N&V0&I\end{pmatrix}$ .

We obtain  $(AB-BA)^3=\begin{pmatrix}-N^3&-N^2V0&0\end{pmatrix}$ .
EDIT.
According to the Flanders theorem (about the Jordan forms of  $AB$  and  $BA$ ), cf.
[ see here ](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0024379568900475)
one has  $dim(\ker(BA)^2)=n-r$ . Note that  $(BA)^2[x,y]^T=0$  iff  $N^2x=0,y=0$ ;
 then  $N^2=0$  and we are done.  $\square$

candidates: Does this problem have a normal solution? (E.g. just matrix multiplication manipulations and no heavy theory.)
Nice solution

Let's call  $f=AB$ ,  $g=BA$ , and note that  $f$  and  $g$  have the same characteristic polynomial  $p(x)$ .

We have  $fg^k=f$  for all  $k$ , so the generalized eigenspace for  $g$  relative to 0,  $V'_0(g)=\ker( g^n)$  is containded in  $\ker (f)\subset V'_0(f)$ .
But the dimension of  $V'_0(g)$  and  $V'_0(f)$  are both equal to the multiplicity of 0 as root of  $p$ , hence $V'_0(g)=\ker(f)=V'_0(f)$ , and we have that if 0 is an eigenvalue of  $f$ , then it is a semisimple eigenvalue.

Moreover we have, for  $\lambda\in\mathbb{C}$ ,  $f(g-\lambda id)^k=(1-\lambda)^kf$  for all  $k$ , so for all generalizad eigenspaces with  $\lambda\neq1$ ,
  $V'_\lambda(g)\subset\ker(f)=V'_0(g)$ .
But generalized eigenspaces form a direct sum, this means that  $Spec(g)\subset\{0,1\}$ , so  $p(x)=x^h(x-1)^{n-h}$  for some  $h$  (and  $Spec(f)\subset\{0,1\}$  too). We also have  $\mathbb{C}^n=V'_0(g)\oplus V'_1(g)$ .

Suppose now that 1 is a non-semisimple eigenvalue for  $g$ . Than there exist  $v,w\in\mathbb{C}^n$  linearly independent such that  $g(v)=v+w$ ,  $g(w)=w$  (the first two vectors of a Jordan block of order >1 for  $g$  relative to the eigenvalue 1). Then  $f(v)=f(v)+f(w)$  implies  $w\in\ker(f)=V'_0(g)$ , which is impossible.
So, if 1 is an eigenvalue of  $g$ , then it is a semisimple eigenvalue.

Note that  $A$  sends  $\ker(BA-I)$  injectively into  $\ker(AB-I)$  ( $BAv=v$   $\Rightarrow$   $AB(Av)=Av$ ), so  $\dim(V'_1(g))=\dim(\ker(g-id))\leq\dim(\ker(f-id))\leq\dim(V'_1(f)$ , and again the generalized eigenspaces have both dimension  $n-h$ , so
if 1 is an eigenvalue of  $f$ , then it is a semisimple eigenvalue.

We now have that the minimal polynomial of  $f$  divides  $x(x-1)$ , that is,  $f^2=f$ .

Moreover, if  $v\in\ker (BA)^3$ ,  $BABABAv=0$ ,  then  $(AB)^3(Av)=0$ , i.e.  $Av\in\ker(f^3)=\ker(f)$ , thus  $ABAv=0$ , so  $v\in\ker(BA)^2$ .
This means that  $V'_0(g)=\ker(g^2)$ , so that  the minimal polynomial of  $g$  divides  $x^2(x-1)$ , that is,  $g^3=g^2$ .

Take now a Jordan basis for  $g$  for which the Jordan matrix has the form  $\begin{pmatrix}C&0_{n-h}0_h&I\end{pmatrix}$  with  $C^2=0$ .
In the same basis,  $f$  has  a matrix of the form  $\begin{pmatrix}0_h&D0_h&E\end{pmatrix}$  with  $DE=D$  and  $E^2=E$ .

Note that the characteristic polynomial of  $E$  is  $(x-1)^{n-k}$ , so  $E$  is invertible and  $E=I$ Then  $f-g$  has matrix  $M=\begin{pmatrix}-C&D0&0\end{pmatrix}$ , and so  $M^2=\begin{pmatrix}C^2&-CD0&0\end{pmatrix}$  and  $M^3=\begin{pmatrix}-C^3&C^2D0&0\end{pmatrix}=0$  and we have  $(AB-BA)^3=0$ .

Note that we can conclude without using a Jordan basis: $(f-g)^2=f^2-fg-gf+g^2=g^2-gf$ , $(f-g)^3=fg^2-fgf-g^3+g^2f=f-f^2-g^2+g^2f=g^2(id-f)$ and we have  $\text{Ima}(id-f)=\ker (f)=\ker (g^2)$ .

And we can't do better than  $(AB-BA)^3=0$ . cf. this solution where  $(AB-BA)^2\not= 0$ . $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&a0&0&00&0&u\end{pmatrix}$ , $B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&c0&0&d0&0&1/u\end{pmatrix}$ , where  $d$ , $u$  are non-zero.

There are several sufficient conditions for two matrices  $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb{C})$   to be simultaneously triangularizable. For example:
i)  $AB=BA$ .
ii)  $AB=0$ .
iii)  $rank(AB-BA)\leq 1$ .
iv)  $AB-BA=aA+bB$ .
v) McCoy theorem.
These results and many others are exposed in the first part of the bible: "simultaneous triangularization" by Radjavi, Rosenthal.

Official solution The given condition is written as follows: \[AB(BA-I_{n})=O_{n}.\] We use Sylvester's inequality for ranks. It is: \[0 = \text{rank}(AB(BA-I_{n})) \geq \text{rank}(AB) + \text{rank}(BA-I_{n}) - n = \text{rank}(AB) + \text{rank}(AB-I_{n}) - n\] from the known Lemma (Summand). We also have: \[\text{Null}(AB-I_{n}) \subseteq \text{Im}(AB),\] since \(X \in \text{Null}(AB-I_{n}) \implies (AB-I_{n})X=O_{n} \implies ABX=X \implies X \in \text{Im}(AB),\) so the equality case holds for Sylvester. \[\text{rank}(AB-I_{n}) + \text{rank}(AB) - n = \text{rank}((AB-I_{n})AB) \leq 0 \implies \text{rank}(AB(AB-I_{n})) = 0 \implies (AB-I_{n})AB=O_{n},\] which was the required result. Regarding part (β): \[(AB-BA)^{2} = (AB-BA)(AB-BA) = (AB)^{2} - AB^{2}A - BA^{2}B + (BA)^{2} = AB - AB^{2}A - BA^{2}B + (BA)^{2} = -BA(AB-BA),\] \[(AB-BA)^{3} = -BA(AB-BA)^{2} = (BA)^{2}(AB-BA),\] \[(AB-BA)^{4} = (BA)^{2}(AB-BA)^{2} = -(BA)^{3}(AB-BA) = -B(AB)^{2}A(AB-BA) = -(BA)^{2}(AB-BA) = -(AB-BA)^{3}.\] If \(m_{AB-BA}(x)\) is the minimal polynomial of \(AB-BA\), then obviously \(m_{AB-BA}(x) \vert x^{4}+x^{3}\), so \(AB-BA\) has possible eigenvalues 0, -1. However, \(\text{Tr}(AB-BA)=0\), so \(AB-BA\) cannot have eigenvalue -1, since it would then have negative trace. Therefore, \(m_{AB-BA}(x)=x^{k}\), \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\), and the known equality \(m_{AB-BA}(AB-BA)=O_{n}\) gives us the desired result.

stem_md: Let  $a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}$  be such that  $$ a + b + c = a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1, \hspace{8px} a^3 + b^3 + c^3 \neq 1. $$  We say that a function  $f$  is a *Palić function* if  $f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ ,  $f$  is continuous and satisfies  $$ f(x) + f(y) + f(z) = f(ax + by + cz) + f(bx + cy + az) + f(cx + ay + bz) $$  for all  $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}.$ Prove that any Palić function is infinitely many times differentiable and find all Palić functions.
solution_md:
Let  $F'=f$  with  $F(0)=0$ . Integrating the relation in the hypothesis from  $0$  to  $1$  with respect to  $x$ , we get  $F(1)+f(y)+f(z)=\left(\frac{F(ax+by+cz)}{a}+\frac{F(bx+cy+az)}{b}+\frac{F(cx+ay+bz)}{c} \right)\bigg\rvert_{0}^{1}$ . If we keep  $z$  fixed, and treat  $y$  as a variable, we infer that  $f$  is differentiable. Now, differentiate the relation in the hypothesis by  $x$ ,  $y$ , and finally by  $z$  to get $f'(x)=af'(ax+by+cz)+bf'(bx+cy+az)+cf'(cx+ay+bz)$ (1) $f'(y)=bf'(ax+by+cz)+cf'(bx+cy+az)+af'(cx+ay+bz)$  $f'(z)=cf'(ax+by+cz)+af'(bx+cy+az)+bf'(cx+ay+bz)$ Add them up to infer that  $f'$  verifies the same condition as  $f$ . By induction,  $f$  is infinitely differentiable.
Now, differentiate  $(1)$  with respect to  $y$ , and get  $0=abf''(ax+by+cz)+bcf''(bx+cy+az)+caf''(cx+ay+bz)$ . Differentiate this further with respect to  $x$ , and set  $x=y=z$  to finally obtain  $0=abcf'''(x)$ . If  $abc=0$  then  $a^3+b^3+c^3=3abc+(a+b+c)(a^2+b^2+c^2-ab-bc-ca)=1$ , contradiction.
Thus  $f'''(x)=0$ , and so  $f$  is a quadratic function, and conversly any quadratic works.

stem_md: Let  $\alpha \in \mathbb{C}\setminus \{0\}$  and  $A \in \mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})$ ,  $A \neq O_n$ , be such that  $$ A^2 + (A^*)^2 = \alpha A\cdot A^*, $$  where  $A^* = (\bar A)^T.$  Prove that  $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ ,  $|\alpha| \le 2$ . and  $A\cdot A^* = A^*\cdot A.$
solution_md:
A partial solution. $\textbf{Part 1.}$  $\bullet$   $AA^*$  is hermitian  $\geq 0$  and has  $\geq 0$  eigenvalues. Since  $A\not=0$ ,  $AA^*\not= 0$  and has a  $>0$  eigenvalue  $\lambda$ . $A^2+(A^*)^2$  is hermitian and has real eigenvalues, for example  $\alpha\lambda$ . Since  $\alpha\not=0$ ,  $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^*$ .  $2Re(tr(A^2))=\alpha tr(AA^*)\not= 0$ ; then  $A^2$  is not nilpotent and neither is  $A$ . $\bullet$  Let  $u\in spectrum(A)$ . Up to an orthonormal change of basis, we may assume that  $A=[a_{i,j}]$  is upper-triangular with  $a_{n,n}=u$ .
Considering the  $(n,n)$  entry of  $A^2+(A^*)^2-\alpha AA^*$ , we obtain $u^2+\bar{u}^2-\alpha u\bar{u}=0$ .
 Putting  $u=a+ib$  with real  $a,b$ , we deduce that  $(2-\alpha)a^2=(2+\alpha)b^2$ . 
We can choose  $u\not= 0$  -cf. above-; then necessarily  $\alpha\in [-2,2]$ . We put  $\alpha=2\cos(\theta)$  where  $\theta\in [0,\pi]$ .
Now  $u$  is any eigenvalue of  $A$ . Note that if  $A$  is a solution, then  $\lambda A$  too, where  $\lambda\in \mathbb{R}^*$ .
If  $\alpha=2$ , then the eigenvalues of  $A$  are real.
If  $\alpha\not=2$ , then, up to a real factor,  $(a,b)=(\pm \sqrt{2+\alpha},\pm \sqrt{2-\alpha})=2(\pm \cos(\theta/2),\pm\sin(\theta/2))$ .
Finally,  $u=0$  or  $u=\lambda e^{\pm i\theta/2}$ . $\bullet$  Putting  $A=iB$ , we obtain  $B^2+(B^*)^2=-\alpha BB^*$ . Then we may assume that  $\alpha \in (0,2]$  and we put  $\alpha=2\cos(\theta)$ , where  $\theta\in [0,\pi/2)$ .
Then  $e^{2i\theta}\not= 1$  except when  $\alpha =2$ . $\textbf{Part 2.}$  Let  $U=A-A^*e^{i\theta},V=A^*-Ae^{i\theta}$ . Then  $UV=e^{2i\theta}(A^*A-AA^*),VU=A^*A-AA^*$  and  $UV=VUe^{2i\theta}$ . $\textbf{Hypothesis.}$  We assume that  $e^{2i\theta}$  is not a root of unity (that is,  $\theta\not= k\pi/n$ ).

Then, by a result due to Drazin,  $U,V$  are simultaneously triangularizable and, consequently,  $A,A^*$  too.

Thus  $A^*A-AA^*$  is a nilpotent hermitian matrix, then a nilpotent diagonalizable matrix and  $AA^*=A^*A$ . $\textbf{Remark.}$  It remains to study the case when  $\theta =k\pi/n$ .
Note that when  $\theta=0$ , we consider a matrix equation in the form  $A^2+B^2=2AB$ . It's well-known that  $A,B$  are simult. triang. and we finish the proof as above.

Official solution Firstly, let \( a \) be real since we want the Adjunct Member to be Hermitian. Now onto the rest of the problem. First, we will show: \[ \ker(A) = \ker(A^*) = \ker(A^2) = \ker((A^*)^2) \] Indeed: 1. If \( A^2v = 0 \), then multiplying the given equation by \( v \) from the right and \( v^* \) from the left, we obtain: \[ 0 = v^*A^2v + v^*(A^*)^2v = \alpha v^*AA^*v = (A^*v)^*A^*v \] so \( A^*v = 0 \). 2. Similarly, if \( (A^*)^2 = 0 \). 3. If \( A^*v = 0 \), simply multiplying by \( v \) from the right yields \( A^2v = 0 \). In summary: \[ \ker(A) \subseteq \ker(A^2), \ker((A^*)^2) \subseteq \ker(A^*) \subseteq \ker(A^2), \ker((A^*)^2) \] Since now \( n(A) = n(A^*) \) and \( n(A^2) = n((A^*)^2) \), equality must hold in all of the above inclusions. So, working in \( (\ker A)^\perp \) (non-empty since \( A \) is non-zero), we can assume without loss of generality that \( A \) is invertible. Let \( B = A^{-1}A^* \). The given, after multiplying by \( A^{-1} \) from the left and \( (A^*)^{-1} \) from the right, is written as: \[ B^* + B = \alpha I \] Thus, \( B \) is normal, meaning it's unitarily diagonalizable. Finally, we'll show that \( B \) is orthogonal. If \( \lambda \) is an eigenvalue of \( B \) with corresponding eigenvector \( v \), then \( Bv = \lambda v \) implies \( A^*v = \lambda Av \), thus: \[ A^2v + \lambda^2A^2v = \lambda \alpha A^2v \] which, since \( A^2 \) is invertible, gives the relation: \[ \lambda^2 + 1 = \alpha \lambda \] So, \( |\lambda| = 1 \), \( \lambda + \frac{1}{\lambda} = \alpha \). Therefore: \( \alpha \) is real, \( |\alpha| \leq 2 \), and \( B \) has eigenvalues \( \lambda \) and \( \frac{1}{\lambda} \) with some multiplicities. So, \( B \) is orthogonal (unitarily diagonalizable + eigenvalues on the unit circle). Thus, we have \( BB^* = I \), hence: \[ A^{-1}A^*AA^* = I \] which gives: \[ A^*A = AA^* \] (the desired result). The inequality \( |\alpha| \leq 2 \) can be shown independently, for example, using the inequality \( |tr(A^2+(A^*)^2)| \leq 2tr(AA^*) \).

stem_md: Let  $\mathcal{F}$  be the family of all nonempty finite subsets of  $\mathbb{N} \cup \{0\}.$  Find all real numbers  $a$  for which the series  $$ \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{\sum_{k \in A}a^k} $$  is convergent.
solution_md: Very neat problem! (By the way, the original formulation asks for  $a>0$  only.) The case  $a\leq 1$  is clear, as  $\sum_{A\in \mathcal{F}}\frac{1}{|A|} > \sum_{i=1}^{\infty} 1$  diverges; let  $a>1$ . Denote by  $S_n$  the partial sum running through the subsets whose elements do not exceed  $n$ . Then  $S_n = S_{n-1} + \sum_{A\subseteq \{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}}\frac{1}{a^n + \sum_{k\in A}a^k}$  where the latter  $\sum$  consists of  $2^n$  summands, each not exceeding  $\frac{1}{a^n}$  and being at least  $\frac{1}{\sum_{k=0}^n a^k} = \frac{a-1}{a^{n+1} - 1}$ . In particular,  $S_n \leq \sum_{j=0}^n \left(\frac{2}{a}\right)^j$  and the latter converges for  $a>2$ . Also,  $S_n \geq (a-1)\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{2^n}{a^{n+1} - 1} \geq \frac{a-1}{4}\sum_{j=0}^n  \left(\frac{2}{a}\right)^{n+1} \geq \frac{a-1}{4}n \to \infty$  for  $a\leq 2$   and hence  $S_n$  diverges in this case.

Official solution Αn important note is that the problem should state non-empty subsets, as otherwise the sum is not defined. We will show that it converges if and only if \( a > 2 \). It's obvious that it diverges for \( a \leqslant 1 \) since it's a sum of positive terms among which are \( 1, \frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{a^2}, \ldots \). Thus, we can assume \( a > 1 \). Then, for every finite \( A \) we have: \[ a^{\max{A}} \leqslant \sum_{k \in A} a^k \leqslant |A|a^{\max{A}} \] There are exactly \( 2^n \) subsets \( A \) with \( \max{A} = n \) since we can independently decide for each of \( 0,1,2,\ldots,n-1 \) whether they belong to \( A \) or not. Hence, \[ \sum\limits_{A\in\mathcal{F}}\dfrac{1}{\sum\limits_{k\in A}a^k} \leqslant \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{a^{\max{A}}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{2^n}{a^n} \] which shows convergence for \( a > 2 \). Moreover, there are exactly \( \binom{n}{k} \) subsets \( A \) of size \( k+1 \) with \( \max{A} = n \). Therefore, \[ \sum\limits_{A\in\mathcal{F}}\dfrac{1}{\sum\limits_{k\in A}a^k} \geqslant \sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \frac{1}{|A|a^{\max{A}}} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a^n}\sum_{k=0}^{n} \frac{\binom{n}{k}}{k+1} \] Writing \[ f(x) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} x^k = (1+x)^n \] we have \[ \int_{0}^{1} f(x)\,\mathrm{d}x = \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k} \frac{1}{k+1} = \frac{2^{n+1}-1}{n+1} \geqslant \frac{2^n}{n+1} \] So, \[ \sum\limits_{A\in\mathcal{F}}\dfrac{1}{\sum\limits_{k\in A}a^k} \geqslant \frac{2^n}{(n+1)a^n} \] which diverges for \( a \leqslant 2 \) (from the comparison test for \( a < 2 \) and from the harmonic series for \( a = 2 \)).

We start by showing the easy implication. $\Leftarrow)$  We have :  $$ (A + B)^3 = (A + B)(A + B)(A + B) $$    $$  = A^3 + A^2B + ABA + AB^2 + BA^2 + BAB + BA^2 + B^3 $$  By using the hypothesis, we get:   $$ (A + B)^3 = A^3 + B^3 + BA^2 + B^2A $$  Since  $AB = 0_{n}$  and  $A, B$  are symmetric matrices, we get:   $$ (AB)^t = BA = 0_{n} $$  Hence, we get the desired result.

Now, we go to the other implication. $\Rightarrow)$  $\textbf{Claim 1:}$    $tr(ABA) + tr(BAB) = 0$   $\textbf{Proof:}$ We have  $(A + B)^3 = A^3 + B^3$ , then:   $$ A^2B + ABA + AB^2 + BA^2 + BAB + B^2A = 0_{n} $$   $\Rightarrow$    $$ tr(A^2B + ABA + AB^2 + BA^2 + BAB + B^2A) = 0 $$  As the trace of a matrix is a linear operator, and by using the property that it's invariant under cyclic permutation, we get:   $$ tr(ABA) = - tr(BAB)\;\;\cdots (\ast) $$  Thus, our claim  $1$  is proved. $\textbf{Claim 2:}$  All eigenvalues of  $BAB$  and  $ABA$  are nonnegative. $\textbf{Proof:}$   Since  $A$  and  $B$  are symmetric, then the matrices  $ABA$  and  $BAB$  are also symmetric.
Let  $\lambda$  be an eigenvalue of  $BAB$ , and let  $v$  be the associated eigenvector, we have:
   $$ \lambda<v, v>\;=\; < \lambda v, v >\; = \;< BAB v, v >\; =\;<ABv, Bv>\; =\; (Bv)^tA(Bv)\;\;\cdots (\ast \ast)  $$  (This is just because  $BAB, A$  and  $B$  are symmetric).
As  $A$  is symmetric and all eigenvalues are nonnegative, then  $A$  is positive semi-definite and we get:   $$ (Bv)^tA(Bv) \ge 0 $$  Hence, from  $(\ast \ast )$  we get:   $$ \lambda<v, v>\;=\;(Bv)^tA(Bv) \ge 0 $$  which implies directly that:  $\lambda \ge 0$ as desired.
Similarly, we can prove that the eigenvalues of  $ABA$  are nonnegative. stem_md:
For every  $n\geq 1$  define  $x_n$  by   $$ x_n=\int_0^1 \ln(1+x+x^2+\dots +x^n)\cdot\ln\frac{1}{1-x}\mathrm dx. $$  a) Show that  $x_n$  is finite for every  $n\geq 1$  and  $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}x_n=2$ .
b) Calculate  $\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\frac{n}{\ln n}(2-x_n)$ .
solution_md:
Nice problem!  $$ I(n)=\int_0^1 \ln(1+x+x^2+\dots +x^n)\cdot\ln\frac{1}{1-x}dx=\int_0^1\ln\frac{1-x^{n+1}}{1-x}\ln\frac1{1-x}dx=I_1+I_2 $$  where  $$ I_1=\int_0^1\ln^2(1-x)dx=2\quad(1) $$  Denoting for a while  $n+1=m$   $$ I_2=-\int_0^1\ln(1-x)\ln(1-x^m)dx\overset{x^m=t}{=}-\frac1m\int_0^1\ln(1-t^{\frac1m})\ln(1-t)t^{\frac1m-1}dt\overset{t=e^{-x}}{=}-\frac1m\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\ln(1-e^{-\frac xm})dx $$    $$ =-\frac1m\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\ln\frac{1-e^{-\frac xm}}{\frac xm}dx-\frac1m\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\ln\frac xm\,dx $$  The function  $\,f(t)=\Big|e^{-t}\ln\frac{1-e^{-t}}t\Big|$  is zeto at  $\,t=0;\infty$  and reaches its maximum at some point  $\,t=t_0;\,t_0\in(0;\infty)$ . Denoting  $\,\max f(t)=C$ , the first integral is dominated by the integrable on  $[0;\infty)$  function  $$ \Big|\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\ln\frac{1-e^{-\frac xm}}{\frac xm}\Big|<-C\ln(1-e^{-x})  $$  Based on the dominated convergence theorem we are taking the limit under the integral sign:  $$ \lim_{m\to\infty}\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\ln\frac{1-e^{-\frac xm}}{\frac xm}dx=\int_0^\infty \left(\lim_{m\to\infty}e^{-\frac xm}\ln\frac{1-e^{-\frac xm}}{\frac xm}\right)\ln(1-e^{-x})dx=0 $$  It means that  $$ I_2=-\frac1m\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})e^{-\frac xm}\big(\ln x-\ln m\big)dx+o(1/m)=\frac{\ln m}m\int_0^\infty\ln(1-e^{-x})dx-\frac1m\int_0^\infty \ln x\ln(1-e^{-x})dx+o(1/m) $$  Integrating by parts, we finally get  $$ I_2=-\frac{\pi^2}6\,\frac{\ln m}m+\Big(\zeta'(2)-\frac{\pi^2}6\gamma\Big)\frac1m+o(1/m)\qquad(2) $$  Coming back to  $\,m=n+1$ ,  our initial integral has the following asymptotics at  $n\to\infty$   $$ \boxed{\,\,I=2-\frac{\pi^2}6\,\frac{\ln n}{n}+\Big(\zeta'(2)-\frac{\pi^2}6\gamma\Big)\frac1{n}+O\Big(\frac{\ln n}{n^2}\Big)\,\,} $$  Numeric check (WA) confirms the answer.
The limit follows.

stem_md: Let  $n\in\mathbb{N}$ ,  $n\geq 2$ . Find all values of  $k\in\mathbb{N}$ ,  $k\geq 1$ , for which the following statement holds:   $$ \text{"If }A\in\mathcal{M}_n(\mathbb{C})\text{ is such that }A^kA^*=A\text{, then }A=A^*\text{."} $$   (here,  $A^*$  denotes the conjugate transpose of  $A$ ).
solution_md:
$\textbf{Proposition.}$  The statement holds only for  $k=1,3,4$ . $\textbf{Proof.}$  According to @Tim23, since  $dim(\ker(A))=dim(\ker(A^*))$ , we deduce that  $\ker(A)=\ker(A^*)$  and  $A$  is normal
and then diagonalizable in an orthonormal basis. We may assume that  $A=diag((\lambda_i))$ ,
 where  $\lambda_i^k\overline{\lambda_i}=\lambda_i$ . Thus  $\lambda_i=0$  or  $|\lambda_i|=1$ ; in the last case,  ${\lambda_i}^{k-2}=1$ . $\bullet$   $k$  is convenient only if each possible  $\lambda_i$  is real.
If  $k=1$ , then  $A$  is an hermitian projector.
If  $k=2$ , then  $|\lambda_i|=1$  doesn't imply that  $\lambda_i$  is real.
If  $k=3$ , then  $\lambda_i=1$ . If  $k=4$ , then  $\lambda_i=\pm 1$ .
If  $k\geq 5$ , then  ${\lambda_i}^{k-2}=1$  admits non real solutions.    $\square$

stem_md: Let  $A$  be an  $n\times n$  matrix with strictly positive elements and two vectors  $u,v\in\mathbb{R}^n$ , also with strictly positive elements, such that   $$ Au=v\text{ and }Av=u. $$   Prove that  $u=v$ .
solution_md:
Note that  $A^2$  has  $>0$  entries.
One has  $A^2u=u$  and  $A^2v=v$ ; according to Perron-Frobenius theorem,  $A^2$  has only one (up to a  $>0$  factor) 
positive eigenvector; then  $u=av$  where  $a>0$ . Then  $Au=v=\dfrac{1}{a}u=aAv=au$ .
Finally,  $a^2=1$  and therefore  $a=1$ .   $\square$

stem_md: Calculate   $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}n\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x}\sqrt[n]{e^x - 1 -\frac{x}{1!} - \frac{x^2}{2!} - \dots -\frac{x^n}{n!}}\,dx. $$
solution_md: $$ e^x - 1 -\frac{x}{1!} - \frac{x^2}{2!} - \dots -\frac{x^n}{n!}=\frac{x^n}{\Gamma(n)}\sum_{k=1}^\infty\frac{\Gamma(k+1)\Gamma(n)}{\Gamma(n+1+k)}\frac{x^k}{k!}=\frac{x^n}{\Gamma(n)}\sum_{k=1}^\infty B(k+1,n)\frac{x^k}{k!} $$  Changing the order of summation/intergation  $$ =\frac{x^n}{\Gamma(n)}\sum_{k=1}^\infty \int_0^1(1-t)^{n-1}\left(\sum\frac{x^kt^k}{k!}\right)dt=\frac{x^n}{\Gamma(n)}\int_0^1\frac{e^{xt}-1}{(1-t)^{n-1}}dt $$    $$ \int_0^1\frac{e^{xt}-1}{(1-t)^{n-1}}dt<\int_0^1(e^{xt}-1)dt=\frac{e^x-x-1}x $$  Therefore, for  $n>2$   $$  n\,e^{-x}\sqrt[n]{e^x - 1 -\frac{x}{1!} - \frac{x^2}{2!} - \dots -\frac{x^n}{n!}}<\frac n{\sqrt[n]{\Gamma(n)}}e^{-x}x\left(\frac{e^x-x-1}x\right)^{\frac1n}< const\,\cdot \, e^{-x}x\left(\frac{e^x-x-1}x\right)^{\frac12} $$  - the integrand is majorised by the integrable function. Taking the pointwise limit under the integral sign  $$ \lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}n\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x}\sqrt[n]{e^x - 1 -\frac{x}{1!} - \frac{x^2}{2!} - \dots -\frac{x^n}{n!}}\,dx=\int_0^1 e^{-x}x\left(\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac n{\sqrt[n]{\Gamma(n)}}\left(\int_0^1\frac{e^{xt}-1}{(1-t)^{n-1}}dt\right)^{\frac1n}\right)dx $$    $$ =e\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x\,dx=e $$  In fact, we can proceed further and find next asymptotic terms. Using the Watson' lemma  $$ \int_0^1(1-t)^{n-1}(e^{xt}-1)dt=\frac x{n^2}\left(1+\frac{x+1}n+O\Big(\frac1{n^2}\Big)\right) $$    $$ n\int_0^{\infty} e^{-x}\sqrt[n]{e^x - 1 -\frac{x}{1!} - \frac{x^2}{2!} - \dots -\frac{x^n}{n!}}\,dx=\frac n{\sqrt[n]{n!}\sqrt[n]{n}}\int_0^\infty e^{-x}x^{1+\frac1n}\left(1+\frac{x+1}n+O\Big(\frac1{n^2}\Big)\right)^{\frac1n}dx $$    $$ =e\left(1-\frac32\frac{\ln n}n+\frac{2-2\gamma-\ln(2\pi)}{2n}+O\Big(\frac{\ln^2 n}{n^2}\Big)\right) $$  what is in a good numeric agreement already at small  $n\sim 10$

stem_md: Let  $(a_n)_{n\geq 1}$  be a monotone decreasing sequence of real numbers that converges to  $0$ . Prove that  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{a_n}{n}$  is convergent if and only if the sequence  $(a_n\ln n)_{n\geq 1}$  is bounded and  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (a_n-a_{n+1})\ln n$  is convergent.
solution_md:
With partial summation we find  $\sum_1^n {{a_k}\over k}=a_nH_n+\sum_1^{n-1}(a_k-a_{k+1})H_k$  and both terms on the RHS are  $\ge 0$ .
Hence  $\sum_1^\infty {{a_n}\over n}<\infty$  iff  $a_nH_n$  bounded and  $\sum_1^\infty (a_n-a_{n+1})H_n<\infty$ .
The result now follows from  $H_n\sim \ln n$ .

stem_md: Let  $z=z(x,y)$  be implicit function with two variables from  $2sin(x+2y-3z)=x+2y-3z$ . Find  $\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}$ .
solution_md:
Consider the mapping  $F(x,y,z(x,y)):=2\sin(x+2y-3z)-(x+2y-3z)$  and suppose that  $F(x,y,z(x,y))=0$  implicitly defines  $z$  as a continuously differentiable function of  $x$  and  $y$  (i.e.,  $F\in \mathcal{C}^{1}$  over its domain). If  $F_{z}\not=0$ , then  by the [Implicit Theorem function](https://www.math.ucla.edu/~archristian/teaching/32a-f16/implicit-function-theorem.pdf) we have that,
\[
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}=-\frac{F_{x}}{F_{z}}=-\frac{-1+2\cos(x+2y-3z)}{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)}
\]
and
\[
\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\frac{F_{y}}{F_{z}}=-\frac{-2+4\cos(x+2y-3z)}{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)}
\]
So,
\[
\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=-\left(\frac{-1+2\cos(x+2y-3z)}{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)}\right)+\left(-\frac{-2+4\cos(x+2y-3z)}{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)} \right)=\frac{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)}{3-6\cos(x+2y-3z)}=1
\]
which implies that,
\[
\color{blue}{\frac{\partial z}{\partial x}+\frac{\partial z}{\partial y}=1}
\]

stem_md: Let  $f(x)$  be a continuous function, where  $f(0)\neq0$ . Find  $\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{2\int_{0}^{x}(x-t)f(t)dt}{x\int_{0}^{x}f(x-t)dt}$ .
solution_md:
<details><summary>alternate solution to original problem</summary>Since the numerator and denominator both go to  $0$ , we use lhospital's. We need to calculate the derivative of the numerator. This is  $$ 2\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\int_0^{x+h}(x+h-t)f(t) dt-\int_0^x (x-t)f(t) dt}{h} $$    $$ =2\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\int_0^{x+h} hf(t) dt +\int_0^{x+h}(x-t)f(t) dt-\int_0^x (x-t)f(t) dt}{h} $$    $$ =2\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\int_0^{x+h} hf(t) dt+\int_x^{x+h} (x-t)f(t) dt}{h} $$    $$ =2\lim_{h\to 0}\frac{\int_0^{x+h} hf(t) dt}{h} $$    $$ =2\int_0^x f(t) dt $$  The derivative of the denominator is  $xf(x)+\int_0^x f(t)dt$ . So the limit is equal to the limit of  $$ \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{2\int_0^x f(t) dt}{xf(x)+\int_0^x f(t)dt} $$  If we look at the reciprocal of this, we have  $$ \frac{1}{2}+\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{xf(x)}{2\int_0^x f(t) dt} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{\lim_{x\to 0} f(x)}{2\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{1}{x}\int_0^x f(t)dt} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{f(0)}{2f(0)} $$    $$ =1 $$  So the original limit is also  $1$ .</details>
<details><summary>solution to raised bar</summary>Let's say we assume additionally that  $f'(0)$  exists and is not  $0$ . Continuing from calculating  $\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{xf(x)}{2\int_0^x f(t)dt}$ . We apply lhospital's  $$ \lim_{x\to 0}\frac{f(x)+xf'(x)}{2f(x)} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}+\lim_{x\to 0} \frac{xf'(x)}{f(x)} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{f'(0)}{f'(0)} $$  So now the original limit is  $\frac{1}{2}$ .</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/The Chinese Mathematics Competition/2021 The Chinese Mathematics Competition/2967458.json

stem_md:
Find the equation of cylinder that passes three straight lines $L_1=
\begin{cases}
x=0
y-z=2
\end{cases},
L_2=
\begin{cases}
x=0
x+y-z+2=0
\end{cases},
L_3=
\begin{cases}
x=\sqrt{2}
y-z=0
\end{cases}$ .
solution_md:
The three lines have directional vector  $(0,1,1)$  hence the carrying line of the cylinder will be parallel. Hence the cylinder will be of the form  $d(v,l)=C$  where  $l=p+R(0,1,1)$ . First we determine a candidate for  $p$ .
A plane  $V$  normal to  $L_1,L_2,L_3$  is given by  $y+z=0$  and  $L_1\cap V=\{(0,1,-1)\}, L_2\cap V=\{(0,-1,1)\},L_3\cap V=\{(\sqrt{2},0,0)\}$ . We are in luck, since the circumcenter of this triangle is  $(0,0,0)$ .
Hence we can take  $p=(0,0,0)$  and  $l=R(0,1,1)$ .
Now take  $a:=(0,1,1),b:=(0,1,-1),c:=(1,0,0)$  which is an orthogonal basis of  $R^3$ .
If  $v=(x,y,z)=({{y+z}\over 2})a+({{y-z}\over 2})b+xc=\lambda a+\mu b+\nu c$  then  $d(v,l)^2=||\mu b+\nu c||^2=2\mu^2+\nu^2=D$ . The constant  $D$  can be found by taking  $v=(0,2,0)\in L_1$ .
Hence  $2\mu^2+\nu^2=2\iff 2x^2+(y-z)^2=4$ .

stem_md: Let  $x_1=2021$ ,  $x_n^2-2(x_n+1)x_{n+1}+2021=0$  ( $n\geq1$ ). Prove that the sequence  ${x_n}$  converges. Find the limit  $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n$ .
solution_md:
A standard recursion based on  Newton-Raphson. Write  $a:=2021,\alpha:=\sqrt{a+1}-1$  and define  $f(x)={{x^2+a}\over {2(x+1)}}$  on  $[0,\infty)$ . Note that  $f(\alpha)=\alpha$ .
-  $f$  strictly increases on  $[\alpha,\infty)$ . Indeed, consider  $g(x)={{x^2+a}\over {x+1}}=x-1+{{a+1}\over {x+1}}$ . Then  $g'(x)=1-{{a+1}\over {(x+1)^2}}$  and for  $x> \alpha$  we have  $(x+1)^2> a+1$ , hence  $g'(x)>0$ .
- for  $x>\alpha$  we have  $\alpha<f(x)<x$ . The first part follows since we have  $f(x)>f(\alpha)$ . The second part is easy rewriting.
We see that  $x_n$  is decreasing and bounded below by  $\alpha$ . Hence  $x_n\rightarrow t\ge \alpha$ . Since  $f(t)=t$  we have  $t=\alpha$  and  $x_n\downarrow \alpha$ .

stem_md:
Let  ${a_n}$  and  ${b_n}$  be positive real sequence that satisfy the following condition:
(i)  $a_1=b_1=1$ (ii)  $b_n=a_n b_{n-1}-2$ (iii)  $n$  is an integer larger than  $1$ .
Let  ${b_n}$  be a bounded sequence. Prove that  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{a_1a_2\cdots a_n}$  converges. Find the value of the sum.
solution_md:
<details><summary>reverse engineered solution</summary>Note that we have  $$ \frac{1}{a_1\cdots a_n}=\frac{b_{n-1}}{a_1\cdots a_{n-1}(b_n+2)} $$    $$ =\frac{b_{n-1}}{a_1\cdots a_{n-1}(b_n+2)}-\frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}}+\frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}} $$    $$ =\frac{2b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}(b_n+2)}-\frac{b_{n-1}(b_n+2)}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}(b_n+2)}+\frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}} $$    $$ =\frac{-b_{n-1}b_n}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}(b_n+2)}+\frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}} $$    $$ =\frac{-b_n}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}a_n}+\frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}} $$  So we have that  $$ \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{a_1\cdots a_n} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{a_1}+\sum_{n=2}^N \frac{b_{n-1}}{2a_1\cdots a_{n-1}}-\frac{b_n}{2a_1\cdots a_n} $$    $$ =\frac{1}{a_1}+\frac{b_1}{2a_1}-\frac{b_N}{2a_1\cdots a_N} $$    $$ =\frac{b_1+2}{2a_1}-\frac{b_N}{2a_1\cdots a_N} $$    $$ =\frac{b_1+2}{2a_1}-\frac{b_1\cdots b_N}{2(b_1+2)\cdots (b_N+2)} $$  If  $b_n$  is bounded above by  $M$  we have that  $0<\frac{b_n}{b_n+2}\leq \frac{M}{M+2}<1$ , so  $\frac{b_1\cdots b_N}{2(b_1+2)\cdots (b_N+2)}$  vanishes and we are left with  $\frac{b_1+2}{2a_1}$ .</details>

solution_md:
1) We have  $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1)+t(a,b,c)=(1+at,1+bt,1+ct)$ .
- If  $c\not=0$  then  $z=1+ct$  implies  $x^2+y^2=(1+at)^2+(1+bt)^2= 1+2(a+b)t+(a^2+b^2)t^2=1+2(a+b)({{z-1}\over c})+(a^2+b^2)({{z-1}\over c})^2$ .

Discuss the solvability of the equations
\begin{align*}\lambda x+y+z&=ax+\lambda y+z&=bx+y+\lambda z&=c\end{align*}for all numbers  $\lambda,a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ .
solution_md:
Discuss the solvability of the equations \begin{align*}\lambda x+y+z&=ax+\lambda y+z&=bx+y+\lambda z&=c\end{align*}for all numbers $\lambda,a,b,c\in\mathbb R$ .
From $\begin{vmatrix}\lambda & 1 & 1 1 & \lambda & 1 1 & 1 & \lambda \end{vmatrix}=(\lambda -1)^2(\lambda +2)$ we get that if $\lambda \neq 1,-2$ then the system is always solvable, because the matrix of coefficients is invertible. If $\lambda =1$ then the column space of the matrix of coefficients is $\left \{\begin{pmatrix}sss\end{pmatrix}:s\in \mathbb{R}\right \}$ , so the system is solvable iff $a=b=c$ . If $\lambda =-2$ then the rows of the matrix of coefficients add up to $0$ , so its column space is contained in $\begin{pmatrix}111\end{pmatrix}^\perp$ , and from $\begin{vmatrix}-2&11&-2\end{vmatrix}=3\neq 0$ we get that the matrix of coefficients has rank $2$ , so its column space equals $\begin{pmatrix}111\end{pmatrix}^\perp$ . In conclusion, for $\lambda \neq 1,-2$ the system is alwasy solvable, for $\lambda =1$ the system is solvable iff $a=b=c$ and for $\lambda =2$ the system is solvable iff $a+b+c=0$ .

stem_md: On the ellipse  $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$  find the point  $T=(x_0,y_0)$  such that the triangle bounded by the axes of the ellipse and the tangent at that point has the least area.
solution_md:
On the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2}+\frac{y^2}{b^2}=1$ find the point $T=(x_0,y_0)$ such that the triangle bounded by the axes of the ellipse and the tangent at that point has the least area.
The equation of the tangent line at $(x_0,y_0)$ is $\frac{xx_0}{a^2}+\frac{yy_0}{b^2}=1$ , hence the intersection with the axes are $\left (\frac{a^2}{x_0},0\right )$ and $\left (0,\frac{b^2}{y_0}\right )$ , where we are of course assuming that $x_0y_0\neq 0$ (else we don't get a triangle). The area of the resulting triangle is $\frac{a^2b^2}{2|x_0y_0|}$ , and therefore we need to maximize $|x_0y_0|$ . Using AM-GM we have $$ \frac{1}{2}=\frac{\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}+\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}}{2}\geq \sqrt{\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}}=\frac{|x_0y_0|}{|ab|} $$ so $|x_0y_0|\leq \frac{|ab|}{2}$ with the equality if and only if $\frac{x_0^2}{a^2}=\frac{y_0^2}{b^2}$ if and only if $y_0^2=\frac{b^2}{a^2}x_0^2$ if and only if $x_0^2=\frac{a^2}{2}$ if and only if $\left (x_0^2,y_0^2\right )=\left (\frac{a^2}{2},\frac{b^2}{2}\right )$ . Of course, any of the four points verifying that give s triangle with minimal area.

stem_md: Prove that the equation  $$ \frac x{1+x^2}+\frac y{1+y^2}+\frac z{1+z^2}=\frac1{1996} $$  has finitely many solutions in positive integers.
solution_md:
WLOG, let  $x\le y\le z$ , then as we have  $x,y,z\in\mathbb{N}$  we have  $(xy-1)(y-x)\ge 0\implies x(y^2+1)=xy^2+x\ge x^2y+y=y(x^2+1)\implies \frac{x}{1+x^2}\ge \frac{y}{1+y^2}$ Hence we have  $\frac{x}{1+x^2}\ge \frac{y}{1+y^2}\ge \frac{z}{1+z^2}$ Now  $\frac1{1996}=\frac x{1+x^2}+\frac y{1+y^2}+\frac z{1+z^2}\le \frac {3x}{1+x^2}\implies x^2-3*1996x+1\le 0$  

This implies the number values  $x\in\mathbb{N}$  can take is finitely many, and hence  $a_x=\frac{1}{\frac1{1996}-\frac{x}{x^2+1}}$  is bounded

Now  $\frac{2y}{1+y^2}\ge \frac{y}{1+y^2}+\frac{z}{1+z^2}=\frac1{1996}-\frac{x}{x^2+1}=\frac{1}{a_x}\implies y^2-2a_xy+1\le 0$ this again implies  $y\in\mathbb{N}$  has finitely many solutions, and  $b_{x,y}=\frac{1}{\frac{1}{1996}-(\frac{x}{1+x^2}+\frac{y}{1+y^2})}$  is bounded

Then  $\frac{z}{1+z^2}=\frac{1}{1996}-(\frac{x}{1+x^2}+\frac{y}{1+y^2})=\frac{1}{b_{x,y}}\implies z^2-b_{x,y}z+1=0$  which have finitely many solutions for  $z\in\mathbb{N}$ Hence we have  $(x,y,z)\in\mathbb{N}^3$  has finitely many solutions.

solution_md:
Suppose  $f$  has infinitely many distinct roots  $a_1,a_2,\cdots$  in  $\overline{D}(0,2)$ . Passing to a subsequence we may assume  $a_n\rightarrow a$ , and then  $f\equiv 0$ , since  $a$  is a non-isolated root. Contradiction.
Choose  $r\in (1,2)$  such that all roots of in  $D(0,r)$  lie in  $D(0,1)$ : call them  $a_1,\cdots,a_n$  (with multiplicity) and let  $g(z):=f(z)/\Pi_1^n {{z-a_i}\over {1-\overline{a_i}z}}$ . 
Then  $g$  is analytic and non-zero on  $D(0,r)$  and  $|g(z)|=1$  for  $z\in T$ . Note that  $|g(z)|\le 1$  on  $D$  by the maximum principle.
The same argument with  $1/g$  gives  $|g(z)|\ge 1$  on  $D$ . Hence  $g:D\rightarrow T$  and  $g$  is constant on  $D$ .
It follows that  $f(z)=c \Pi_1^n {{z-a_i}\over {1-\overline{a_i}z}}$  on  $U:=C\setminus\{1/\overline{a_1},\cdots,1/\overline{a_n}\}$ , since  $U$  is a domain and the functions coincide on  $D$ .
Since  $f$  is an entire function, we have  $a_i=0$  for all  $i$  and  $|c|=1$ . The result follows.

stem_md: Prove that  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{n^2}{(7n)!}=\frac1{7^3}\sum_{k=1}^2\sum_{j=0}^6e^{\cos(2\pi j/7)}\cdot\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi j}7+\sin\frac{2\pi j}7\right). $$
solution_md:
Consider  $f(x)=\sum_1^\infty {{n^2x^n}\over {n!}}=\sum_1^\infty {{nx^n}\over {(n-1)!}}=\sum_1^\infty {{(n-1+1)x^n}\over {(n-1)!}}=x\sum_0^\infty {{nx^n}\over {n!}}+xe^x=(x^2+x)e^x$ .
Let  $\alpha:=2\pi /7$  and  $\zeta:=e^{i\alpha}$ . Extracting the terms with  $n\equiv 0(7)$  with a root-of-unity filter we get  $49 \sum_1^\infty {{n^2 x^{7n}}\over {(7n)!}}=1/7 \sum_0^6 f(\zeta^k x)$ . Taking  $x=1$  gives  $\sum_1^\infty {{n^2}\over {(7n)!}}={1\over {7^3}} \sum_0^6 f(\zeta^k )={1\over {7^3}} \sum_0^6 {\rm Re }f(\zeta^k )$ , since the first sum is real.
We have  $f(\zeta^k)=(\zeta^{2k}+\zeta^k)\exp(\zeta^k)$ . Since  $e^{x+iy}=e^x (\cos y+i\sin y)$  we have  ${\rm Re} (\zeta^{2k}\exp(\zeta^k))={\rm Re} \exp(2ki\alpha+\zeta^k)=\exp(\cos k\alpha) \cos (2k\alpha+\sin k\alpha)$ .
Similarly for the other term and adding gives the result.

stem_md: Give an example of a sequence of continuous functions on  $\mathbb R$  converging pointwise to  $0$  which is not uniformly convergent on any nonempty open set.
solution_md:
In fact, the above method only guarantees a sequence of functions converging almost everywhere to  $0$ . We cannot avoid the uncertainty on a set of measure  $0$ . Here is a different approach.

Fix some rational number  $r=p/q, (p,q)=1$  and consider the sequence of functions  $\varphi_{r,n}(x), n=1,2,\dots$  defined as follows.   $$ \varphi_{r,n}(x):=
\begin{cases}
0 & x\notin(r,r+\frac{1}{n})
\frac{1}{q}	& x=r+\frac{1}{2n}
\text{is piecewise linear inside } (r,r+\frac{1}{n})  
\end{cases} $$  So,  $\varphi_{r,n}$  is like a saw tooth with height  $1/q$  and width  $1/n$  that approaches  $r$  as  $n\to\infty$  and apparently  $\lim_{n\to\infty} \varphi_{r,n}(x)=0,\forall x\in \mathbb{R}$ . Note that  $\varphi_{r,n},n=1,2,\dots$  does not converge uniformly to  $0$  on any open interval  $(r-\varepsilon, r+\varepsilon)$  where  $\varepsilon>0$ . 
Now, we enumerate the rational numbers as  $r_1,r_2,\dots$  and get two dimensional array of functions  $\varphi_{m,n}(x):=\varphi_{r_m,n}(x)$  which we arrange diagonally (like the standart enumeration of the rationals) as  $\varphi_k(x),k=1,2,\dots .$  
Let us show that  $\lim_{k\to\infty}\varphi_k(x)=0,\forall x\in\mathbb{R}.$  Fix some  $x\in\mathbb{R}$  and let  $N\in \mathbb{N}$ . There are finitely many rational numbers inside  $(x-1,x+1)$  with denominator at most  $N$ . That is, there are finitely many functions  $\varphi_{r,n}$  which support contains  $x$  and  $r$  has denominator at most  $N$ . It means that for sufficiently large  $k$  it holds  $|\varphi_k(x)|\le 1/N.$ It remains to see  $\varphi_k$  is not uniformly convergent on any open set. Indeed if  $U$  is an open set, there exists  $r\in\mathbb Q$  and  $\varepsilon >0$  such that  $(r-\varepsilon, r+\varepsilon)\subset U.$  But  $\varphi_{r,n},n=1,2,\dots$  (which is a subsequence of  $\varphi_k$  ) does not converge uniformly on  $(r-\varepsilon, r+\varepsilon)$ .

stem_md: Let  $a$  and  $d$  be two positive integers. Prove that there exists a constant  $K$  such that every set of  $K$  consecutive elements of the arithmetic progression  $\{a+nd\}_{n=1}^\infty$  contains at least one number which is not prime.
solution_md:
If  $a,d$  are not coprime, then clearly  $K=1$  works since every number  $a+nd$  is divisible by that gcd, but larger than it, hence not prime.
On the other hand, if  $a,d$  are coprime,  $K=d$  works, since among any  $d$  successive numbers  $a+nd$ , there is exactly one divisible by  $d$  (and of course larger than  $d$ , hence not prime).

stem_md: Show that all complex roots of the polynomial  $P(z)=a_0z^n+a_1z^{n-1}+\ldots+a_{n-1}z+a_n$ , where  $0<a_0<\ldots<a_n$ , satisfy  $|z|>1$ .
solution_md:
Just note that
\[(1-z)P(z)=-a_0z^{n+1}+(a_0-a_1)z^n+(a_1-a_2)z^{n-1}+\dots+(a_{n-1}-a_n)z+a_n\]
and by the triangle inequality we have
\[\vert (z-1)P(z)\vert \ge a_n-(a_n-a_{n-1})\vert z\vert-(a_{n-1}-a_{n-2})\vert z\vert^2-\dots-(a_0-a_1)\vert z\vert^{n}-a_0\vert z\vert^{n+1}.\]
For  $\vert z\vert \le 1$ , this becomes
\[\vert (z-1)P(z)\vert \ge a_n-(a_n-a_{n-1})-\dots-(a_0-a_1)-a_0=0\]
so that equality must hold everywhere, in particular  $\vert z\vert=1$  and  $z$  must be real and positive, hence  $z=1$ .
However, obviously  $z=1$  is not a root of  $P$ . Done.

stem_md:
A function  $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$  has the property that for every $x,y\in\mathbb R$  there exists a real number  $t$  (depending on  $x$  and  $y$ ) such
that  $0<t<1$  and  $$ f(tx+(1-t)y)=tf(x)+(1-t)f(y). $$  Does it imply that  $$ f\left(\frac{x+y}2\right)=\frac{f(x)+f(y)}2 $$  for every  $x,y\in\mathbb R$ ?
solution_md:
No, it doesn't. Let's construct an example. Consider the Cantor's set  $C.$  For each open interval  $(a,b)$ , that is removed in order to get  $C,$  we define  $f$  as  $f(a)=-1, f(b)=1$  and linear inside  $(a,b)$ .
We set  $f(x)=0$  for all points of  $C$  where  $f$  is not yet defined, that is, any points of  $C$  which is not an end point of some open interval  $(a,b)$  removed in the classical construction of  $C$ .
Thus,  $f$  is defined at every point of  $[0,1]$ . We extend  $f$  periodically outside  $[0,1]$ . It can be checked that this function satisfies the requirements, but there are points  $x,y$  with  $$ f\left(\frac{x+y}2\right)\neq \frac{f(x)+f(y)}2 $$

solution_md: $$ n!\sim \left(\frac{n}{e}\right)^n\sqrt{2\pi n}\Longrightarrow  \prod_{k=1}^{n}\frac{k}{k+n}\sim \frac{\sqrt{\pi n}}{4^n}=A $$    $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\prod_{k=1}^n\frac {k}{k+n}\right)^{e^{\frac{1999}{n}-1}}=\lim_{n\to \infty}A^{e^{\frac{1999}{n}-1}} $$    $$ \lim_{n\to \infty}\left(e^{\frac{1999}{n}}-1\right)\ln{A}=\lim_{n\to \infty}\left(\frac{1}{2}\left(e^{\frac{1999}{n}}-1\right)\ln{n}+n\left(e^{\frac{1999}{n}}-1\right)\ln{4}\right)=1999\ln{4}\Longrightarrow \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\prod_{k=1}^n\frac k{k+n}\right)^{e^{\frac{1999}n}-1}=4^{1999} $$

stem_md: Let  $u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n\in C([0,1]^n)$  be nonnegative and continuous functions, and let  $u_j$  do not depend on the  $j$ -th variable for  $j=1,\ldots,n$ . Show that  $$ \left(\int_{[0,1]^n}\prod_{j=1}^nu_j\right)^{n-1}\le\prod_{j=1}^n\int_{[0,1]^n}u_j^{n-1}. $$
solution_md:
Let $u_1,u_2,\ldots,u_n\in C([0,1]^n)$ be nonnegative and continuous functions, and let $u_j$ do not depend on the $j$ -th variable for $j=1,\ldots,n$ . Show that $$ \left(\int_{[0,1]^n}\prod_{j=1}^nu_j\right)^{n-1}\le\prod_{j=1}^n\int_{[0,1]^n}u_j^{n-1}. $$
Induction over $n$ . The base cases $n=1,2$ are obvious. For $n>2$ we have by applying Hölder twice and the induction hypothesis once: \begin{align*} \left(\int_{[0,1]^n}\prod_{j=1}^nu_j\;\mathrm{d}x_n\cdots \mathrm{d}x_1\right)^{n-1}=\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}u_n\left(\int_0^1\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}u_j\;\mathrm{d}x_n\right)\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)^{n-1} \leq\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}u_n^{n-1}\;\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}\left(\int_0^1\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}u_j\;\mathrm{d}x_n\right)^{\frac{n-1}{n-2}}\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)^{n-2} \leq\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}u_n^{n-1}\;\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(\int_0^1u_j^{n-1}\;\mathrm{d}x_n\right)^{\frac{1}{n-2}}\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)^{n-2} \leq\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}u_n^{n-1}\;\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right)\prod_{j=1}^{n-1}\left(\int_{[0,1]^{n-1}}\left(\left(\int_0^1u_j^{n-1}\;\mathrm{d}x_n\right)^{\frac{1}{n-2}}\right)^{n-2}\mathrm{d}x_{n-1}\cdots\mathrm{d}x_1\right) =\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\int_{[0,1]^n}u_j^{n-1}\mathrm{d}x_n\cdots \mathrm{d}x_1\right) \end{align*}

stem_md: Find the minimal  $k$  such that every set of  $k$  different lines in  $\mathbb R^3$  contains either  $3$  mutually parallel lines or  $3$  mutually intersecting lines or  $3$  mutually skew lines.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/Vojtěch Jarník IMC/1999 VJIMC/2635457.json

candidates:
<details><summary>Some preliminary insight</summary>Note how shockingly similar to finding Ramsey numbers this is. Indeed, consider the graph \(K_k\) whose vertices are the given lines and whose edge \((u, v)\) is colored in one of three colors according to the positioning of the lines \(u, v\) (whether they are skew, parallel or intersect). Thus \(k\le R(3, 3, 3)=17\). However we cannot claim that these numbers are the same, since if among three given lines \(u, v, w\) there are two pairs of parallels, e.g. \(u, v\) and \(u, w\), then the third pair \(v, w\) is parallel too. This corresponds to coloring the edge \((v, w)\) in the color of parallel lines if \((u, v)\) and \((u, w)\) are of this color, which is an extra condition for the Ramsey problem.
We could also color the edges of the graph in a different way, in two colors, determining the color of edge \((u, v)\) by skewness or coplanarity of the lines \(u, v\). This would result in a lower bound \(k\ge R(3, 3)=6\). Again we cannot claim equality since for lines \(u, v, w\) with \(u\) intersecting \(v\), \(u\parallel w\) and \(v\parallel w\) they are coplanar but do not count for a monochromatic \(K_3\) in the graph.</details>

We will call pairwise skew, parallel and intersecting triples of lines s-, p- and i-triples, respectively. Note that
(i) If there is no p-triple or i-triple among four coplanar lines then these lines form a parallelogram. Indeed, there should be a pair of parallel lines. The third line should intersect them. So should do the fourth line, which has to be parallel to the third line.
(ii) Among five coplanar lines there is either a p-triple or an i-triple. Indeed, suppose the contrary. According to (i) some four lines form a parallelogram. But then the fifth line will inevitably be either parallel to or intersect two of the lines.

First we prove that \(k=9\) works. Let \(a\) be one of the given \(9\) lines. Note that among the remaining \(8\) lines either there are \(5\) lines each of which is skew with \(a\), or there are \(4\) lines each of which is coplanar with \(a\).

Suppose that there are \(5\) lines skew with \(a\). Let \(L\) denote the set of these \(5\) lines. If some two lines from \(L\) are skew with each other then adding \(a\) we will get an s-triple. So consider the case when lines in \(L\) are pairwise coplanar. If there is a p-triple or i-triple in \(L\) then we are done. So consider the case when there are no such triples. Thus there should be at least one parallel couple and one intersecting couple in \(L\). Let the parallel lines be \(b, c\in L\). Any of the other three lines \(d\in L\) cannot be parallel to \(b\) and \(c\) since they will form a parallel triple, so intersects them. Thus the five lines in \(L\) are coplanar and we are done by (ii).

Suppose now that there are \(4\) lines coplanar with \(a\). Let \(L=\{l_1, l_2, l_3, l_4\}\) denote the set of these \(4\) lines and let \(\pi_i\) be the plane through \(a\) and \(l_i\). Denote \(\Pi=\{\pi_1,\pi_2,\pi_3,\pi_4\}\).
If \(|\Pi|=1\) then all \(\pi_i\) coincide and we have five coplanar lines so we are done by (ii).
If \(|\Pi|=2\) then either WLOG \(\pi_1\ne \pi_2=\pi_3= \pi_4\) or \(\pi_1=\pi_2\ne\pi_3=\pi_4\). <details><summary>Case 1</summary>If there is an i-triple in \(\pi_2\) then we are done, otherwise the lines \(a, l_2, l_3, l_4\) form a parallelogram by (i) (WLOG in this order they are its sidelines). Then if \(l_1\parallel a\) they form a p-triple with \(l_3\). Otherwise \(l_1\) intersects \(a\). Now consider the set \(K\) of the remaining four lines out of the nine given lines. If some \(k\in K\) lies in \(\pi_2\) then we are done by (ii). Otherwise if some \(k\in K\) is parallel to \(a, l_3\) or \(l_2, l_4\) then we find a p-triple. Otherwise if some \(k\in K\) is skew with \(l_1\) then an s-triple is formed with either \(l_2\) or \(l_4\). So consider the case when each \(k\in K\) is coplanar with \(l_1\). If all \(k\in K\) are coplanar and coplanar with \(l_1\) then we are done with (ii). Otherwise there is a skew pair \(k_1, k_2\) in \(K\). If some \(k\in \{k_1, k_2\}\) intersects some \(l\in \{l_2, l_4\}\) then they intersect on \(a\) and an i-triple is found. Otherwise \(k_1, k_2\) form an s-triple with \(l_2\) or \(l_4\) and we are done.</details> <details><summary>Case 2</summary>If some \(m\in\{l_1, l_2\}\) and \(n\in\{l_3, l_4\}\) are parallel or intersecting then they form respectively a p-triple or i-triple with \(a\). So assume \(l_1\) and \(l_2\) are skew with \(l_3\) and \(l_4\). If \(a, l_1, l_2\) is a p-triple or i-triple we are done so assume otherwise; similarly for \(a, l_3, l_4\). Then there is a parallel pair in \(\pi_1\) and a parallel pair in \(\pi_3\). Now consider the set \(K\) of the four remaining lines (not in \(\{a\}\cup L\)). If two of them lie in \(\pi_1\) or \(\pi_3\) then we are done by (ii). So assume that some \(k\in K\) lies neither in \(\pi_1\) nor in \(\pi_3\). Then \(k\) does not intersect one of the parallel lines in \(\pi_1\) and one of the parallel lines in \(\pi_3\). If \(a\) is in none of the parallel pairs in \(\pi_1\) and \(\pi_3\) then \(k\) is skew with one of \(l_1, l_2\) and one of \(l_3, l_4\) so we get an s-triple. Otherwise WLOG \(l_1\parallel l_2\) and \(a\parallel l_3\). If \(k\parallel l_1\) or \(k\parallel a\) we are done. So assume it is not the case. Then \(k\) is skew with one of \(l_1, l_2\) and with one of \(l_3, l_4\) again and we get an s-triple.</details>
If \(|\Pi|\ge 3\) then WLOG \(\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3\) are different. If some two lines in \(l_1, l_2, l_3\) are parallel or intersecting then they form a p-triple or i-triple with \(a\), respectively. Otherwise \(l_1, l_2, l_3\) are pairwise skew and we are done.

It remains to construct a counterexample for \(k=8\). Consider two parallelograms with consecutive sidelines \(a_1, b_1, c_1, d_1\) and \(a_2, b_2, c_2, d_2\) so that  \(b_1\) and \(b_2\) intersect, \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) intersect, but \(a_1\) and \(c_1\) are skew with \(a_2\) and \(c_2\). Then no s-, p- or i-triple is found among these \(8\) lines.
Compare this problem with its [eaiser version](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c6h3394972p32653928).

stem_md: Find all natural numbers  $n\ge1$  such that the implication  $$ (11\mid a^n+b^n)\implies(11\mid a\wedge11\mid b) $$  holds for any two natural numbers  $a$  and  $b$ .
solution_md:
A routine exercise, the answer is all even  $n$ .

Note that  if  $n$  is odd, then as  $a+b\mid a^n+b^n$ , the condition fails by taking, e.g.,   $a\equiv -b\equiv 1\pmod{11}$ . Now, assume  $n$   is even, let  $u:=a^{n/2}$  and  $v:=b^{n/2}$ . Then,  $11\mid  u^2+v^2$ . If  $11\nmid u$  (and thus  $11\nmid v$ ), then  $(u\cdot v^{-1})^2\equiv -1\pmod{11}$ , a contradiction as  $11$  is congruent to 3 modulo 4.

stem_md: Show that the following implication holds for any two complex numbers  $x$  and  $y$ : if  $x+y$ ,  $x^2+y^2$ ,  $x^3+y^3$ ,  $x^4+y^4\in\mathbb Z$ , then  $x^n+y^n\in\mathbb Z$  for all natural n.
solution_md:
So  $2xy=(x+y)^2-(x^2+y^2) \in \mathbb{Z}$ .
Also  $2(xy)^2=(x^2+y^2)^2-(x^4+y^4) \in \mathbb{Z}$ .
So  $(2xy)^2$  is an even integer and a perfect square, hence the square of an even integer and hence  $xy \in \mathbb{Z}$ .
But now we are done since it is classical that any symmetric polynomial is an integer polynomial in the symmetric polynomials  $x+y, xy$ .
In particular any such symmetric polynomial is an integer as well, in particular this holds for  $x^n+y^n$ .
(Note that we did not use  $x^3+y^3$  in our proof.)

stem_md: Prove that if m,n are nonnegative integers and 0<=x<=1 then $(1-x^n)^m + (1-(1-x)^m)^n \ge 1$
solution_md:
<details><summary>Probabilistic Solution</summary>Let there be a board, with dimension  $m \times n$ , with  $n$  rows.
Let there be a coin, which has a probability  $x$  of flipping heads, and  $1-x$  of flipping tails.
For each square, flip a coin and if you flipped heads, color it black, and if you flipped tails, color it white.
Let  $A$  be the probability where no column is colored completely black.
Let  $B$  be the probability where no row is colored completely white. $A = (1-x^{n})^{m}$ , and  $B = (1-(1-x)^{m})^{n}$ Since at least one of  $A$  and  $B$  is true, we are done  $\blacksquare$</details>

stem_md: Let  $a_1,a_2,\ldots$  be a bounded sequence of reals. Is it true that the fact  $$ \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^Na_n=b\enspace\text{ and }\enspace\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1{\log N}\sum_{n=1}^N\frac{a_n}n=c $$  implies  $b=c$ ?
solution_md:
$\underset{N\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{1}{\log N}\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}{\frac{{{a}_{n}}}{n}}=\underset{N\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{\frac{{{a}_{N+1}}}{N+1}-\frac{{{a}_{N}}}{N}}{\ln (N+1)-\ln N}$
That is not correct; the correct one is this $$ \underset{N\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{1}{\log N}\sum\limits_{n=1}^{N}{\frac{{{a}_{n}}}{n}}=\underset{N\to \infty }{\mathop{\lim }}\,\frac{\frac{{{a}_{N+1}}}{N+1}}{\ln (N+1)-\ln N} $$ and that does not give you a counter-example, as you claimed, because there's no counter-example; we always have $b=c.$ In fact, as I've shown in the link I gave in my previous post, a stronger result holds: if $b$ exists (as a finite or infinite number), then $c$ exists too and $b=c.$

stem_md: Let  $\mathcal B$  be a family of open balls in  $\mathbb R^n$  and  $c<\lambda\left(\bigcup\mathcal B\right)$  where  $\lambda$  is the  $n$ -dimensional Lebesgue measure. Show that there exists a finite family of pairwise disjoint balls  $\{U_i\}^k_{i=1}\subseteq\mathcal B$  such that  $$ \sum_{j=1}^k\lambda(U_j)>\frac c{3^n}. $$
solution_md:
Interestingly it seems to be an open problem to determine the optimal constant. As explained [here](https://mathoverflow.net/questions/115455),  $\frac{1}{3^n}$  is not optimal.
For  $n=1$  the optimal constant is clearly  $\frac{1}{2}$  instead of  $\frac{1}{3}$ .
In general, we trivially cannot do better than  $\frac{1}{2^n}$  so one could conjecture that  $\frac{1}{2^n}$  is the optimal constant but this seems to be already open for  $n=2$ .

stem_md: Let  $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$  be given by  $$ f(n)=n^{\frac12\tau(n)} $$  for  $n\in\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$  where  $\tau(n)$  is the number of divisors of  $n$ . Show that  $f$  is an injection.
solution_md:
If not, there exists positive integers  $a<b$  which holds  $f(a)=f(b)$ .
There exists a prime  $p$  such that  $v_p(a) < v_p(b)$ .
Therefore,  $\tau(a) > \tau(b)$ . So, for some prime  $q$ ,  $v_q(a)>v_q(b)$ . But,  $v_q(f(a))=v_q(f(b))$ , which is contradiction. So, f is injection

stem_md: Let us choose arbitrarily  $n$  vertices of a regular  $2n$ -gon and color them red. The remaining vertices are colored blue. We arrange all red-red distances into a non-decreasing sequence and do the same with the blue-blue distances. Prove that the sequences are equal.
solution_md:
Number the vertices from  $0$  to  $2n-1$  let  $R\sqcup B$  their partition into red and blue. Let  $f=\sum_{r\in R} x^r$  and  $g=\sum_{b\in B}x^b$ . By the hypothesis  $f+g=x^{2n-1}+...+1$  and  $f(1)=g(1)$ , so  $|f(z)|=|g(z)|$  for all  $z^{2n}=1$ .
 
Now, let  $r_k,b_k$  denote the number of pairs of red, respectively blue vertices that are  $k$  units apart travelling along the edges of the polygon. It's easy to see that  $\sum_{k=0}^{2n-1}r_kz^k=f(z)f(\overline z)=|f(z)|^2$  and  $\sum_{k=0}^{2n-1}b_kz^k=|g(z)|^2$  for all  $z^{2n}=1$ . Hence  $\sum_{k=0}^{2n-1}(r_k-b_k)z^k=|f(z)|^2-|g(z)|^2=0$  for all such  $z$ , so the polynomial on the left hand side vanishes. Thus  $r_k=b_k$  which easily implies the conclusion.
