stem_md: If we write the sequence  $\text{AAABABBB}$  along the perimeter of a circle, then every word of the length  $3$  consisting of letters  $A$  and  $B$  (i.e.  $\text{AAA}$ ,  $\text{AAB}$ ,  $\text{ABA}$ ,  $\text{BAB}$ ,  $\text{ABB}$ ,  $\text{BBB}$ ,  $\text{BBA}$ ,  $\text{BAA}$ ) occurs exactly once on the perimeter. Decide whether it is possible to write a sequence of letters from a  $k$ -element alphabet along the perimeter of a circle in such a way that every word of the length  $l$  (i.e. an ordered  $l$ -tuple of letters) occurs exactly once on the perimeter.
solution_md:
If we write the sequence $\text{AAABABBB}$ along the perimeter of a circle, then every word of the length $3$ consisting of letters $A$ and $B$ (i.e. $\text{AAA}$ , $\text{AAB}$ , $\text{ABA}$ , $\text{BAB}$ , $\text{ABB}$ , $\text{BBB}$ , $\text{BBA}$ , $\text{BAA}$ ) occurs exactly once on the perimeter. Decide whether it is possible to write a sequence of letters from a $k$ -element alphabet along the perimeter of a circle in such a way that every word of the length $l$ (i.e. an ordered $l$ -tuple of letters) occurs exactly once on the perimeter.
Consider the graph where the vertices correspond to the $k^{l-1}$ words of lenght $l-1$ and the edges correspond to words of lenght $l$ in the following way: For every word of lenght $l$ we take a directed edge from the first $l-1$ letters of the word to the last $l-1$ letters of the word. We can reach any two vertices from each other and every vertex has $k$ incoming and outgoing edges. So there exist an Eulerian path. Now we get the letters on the circle by going along the path and choosing the last letter of the words corresponding to the edges.

stem_md:
Let  $A,B,C$  be nonempty sets in  $\mathbb R^n$ . Suppose that  $A$  is bounded,  $C$  is closed and convex, and  $A+B\subseteq A+C$ . Prove that $B\subseteq C$ .
Recall that  $E+F=\{e+f:e\in E,f\in F\}$  and  $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$  is convex iff  $tx+(1-t)y\in D$  for all  $x,y\in D$  and any  $t\in[0,1]$ .
solution_md:
Assume for the sake of contradiction that there exists  $b \in B \backslash C$ . 
By the [url = https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperplane_separation_theorem]Hyperplane Separation Theorem[/url], applied to the disjoint closed convex sets  $\{ b \}$  and  $C$ , there exist  $v \in \mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\varepsilon > 0$  such that  $\langle v , c \rangle > \langle v , b \rangle + \varepsilon$  for all  $c \in C$ .
Since  $A $  is bounded, we have  $\inf_{a \in A} \langle v ,a \rangle \in \mathbb{R}$ . Choose  $a_0 \in A$  which satisfies  $\langle v, a_0 \rangle < \varepsilon + \inf_{a \in A} \langle v ,a \rangle$ . Then we have for all  $a \in A$ ,  $c \in C$  that  $$  \langle v , a+c \rangle > \langle v , a_0 \rangle - \varepsilon + \langle v , b \rangle + \varepsilon = \langle v , a_0 + b \rangle. $$  This shows that  $a_0 + b \notin A+C$ , which is a contradiction.

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be a continuous function. Define a sequence of functions  $f_n:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  in the following way:  $$ f_0(x)=f(x),\qquad f_{n+1}(x)=\int^x_0f_n(t)\text dt,\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots. $$  Prove that if  $f_n(1)=0$  for all  $n$ , then  $f(x)\equiv0$ .
solution_md: I didn't like the official solution much , so here is an alternative and interesting approach : $f$  is (uniformly) continuous on  $[0,1]$  , hence there is some  $M>0$  such that  $|f(x)|\leq M$  for all  $x\in[0,1]$  . Then it's not hard to see by induction   $$ |f_n(x)|\leq\frac{Mx^n}{n!}\leq\frac{M}{n!} $$   since  $x\in[0,1]$  . This shows that  $\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n$  converges uniformly on  $[0,1]$  . Now also  $f_0=f$  is continuous on  $[0,1]$  , so we can safely apply FCT on  $ f_{n+1}(x)=\int^x_0f_n(t)dt$  which gives   $$ f_{n+1}'(x)=f_n(x) \  \ \forall \ \ n\in\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\} $$   Taking summation both sides   $$ \sum_{n=0}^\infty f_{n+1}'(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty f_n(x) $$   Define  $F(x)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)$  . Then term by term differentiation follows from uniform convergence and   $$ F'(x)=f(x)+F(x) $$     $$ \implies F(x)=e^x\int_0^xe^{-t}f(t)dt $$     $$ \implies\sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)=e^x\int_0^xe^{-t}f(t)dt $$    $x=1$  on both sides and  $f_n(1)=0$  for all  $n$  give   $$ 0=e\int_0^1e^{-t}f(t)dt $$     $$ \implies\int_0^1e^{-t}f(t)dt=0 $$   Since  $e^{-t}>0$  for all  $t\in[0,1]$  , by continuity of  $f$  we must have  $\color{blue}f(x)\equiv0$  for all  $x\in[0,1]$  . Proved .

stem_md: Let  $f:(0,+\infty)\to(0,+\infty)$  be a decreasing function which satisfies  $\int^\infty_0f(x)\text dx<+\infty$ . Prove that  $\lim_{x\to+\infty}xf(x)=0$ .
solution_md:
Let G(x):= integration 0 to x f(t) dt
Then use L Hospitals theorem and FTC to calculate the limit :
lim x-> infinity G(x)/ln(x) 
It gives 0 = x.G'(x)= xf(x). 
This is applicable since both G, ln(x) are defined and differentiable on (0, +infinity), the derivative of ln(x) doesn't vanish in (0, +infinity), lim x-> infinity G'(x)/(1/x) exists, since G' is a decreasing function bounded below by 0. Also ln x is unbounded as goes to + infinity as x-> + infinity. 
Q.E.D.

(This proof works only if we assume f is continuous on (0, +infinity) because it's a necessary part to use FTC).

solution_md:
Let $R$ be an associative non-commutative ring and let $n>2$ be a fixed natural number. Assume that $x^n=x$ for all $x\in R$ . Prove that $xy^{n-1}=y^{n-1}x$ holds for all $x,y\in R$ .
$R$ has no nontrivial nilpotents. We have $(xy^{n-1}-y^{n-1}xy^{n-1})^2=0$ . So $xy^{n-1}=y^{n-1}xy^{n-1}$ . Analogously $y^{n-1}x=y^{n-1}xy^{n-1}$ . So $xy^{n-1}=y^{n-1}xy^{n-1}=y^{n-1}x$ .

stem_md: Differentiable functions  $f_1,\ldots,f_n:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$  are linearly independent. Prove that there exist at least  $n-1$  linearly independent functions among  $f_1',\ldots,f_n'$ .
solution_md: Official Solution Select a maximal independent set from derivatives. WLOG it can be assumed that the set is $f^{\prime}_1 , \dots , f^{\prime}_m$ where $m \leq n$ . If $m \leq n-2$ then $f^{\prime}_{n-1}$ and $f^{\prime}_n$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $f^{\prime}_1 , \dots , f^{\prime}_m$ hence there exists real numbers $a_1 , \dots , a_m$ and $b_1 , \dots b_m$ such that \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i f^{\prime}_i - f^{\prime}_{n-1} = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{m} a_if_i - f_{n-1} \right)^{\prime} = 0 \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{m} b_i f^{\prime}_i - f^{\prime}_n = \left(\sum_{i=1}^{m} b_i f_i - f_n \right)^{\prime} = 0 \end{align*} This implies that the functions \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{m} a_i f_i - f_{n-1} \end{align*} and \begin{align*} \sum_{i=1}^{m} b_i f_i - f_n \end{align*} are constant. Eliminating these constants , a linear combination of $f_1 , \dots , f_n$ is found which vanishes. $\blacksquare$

stem_md: A ring  $R$  (not necessarily commutative) contains at least one non-zero zero divisor and the number of zero divisors is finite. Prove that  $R$  is finite.
solution_md:
Let  $m$  be the number of zero divisors and  $u ,v \in \Re$  be two non zero elements such that  $uv = 0$ We generate e more zero divisors in the following way. For an arbitrary  $x \in \Re$  , the element  $xu$  is either  $0$  or or also a zero divisor since  $(xu)v = x(uv) = 0$ If  $(xu) = yu$  for some different elements  $x , y \in \Re$  then  $(x-y)u = 0$  and  $x-y$  is a zero divisor. This implies that  $0$  or an arbitrary zero divisor can be obtained at most  $m+1$  times in the form  $xu$ .  
Thus each of  $0$  and the  $m$  zero divisors is obtained at most  $m$  times and the number if elements in  $\Re$  cannot exceed  $(m+1)^2$   $\blacksquare$

stem_md: Let  $E$  be the set of all continuous functions  $u:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  satisfying  $$ u^2(t)\le1+4\int^t_0s|u(s)|\text ds,\qquad\forall t\in[0,1]. $$  Let  $\varphi:E\to\mathbb R$  be defined by  $$ \varphi(u)=\int^1_0\left(u^2(x)-u(x)\right)\text dx. $$  Prove that  $\varphi$  has a maximum value and find it.
solution_md: Let  $v(t)=1+4\int_0^ts|u(s)|\,ds$ . Then by hypothesis   $$ v'(t)=4t|u(t)|\leq4t\sqrt{v(t)}\implies\frac{v'(t)}{2\sqrt{v(t)}}\leq2t $$   Hence using  $v(0)=1$    $$ \sqrt{v(t)}-1=\int_0^t\frac{v'(s)}{2\sqrt{v(s)}}\,ds\leq2\int_0^ts\,ds=t^2\implies |u(t)|\leq\sqrt{v(t)}\leq t^2+1 $$   Therefore   $$ |\varphi(u)|\leq\int_0^1|u(x)||u(x)-1|\,dx\leq\int_0^1(x^2+1)(x^2+2)\,dx=\color{blue}\frac{16}5 $$   Equality is achieved if  $|u(t)|=t^2+1$  and  $|u(t)-1|=t^2+2$ , this happens exactly when  $\color{blue}u(t)=-t^2-1$ .

stem_md: Let  $p>3$  be a prime number and  $n=\frac{2^{2p}-1}3$ . Show that  $n$  divides  $2^n-2$ .
solution_md:
Clearly  $n$  is odd. Hence, it suffices to show  $n\mid 2^{n-1}-1$ , that is,
\[
\frac{2^{2p}-1}{3} \mid 2^{n-1}-1.
\]
We will prove a stronger conclusion: we claim  $2^{2p}-1\mid 2^{n-1}-1$ . For this, it suffices to verify  $2p\mid n-1$ , that is
\[
2p\mid \frac{2^{2p}-4}{3} = \frac{4^p-4}{3}.
\]
Notice that   $p\mid 4^p-4$  by Fermat, and since  $p>3$ ,  $p\mid (4^p-4)/3$ . Likewise,  $(4^p-4)/3$  is clearly even. This concludes the proof as  $p>2$ .

stem_md: Let  $ \{D_1, D_2, ..., D_n \}$  be a set of disks in the Euclidean plane. Let  $ a_ {i, j} = S (D_i \cap D_j) $  be the area of  $ D_i \cap D_j $ . Prove that   $$  \sum_ {i = 1} ^ n \sum_ {j = 1} ^ n a_ {i, j} x_ix_j \geq 0  $$   for any real numbers  $ x_1, x_2, ..., x_n $ .
solution_md:
Not sure that this works? Suppose only discs $D_1$ and $D_2$ have a non-trivial intersection, say with area $A > 0$ , and all other pairs of discs have zero intersections. Then pick $x_1 = -x_2 = 1$ and any arbitrary choices for the remaining $x_i$ . Then $$ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ n \sum_ {j = 1} ^ n a_ {i, j} x_ix_j = 2Ax_1 x_2 = -2A < 0 $$
This counterexample does not work. Note that $i=j$ is also allowed in the sum, and all such terms are nonnegative. Hence we obtain $$ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ n \sum_ {j = 1} ^ n a_ {i, j} x_ix_j \geq a_{1,1} x_1^2 + a_{2,2} x_2^2 + 2a_{1,2} x_1 x_2 \geq A ( x_1^2 + x_2^2 + 2x_1x_2) \geq 0. $$ In fact, the statement is true for arbitrary measurable sets $D_i \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with finite measure. Indeed, for all $i,j$ we have $$ a_{i,j} x_i x_j = x_i x_j \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \mathbf{1}_{D_i \cap D_j} ( y ) \, dy = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} x_i x_j \mathbf{1}_{D_i} ( y ) \mathbf{1}_{ D_j} ( y ) \, dy . $$ This implies that $$ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ n \sum_ {j = 1} ^ n a_ {i, j} x_ix_j = \int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \sum_{i,j=1}^n (x_i x_j \mathbf{1}_{D_i} ( y ) \mathbf{1}_{ D_j} ( y ) ) \, dy =\int_{\mathbb{R}^2} \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_i \mathbf{1}_{D_i} ( y ) \right) ^2 \, dy \geq 0. $$

Let  $f(n)=n(n+2)$  Then,  $f(n)=n\sqrt{n^2+4n+4} =n\sqrt{1+(n+1)(n+3)} =n\sqrt{1+f(n+1)} =n\sqrt{1+(n+1)\sqrt{1+(n+2)\sqrt{1+(n+3)}}}$ .

stem_md: Two real square matrices  $A$  and  $B$  satisfy the conditions  $A^{2002}=B^{2003}=I$  and  $AB=BA$ . Prove that  $A+B+I$  is invertible. (The symbol  $I$  denotes the identity matrix.)
solution_md:
The problem in that form is not interesting really. So let me propose a better one: 

find all positive integers  $m,n$  such that  $A+B+I$  is invertible for any complex square matrices  $A,B$  that satisfy the following conditions  $$ A^m=B^n=I, \ \ AB=BA. $$   
We claim that the answer is all positive integers  $m,n$  such that  $3 \nmid \gcd(m,n).$  
Suppose first that  $3 \mid \gcd(m,n)$  and choose  $A=e^{2\pi i/3}I, \ B=e^{-2\pi i/3}I.$  Then  $A^m=B^n=I, \ \ AB=BA,$  but  $A+B+I=0,$  which is not invertible. 
Conversely, let  $m,n$  be positive integers such that  $3 \nmid \gcd(m,n)$  and suppose that there exist matrices  $A,B$  such that  $A^m=B^n=I, \ AB=BA.$  We need to show that  $A+B+I$  is invertible. Since  $A,B$  commute, there exists an invertible matrix  $P$  such that both  $U:=P^{-1}AP, \ V:=P^{-1}BP$  are (upper) triangular. Let  $U=[u_{rs}], \ V=[v_{rs}].$  From  $A^m=B^n=I,$  we get  $U^m=I, \ V^n=I$  and so  $u_{rr}^m=1, \ v_{rr}^n=1,$  for all  $r.$  Fixing an  $r,$  we get   $$ u_{rr}=e^{2\pi ji/m}, \ \ \ v_{rr}=e^{2\pi k i/n}, $$   
for some integers  $0 \le j \le m-1, \ 0 \le k \le n-1.$  On the other hand  $A+B+I=P(U+V+I)P^{-1}$  is invertible if and only if  $W:=U+V+I$  is invertible. But  $W$  is an (upper) triangular matrix and so it is invertible if and only if its diagonal entries are all non-zero. The  $(r,r)$ -entry of  $W$  is  $$ w_{rr}=u_{rr}+v_{rr}+1=e^{2\pi ji/m}+e^{2\pi k i/n}+1=\cos(2\pi j/m)+\cos(2\pi k/n)+1+(\sin(2\pi j/m)+\sin(2\pi k/n))i. $$  So  $w_{rr}=0$  if and only if   $$ \cos(2\pi j/m)+\cos(2\pi k/n)=-1, \ \ \ \sin(2\pi j/m)+\sin(2\pi k/n)=0, $$  which holds if and only if  $j/m=p \pm \frac{1}{3}, \ \ k/n=q \mp \frac{1}{3}$  for some integers  $p,q.$  But that implies  $3 \mid m, \ 3 \mid n,$  which contradicts our assumption that  $3 \nmid \gcd(m,n).$  So  $w_{rr} \ne 0$  for all  $r$  and hence  $W$  is invertible, implying that  $A+B+I$  is invertible.

stem_md: Let  $d(k)$  denote the number of natural divisors of a natural number  $k$ . Prove that for any natural number  $n_0$  the sequence  $\left\{d(n^2+1)\right\}^\infty_{n=n_0}$  is not strictly monotone.
solution_md: The idea here is that the function $d$ grows really slowly. We'll show a stronger bound that we need: Claim. $d(n) = n^{o(1)}$ . (That is, for every $\epsilon > 0$ there exists some constant $C_{\epsilon}$ such that $d(n) < C_{\epsilon}n^{\epsilon}$ ) *Proof* For a number $n = p_1^{\alpha_1}\cdots p_k^{\alpha_k}$ consider $$ \frac{d(n)}{n^{\epsilon}} = \prod_{i=1}^k\frac{\alpha_i+1}{p_i^{\alpha\epsilon}}. $$ Now, if $p_i > e^{1/\epsilon}$ we get that $\alpha_i+1 < e^{\alpha_i} < p_i^{\alpha\epsilon}$ . Here we chosed $e$ becuse it is comfortable, but we could have chosen $3$ , that gives a worse bound but does not matter. Now, this tells us that $d(n)/n^{\epsilon}$ gets smaller when $n$ has primes greater than $e^{1/\epsilon}$ . Now, we can also bound $\frac{\alpha_i+1}{p_i^{\alpha_i\epsilon}}$ for small primes. In fact, we just need to check that when taking $\alpha_i\to \infty$ the denominator is exponential while the numerator is linear, so it approaches $0$ . So basically for $\alpha_i$ integer we get that $\frac{\alpha_i+1}{p_i^{\alpha_i\epsilon}}$ has a maximum, call it $\beta_i$ . This concludes the proof of the claim, as it tells us that if $p_t$ is the biggest prime smaller than $e^{1/\epsilon}$ , then $$ \frac{d(n)}{n^{\epsilon}} \leq \prod_{i=1}^{t}\frac{\alpha_i}{p_i^{\alpha_i\epsilon}}\leq \prod_{i=1}^t \beta_i, $$ which is a constant only dependent on $\epsilon$ . $\hfill\blacksquare$ The problem now follows easily, as the eventual monotonicity of $d(n^2+1)$ would imply that assimtotically $d(n^2+1)$ is bigger than or equal to something linear as $n-t$ for some $t$ , but this contradicts the claim taking $\epsilon < 1/2$ . Now that we are done let me solve a slightly harder problem. Show that $\{d(n^2+1)\}_{n\geq n_0}$ is not non-increasing nor non-decreasing for any $n_0$ . That is, the original problem, but allowing terms of the sequence to be equal. This problem is solved similarly, but in needs a couple of extra steps. Observation $1$ . $(n^2+1)((n+1)^2+1) = (n^2+n+1)^2+1$ Check this already tells us that the sequence can't be non-increasing. A remark on how to get here, if one wants to show the sequence is non-decreasing it is motivated to try to solve $n^2+1 \mid m^2+1$ , which turns equivalent to showing $n^2+1 \mid m^2-n^2 = (m+n)(m-n)$ , so taking $m-n = n^2+1$ does the job. Observation 2. $gcd(n^2+1, (n+1)^2+1))=1$ unless $n\equiv 2$ modulo $5$ . This is done just by applying a couple of time Euclid's algorithm. Now, this is interesting because it tells us that for $n$ not $2$ modulo $5$ then $d((n^2+n+1)^2+1) = d(n^2+1)d((n+1)^2+1)$ , and that for $n\equiv 2$ modulo $5$ then $d((n^2+n+1)^2+1) < d(n^2+1)d((n+1)^2+1)$ . So, if we could show that for some $k$ $d((5k+1)^2+1)=d((5k+2)^2+1)=d((5k+3)^2+1)$ we would be done becuase then $$ d(((5k+1)^2+(5k+1)+1)^2+1) > d(((5k+2)^2+(5k+2)+1)^2+1). $$ Now this would be true if we could find $5$ consecutive terms of the sequence which are the same. So assume that there are not. Now, this together with the fact that the sequence is non-decreasing tells us that $d(n^2+1) > \frac{n}{5}-n_0$ for all $n$ , which contradicts the fact that $d(n) = n^{o(1)}$ .

stem_md: Suppose that  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  is a continuously differentiable function such that  $f(0)=f(1)=0$  and  $f(a)=\sqrt3$  for some  $a\in(0,1)$ . Prove that there exist two tangents to the graph of  $f$  that form an equilateral triangle with an appropriate segment of the  $x$ -axis.
solution_md: **Easy problem...** :fool: $f'(x)$ is continuous. And given $f(0)=f(1)=0$ By Rolle's theorem there exist $c\in(0,1)$ such that $f'(c)=0$ . Now there is a $a\in(0,1)$ such that $f(a)=\sqrt{3}$ . So $f(a)\leq f(c)$ . Now applying LMVT on $(0,c)$ we have a $k_1\in(0,c)$ such that $$ f'(k_1)=\frac{f(c)-f(0)}{c-0}\geq\frac{\sqrt{3}}{c}>\sqrt{3} $$ Similarly applying LMVT on $(c,1)$ we have a $k_2\in(c,1)$ such that $$ f'(k_2)=\frac{f(1)-f(c)}{1-c}\leq\frac{-\sqrt{3}}{1-c}<-\sqrt{3} $$ Now apply IVT on $(k_1,c)$ we have a $y_1\in(k_1,c)$ such that $f'(y_1)=\sqrt{3}$ and similarly we have a $y_2\in(c,k_2)$ such that $f'(y_2)=-\sqrt{3}$ . Easy to see that tangents at $y_1,y_2$ makes an equilateral triangle with finite segment on x axis.

candidates: Actually this doesn't require continuity of the derivative.  There exist two points  $x_1, x_2 \in (0,1) $  such that  $f'(x_1) > 0, f'(x_2) < 0$  (otherwise  $f$  would be strictly increasing or decreasing over the whole interval, contradicting  $f(0) = f(1)$ ).  Hence there exists  $x \in (x_1, x_2)$  for which  $f'(x) = 0$ , because the derivative has the intermediate value property.  Now the absolute maximum of  $f$  must occur at the location of such an  $x$ , hence there actually exists an  $x \in (0,1)$  for which  $f'(x) = 0$  and  $f(x) \ge \sqrt{3}$ .  Then if  $\sigma$  denotes the slope function, note that  $\sigma(0,x) > \sqrt{3}, \sigma(x, 1) < -\sqrt{3}$  and by the mean value, intermediate value properties there exists  $a_1 \in (0,x), a_2 \in (x,0)$  such that  $f'(a_1) = \sqrt{3}, f'(a_2) = -\sqrt{3}$ .  The corresponding tangents to the graph of  $f$  running through  $a_1$  and  $a_2$  (i) intersect the x-axis at  $60^{\circ}$  angles, (ii) do not intersect on the x-axis, and (iii) are not parallel hence intersect (somewhere off the x-axis). stem_md: Evaluate the sum  $$ \sum_{n=0}^\infty\operatorname{arctan}\left(\frac1{1+n+n^2}\right). $$
solution_md: <details><summary>Solution</summary>Note that:  $$ \tan\left(\tan^{-1}(n+1) + \tan^{-1}(n)\right) = \frac{n+1-n}{1+(n+1)n} = \frac{1}{1+n+n^2} $$  So we may write:  $$ \sum_{n=0}^\infty\operatorname{arctan}\left(\frac1{1+n+n^2}\right) =\lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=0}^N \operatorname{arctan}\left(n+1\right) - \operatorname{arctan}\left(n\right) = \lim_{N \to \infty} \operatorname{arctan}(N) = \frac\pi2 $$</details>

stem_md: Denote by  $B(c,r)$  the open disk of center  $c$  and radius  $r$  in the plane. Decide whether there exists a sequence  $\{z_n\}^\infty_{n=1}$  of points in  $\mathbb R^2$  such that the open disks  $B(z_n,1/n)$  are pairwise disjoint and the sequence  $\{z_n\}^\infty_{n=1}$  is convergent.
solution_md:
Yes, sequence like that does exist. Let  $r_n:=1/n,n\in \mathbb{N}$ . The idea is to find a subsequence  $r_{n_i},i=1,2,\dots$  with the following properties. 1)  $\displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^{\infty}r_{n_i}<\infty$ . 2) The sequence  $\displaystyle s_k:=\sum_{i=n_k}^{n_{k+1}-1}r_i, k=1,2,$  converges to  $0$ . 
	
	Suppose now, I have found such subsequnce  $r_{n_i}$ . Put disks with radii  $r_{n_i},i=1,2\dots$  one after another, horizontally aligned (from left to right) and on top of the  $n_i$ -th one, put vertically aligned disks with radii  $r_{n_i+1},\dots, r_{n_{i+1}-1}.$  Denote the center of the disk with radius  $r_i$  as  $z_i.$  Clearly the sequence  $z_i$  converges.
	
	To construct a subsequence satisfying 1) and 2) we take a sequence  $\varepsilon_i>0$  very slowly converging to  $0$  and define  $\displaystyle n_k:=\left\lfloor \prod_{i=1}^k(1+\varepsilon_i)\right\rfloor.$  
	
	I wouldn't go further into technical details, because there is another approach that characterizes all sequences  $r_n$  for which disks with radii  $r_n>0,n\in \mathbb{N}$  could be arranged complying with the same requirements. It happens if and only if  $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r_n^2<\infty.$ 	If  $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r_n^2=\infty$  the total area of the disks is  $\infty$  so there is no hope all of them to disjointly fit into some bounded area. Suppose now  $\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}r_n^2<\infty.$  WLOG we can assume  $r_n$  is a decreasing sequence of numbers less than  $1,$  because we can remove the larger ones and rearange them. We take increasing indices  $1=n_0<n_1<n_2<\dots$  with  $2^{-k-1}<r_i\le 2^{-k}, \forall i\in [n_k,n_{k+1}); k=0,1,\dots.$  That is, the radii  $r_i$  when  $i$  runs from  $n_k$  to  $n_{k+1}$  do not differ too much. Then, we take sufficiently large square  $Q_1$  and begin to put consecutively the disks with radii  $r_i, i=n_k,n_{k}+1,\dots r_{n_{k+1}-1}$  inside subsquares with side length  $2\cdot 2^{-k}.$  In this way we do not waste too much space between the disks. We can put all of them inside  $Q_1$  if it is large enough, but at some moment we take a much smaller square  $Q_2$  horizontally aligned to  $Q_1$  and switch from  $Q_1$  to  $Q_2.$  In this way we put the disks into sequence of squares (with fast decrising sizes). The result follows.

stem_md: Find all pairs  $(m,n)$  of positive integers such that  $m+n$  and  $mn+1$  are both powers of  $2$ .
solution_md:
So write  $m+n=2^{a+1}$  and  $mn+1=2^b$  with  $a \ge 0, b \ge 1$ . W.l.o.g.  $m \ge n$ .
So  $m$  and  $n$  are both even and hence  $d=\frac{m-n}{2}$  is an integer. So  $m=2^a+d, n=2^a-d$ .
So we are looking for solutions to  $4^a-2^b+1=d^2$ , in other words we want  $4^a-2^b+1$  to be a perfect square.
Note that  $4^a-2^b+1<4^a=(2^a)^2$  and hence  $4^a-2^b+1 \le (2^a-1)^2=4^a-2^{a+1}+1$  and hence  $a+1 \le b$ .
So  $2^b \mid d^2-1$  and hence  $2^{a+1} \mid d^2-1=(d-1)(d+1)$ . So one of the factors is divisible by  $2^{a}$  since not both can be divisible by  $4$ .
But  $0<d<2^a$  so this is only possible if  $d=1$  or  $d=2^a-1$ .
So indeed we get exactly the two families of solutions  $(2^{a+1}-1,1)$  and  $(2^a+1,2^a-1)$  (and of course also the other way around).

stem_md: Are the groups  $(\mathbb Q,+)$  and  $(\mathbb Q^+,\cdot)$  isomorphic?
solution_md: Official Solution Suppose for contradiction that there exists an isomorphism $f : (\mathbb{Q} , +) \rightarrow (\mathbb{Q}^+ , .)$ . Then $f(0) = 1$ , because $0$ and $1$ are corresponding neutral elements of $(\mathbb{Q} , +)$ and $(\mathbb{Q}^+ , .)$ . Let $f(1) = \frac{a}{b}$ , $a,b \in \mathbb{N}$ , $(a,b) = 1$ . Similarly let for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ , $n \geq 2$ , $f \left(\frac{1}{n} \right) = \frac{a_n}{b_n}$ . Where $a_n , b_n \in \mathbb{N}$ $(a_n , b_n) = 1$ . Then it is \begin{align*} f(1) = f \left(\frac{1}{n} + \frac{1}{n} + \dots + \frac{1}{n} \right) = \left(f\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)\right)^n = \left(\frac{a_n}{b_n} \right)^n = \frac{a}{b} \end{align*} It is still $((a_n)^n , (b_n)^n) = 1$ so consequently $a = (a_n)^n$ and $b = (b_n)^n$ . If there is $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $a_m \geq 2$ then $a \geq 2$ and $a_n \geq 2$ for all $n$ . That follows $a \geq 2^n$ for all $n$ . Contradiction. Thus for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ it holds $a_n = 1$ , specially $a = 1$ . Same argument gives $b = 1$ . But then $f(1) = \frac{a}{b} = 1 = f(0)$ . $f$ is not injective. **Contradiction**.

stem_md: Let  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n$  be a divergent series with positive nonincreasing terms. Prove that the series  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_n}{1+na_n} $$  diverges.
solution_md: Let  $S_k=\sum_{n=1}^ka_n$  . Since  $\{a_n\}$  is monotonic decreasing , we have  $na_n\leq S_n$  for all  $n\geq1$  . From here  $S_n\geq1$  for arbitrarily large  $n$  .  Hence  $1+na_n\leq2S_n$  for sufficiently large  $n$  . Therefore   $$ \sum_{n=m+1}^k\frac{a_n}{1+na_n}\geq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n=m+1}^k\frac{a_n}{S_n}\geq\frac{1}{2S_k}\sum_{n=m+1}^ka_n=\frac{S_k-S_m}{2S_k}=\frac{1}{2}-\frac{S_m}{2S_k} $$   for large  $m$  and  $k>m$  . For large  $k$  , we have  $S_k\to\infty$  . Hence for all  $m$  there is some  $k>m$  such that   $$ \sum_{n=m+1}^k\frac{a_n}{1+na_n}>\frac{1}{3} $$   which shows that  $\sum_{n=1}^k\frac{a_n}{1+na_n}$  is not Cauchy , hence  $\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_n}{1+na_n}$  is divergent .

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:\mathbb R_{\ge0}\times\mathbb R_{\ge0}\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}$  such that $1$ .  $f(x,0)=f(0,x)=x$  for all  $x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ , $2$ .  $f(f(x,y),z)=f(x,f(y,z))$  for all  $x,y,z\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$  and $3$ . there exists a real  $k$  such that  $f(x+y,x+z)=kx+f(y,z)$  for all  $x,y,z\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}$ .
solution_md:
Setting  $y=0$  in (3) gives  $f(x,x+z)=kx+z=(k-1)x+(x+z)$ . If in this last relationship we change the variables  $u=x$  and  $v=x+z$  (note that we must have  $0\leq u\leq v$ ) then  $f(u,v)=(k-1)u+v$  and symmetrically if  $u\geq v$  we must have  $f(u,v)=u+(k-1)v$ .
Since the first and the last condition are always satisfied, it suffices to check the second one. Assume  $0<x\leq y<z$  . Then we must have  $f((k-1)x+y,z)=f(x,(k-1)y+z)$ Since the maps nonnegative reals to nonnegative reals, we must have  $k\geq 1$ , and so  $x\leq z\leq (k-1)y+z$ , and thus we can reduce the rhs to  $(k-1)x+(k-1)y+z$ . For the LHS we have two cases:
1)  $(k-1)x+y\geq z$ . This brings to  $(k-1)x+y+(k-1)z=(k-1)x+(k-1)y+z\implies (k-2)(y-z)=0$ 2)  $(k-1)x+y\leq z$ . This leads to  $(k-1)^2x+(k-1)y+z=(k-1)x+(k-1)y+z\implies (k-1)(k-2)x=0$ If for some  $(x,y,z)$  the first case holds then we must have  $k=2$ If for some  $(x,y,z)$  the second condition holds then we must have  $k=2$  or  $k=1$ .
This are indeed the only two possible values of  $k$  which both correspond to a valid solution, namely  $k=1$  brings to  $f(x,y)=max(x,y)$  and  $k=2$  brings to  $f(x,y)=x+y$ .

stem_md:
Let  $f:A^3\to A$  where  $A$  is a nonempty set and  $f$  satisfies:
(a) for all  $x,y\in A$ ,  $f(x,y,y)=x=f(y,y,x)$  and
(b) for all  $x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_2,z_3\in A$ ,  $$ f(f(x_1,x_2,x_3),f(y_1,y_2,y_3),f(z_1,z_2,z_3))=f(f(x_1,y_1,z_1),f(x_2,y_2,z_2),f(x_3,y_3,z_3)). $$  Prove that for an arbitrary fixed  $a\in A$ , the operation  $x+y=f(x,a,y)$  is an Abelian group addition.
solution_md:
Let $f:A^3\to A$ where $A$ is a nonempty set and $f$ satisfies: (a) for all $x,y\in A$ , $f(x,y,y)=x=f(y,y,x)$ and (b) for all $x_1,x_2,x_3,y_1,y_2,y_3,z_1,z_2,z_3\in A$ , $$ f(f(x_1,x_2,x_3),f(y_1,y_2,y_3),f(z_1,z_2,z_3))=f(f(x_1,y_1,z_1),f(x_2,y_2,z_2),f(x_3,y_3,z_3)). $$ Prove that for an arbitrary fixed $a\in A$ , the operation $x+y=f(x,a,y)$ is an Abelian group addition.
We have \begin{align*} (x+y)+z=f(f(x,a,y),a,z)=f(f(x,a,y),f(a,a,a),f(a,a,z)) =f(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,a),f(y,a,z))=f(x,a,f(y,a,z))=x+(y+z) x+y=f(x,a,y)=f(f(a,a,x),f(a,a,a),f(y,a,a)) =f(f(a,a,y),f(a,a,a),f(x,a,a))=f(y,a,x)=y+x x+a=f(x,a,a)=x a+x=f(a,a,x)=x x+f(a,x,a)=f(x,a,f(a,x,a))=f(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,a),f(a,x,a)) =f(f(x,a,a),f(a,a,x),f(a,a,a))=f(x,x,a)=a f(a,x,a)+x=f(f(a,x,a),a,x)=f(f(a,x,a),f(a,a,a),f(a,a,x)) =f(f(a,a,a),f(x,a,a),f(a,a,x))=f(a,x,x)=a \end{align*} So $+$ is asssociative, commutative, has $a$ as a unit and $f(a,x,a)$ is an inverse of $x$ . So $(A,+)$ is an abelian group.

stem_md:
Let  $(x_n)_{n\ge2}$  be a sequence of real numbers such that  $x_2>0$  and  $x_{n+1}=-1+\sqrt[n]{1+nx_n}$  for  $n\ge2$ . Find

(a)  $\lim_{n\to\infty}x_n$ ,
(b)  $\lim_{n\to\infty}nx_n$ .
solution_md:
Returning to the serious mathematical discussion, I now have an answer to my question from #5.
Claim:  $x_n \sim \frac{4}{n^2}$  as  $n \to \infty$  i.e.  $\lim_{n \to \infty} n^2x_n=4$ .
<details><summary>Proof</summary>We use the result from #2 that  $y_n=nx_n \to 0$  as  $n \to \infty$ .
We begin by showing that  $z_n=ny_n=n^2x_n$  is bounded and then boost this to show that  $z_n \to 4$ .
Remember that
\[y_{n+1}=(n+1) \cdot \left(\exp\left(\frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n}\right)-1\right) \le (n+1)\cdot \frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n} \cdot \left(1+\frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n}\right) \le \left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right) \cdot \log(1+y_n)\]
for all large  $n$  using that  $y_n \to 0$  and that  $e^x-1 \le x+x^2=x(1+x)$  for  $0 \le x \le 1$  (indeed,  $e^x-x-1 \le (e-2)x^2 <x^2$  for  $0<x<1$ ). The estimate
\[y_{n+1} \le \left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right) \cdot \log(1+y_n)\]
now is a quantitative version (with explicit  $\varepsilon$ ) of the estimate  $y_{n+1} \le (1+\varepsilon)\log(1+y_n)$  from #2 which we there used to prove that  $y_n \to 0$ , and we will use it to make exactly this decay quantitative now.
Indeed, let  $n$  be sufficiently large in terms of the above estimate and let  $C \ge 16$  such that  $y_n \le \frac{C}{n}$  for this  $n$ . Then
\[y_{n+1} \le \left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right) \cdot \log\left(1+\frac{C}{n}\right) \le \left(1+\frac{2}{n}\right) \cdot \frac{C}{n} \cdot \left(1-\frac{C}{4n}\right) \le \frac{C}{n} \cdot \left(1+\frac{2}{n}-\frac{C}{4n}\right) \le \frac{C}{n+1} \cdot \left(1+\frac{4}{n}-\frac{C}{4n}\right) \le \frac{C}{n+1}\]
where we used that  $y_n \to 0$  and that  $\log(1+x) \le x-\frac{x^2}{4}=x\left(1-\frac{x}{4}\right)$  for  $0 \le x \le 1$  (say, the constants are not important for now).
Hence  $y_n \le \frac{C}{n}$  for this choice of  $C$  and all large  $n$  proving that  $z_n=ny_n$  is bounded.
To evaluate the limit, it is convenient to also have a positive lower bound. Indeed, for large  $n$  and  $0<c<\frac{1}{2}$  small enough such that  $y_n \ge \frac{c}{n}$  for this  $n$ , we get from the recursion and  $e^x \ge 1+x$  that
\[y_{n+1} \ge (n+1) \cdot \frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n} \ge (n+1) \cdot \frac{\log(1+\frac{c}{n})}{n} \ge \left(1+\frac{1}{n}\right) \cdot \frac{c}{n} \cdot (1-\frac{c}{n}) \ge \frac{c}{n}>\frac{c}{n+1}\]
for large  $n$ , say, using  $\log(1+x) \ge x-x^2$  for  $0<x<1$ , and hence  $z_n>c$  for all large  $n$  and this choice of  $c$ .
So  $z_n$  is bounded from above and below by some positive constants  $c$  and  $C$ .
Now we need to again be a bit more careful to find the exact limit.
Using  $\log(1+y_n)=y_n-\frac{y_n^2}{2}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^3}\right)$  and  $\exp(x)=1+x+\mathcal{O}(x^2)$ , the recursion now becomes
\[y_{n+1}=(n+1) \cdot \left(\frac{y_n}{n}-\frac{y_n^2}{2n}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^4}\right)\right).\]
Writing  $z_n=ny_n$ , this becomes
\[z_{n+1}=(n+1)^2 \cdot \left(\frac{z_n}{n^2}-\frac{z_n^2}{2n^3}\right)+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right)\]
and hence
\[z_{n+1}=z_n+\frac{4z_n-z_n^2}{2n}+\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n^2}\right).\]
Now finally we can already see where the limit  $4$  comes from, as a solution of  $4z_n-z_n^2=0$ . We also see why the lower bound  $z_n>c>0$  was relevant to exclude the other solution  $z_n \to 0$ . Let's make this precise.
Let  $\varepsilon>0$ . We claim that  $4-\varepsilon<z_n<4+\varepsilon$  for all large  $n$ .
Indeed, first notice that  $z_{n+1}-z_n=\mathcal{O}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right)$  so for large  $n$ , we cannot "jump" over this interval  $(4-\varepsilon,4+\varepsilon)$  when going from  $z_n$  to  $z_{n+1}$ .
So there are three cases:
1) We have  $z_n<4-\varepsilon$  for all large  $n$ .
2) We have  $z_n>4+\varepsilon$  for all large  $n$ .
3) We have  $4-\varepsilon<z_n<4+\varepsilon$  infinitely often.
In case 1), we would have  $z_{n+1} \ge z_n+\frac{c\varepsilon}{3n}$  (say) for all large  $n$  and hence  $z_n \to \infty$  by the divergence of the harmonic series, which is a contradiction to our assumption.
Similarly, in case 2) we would have  $z_{n+1} \le z_n-\frac{C\varepsilon}{3n}$  (say) for all large  $n$  and hence  $z_n \to -\infty$ , again by the divergence of the harmonic series, which is absurd.
Hence we are left with case 3). We claim that if  $4-\varepsilon<z_n<4+\varepsilon$  for one large  $n$ , we will never leave this interval again.
Indeed, if  $z_{n+1}<4-\varepsilon<z_n$ , on recalling  $z_n-z_{n+1} \le \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$  (say), this would mean that  $z_n<4-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$  in which case, however  $z_{n+1} \ge z_n+\frac{c\varepsilon}{5n}$  (say) contradicting our assumption.
Similarly, we get a contradiction if  $z_{n+1}>4+\varepsilon>z_n$ .
Hence, we know that we enter the interval infinitely often, and that once we enter it for some large  $n$ , we never leave it again.
Hence  $4-\varepsilon<z_n<4+\varepsilon$  for all large  $n$ . Since  $\varepsilon>0$  was arbitrary, this shows that indeed  $z_n \to 4$  as  $n \to \infty$ .</details>

<details><summary>Solution for (a)</summary>(a) Easy to prove by induction that  $x_n>0$ .
Using Bernoulli's inequality,  $\sqrt[n]{1+nx_n} \le 1+x_n$ , hence  $x_{n+1} \le x_n$ , so  $x_n$  is positive and monotonically decreasing, hence convergent, say with limit  $L \ge 0$ . Suppose that  $L>0$ . Then  $2Ln>1+nx_n=(1+x_{n+1})^n>\left(1+\frac{L}{2}\right)^n$  for all large  $n$ , which is clearly a contradiction since the LHS grows only linearly, but the RHS grows exponentially. Hence  $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n=L=0$ .</details>
<details><summary>Solution for (b)</summary>Let  $y_n=nx_n$ . So  $y_{n+1}=(n+1) \left[(1+y_n)^{1/n}-1\right]=(n+1) \left[\exp\left(\frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n}\right)-1\right]$ .
We first show that  $y_n$  is bounded and then improve this to show that  $y_n$  converges to  $0$ .
From (a) we know that  $y_n<n$  for all large  $n$  and hence certainly  $\frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n}<1$  for all large  $n$ .
Using  $e^x<1+(e-1)x$  for  $0<x<1$  (e.g. using convexity of  $\exp$ ) it follows that
\[y_{n+1}<(n+1)(e-1) \cdot \frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n}<2(e-1) \cdot \log(1+y_n)\]
for all large  $n$ . Clearly, for all large  $M$  we have  $M>2(e-1) \log(1+M)$ .
Now choose a large  $n$  (in terms of the previous estimate) and a large  $M>y_n$  (in terms of the above inequality for  $M$ ).
Then  $y_{n+1}<2(e-1)\log(1+M)<M$  and hence inductively  $y_n<M$  for all large  $n$ , so  $y_n$  is indeed bounded.
Having established the boundedness of  $y_n$ , we need to go back to our initial recursion and derive a finer estimate since the crude bound  $e^x-1<(e-1)x$  is not good enough any more.
Indeed, let  $L=\limsup y_n$ . Now fix any  $\varepsilon>0$ . As  $z_n=\frac{\log(1+y_n)}{n} \to 0$ , we have  $e^{z_n}-1<(1+\varepsilon)z_n$  for all large  $n$ . Hence for all large  $n$ , we have
\[y_{n+1} \le (1+\varepsilon) \cdot \frac{n+1}{n} \cdot \log(1+y_n) \le (1+2\varepsilon) \cdot \log(1+L).\]
Hence we must have  $L \le (1+2\varepsilon)\log(1+L)$ . Since  $\varepsilon>0$  was arbitrary, this shows that  $L \le \log(1+L)$  and hence  $L=0$  since  $\log(1+x)<x$  for all positive  $x$ . Done.</details>
Of course this leaves us with a natural follow-up question: Can we find the asymptotic behaviour of  $x_n$ ?

stem_md: Let  $S_0=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1,z\ne-1\}$  and  $f(z)=\frac{\operatorname{Im}z}{1+\operatorname{Re}z}$ . Prove that  $f$  is a bijection between  $S_0$  and  $\mathbb R$ . Find  $f^{-1}$ .
solution_md:
Note that  $S_0$  can be written as  $S_0=\{e^{i \theta},\theta \in ]-\pi,\pi[\}$ , and note that  $S_0$  and  $]-\pi,\pi[$  are bijections. Then:  $f(z)=g(\theta)=\frac{\cos \theta}{1+\sin \theta}=\tan(\theta/2)$  which is a clearly a bijective function onto  $\mathbb{R}$ , hence  $f$  is indeed a bijection.

To find the inverse we take  $x \in \mathbb{R}$  and note that  $\tan(\theta/2)=x$ , using standard trigonometric sustitutions is easy to see that  $\cos \theta=\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}$  and  $\sin \theta=\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$  and hence  $f^{-1}(x)=\frac{1-x^2}{1+x^2}+i\frac{2x}{1+x^2}$ .

Regards
Claudio.

stem_md: Find all reals  $\lambda$  for which there is a nonzero polynomial  $P$  with real coefficients such that  $$ \frac{P(1)+P(3)+P(5)+\ldots+P(2n-1)}n=\lambda P(n) $$  for all positive integers  $n$ , and find all such polynomials for  $\lambda=2$ .
solution_md:
Note that  $\lambda (n+1)P(n+1)-\lambda nP(n)=P(2n+1)$ , and since this is true for all positive integers  $n$ , it must be true for all real  $n$ . If  $deg(P)=k, \lambda = \frac{2^k}{k+1}$ . Note also that the solution space is a vector space, so if  $\lambda$  is of this form, the linear map  $P(x) \to \lambda (x+1)P(x+1)-\lambda xP(x)-P(2x+1)$  defines a map from the space of polynomials of degree at most  $k$  to the space of polynomials of degree at most  $k-1$ , so has non-trivial kernel, so such a polynomial does exist.
For  $\lambda=2$ , must have  $k=3$ . Then  $P(1)=0$ , and setting  $x=0$  gives  $P(-1)=0$ . Hence  $P(x)=(x^2-1)(ax+b)$ , and putting this in gives  $b=0$ . It is straightforward to check that these do give solutions.

stem_md: For an arbitrary square matrix  $M$ , define  $$ \exp(M)=I+\frac M{1!}+\frac{M^2}{2!}+\frac{M^3}{3!}+\ldots. $$  Construct  $2\times2$  matrices  $A$  and  $B$  such that  $\exp(A+B)\ne\exp(A)\exp(B)$ .
solution_md:
How was this on a competition? It is really the first property you learn in university on the matrix exponential that in general  $\exp(A+B) \ne \exp(A)\exp(B)$  unless  $A$  and  $B$  commute.
So just take essentially any two matrices  $A$  and  $B$  that do not commute and compute their exponentials.
For instance, one can take  $A=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 10 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$  and  $B=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0-1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$  so that  $\exp A=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 10 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$  and  $\exp B=\begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0-1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$  and hence
\[\exp(A)\exp(B)=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1-1 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
while  $A+B=\begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1-1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$  so that
\[\exp(A+B)=\begin{pmatrix} \cos 1 & \sin 1-\sin 1 & \cos 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
which is certainly different from  $\exp(A)\exp(B)$ .

stem_md: Let  $(a_{i,j})^n_{i,j=1}$  be a real matrix such that  $a_{i,i}=0$  for  $i=1,2,\ldots,n$ . Prove that there exists a set  $\mathcal J\subset\{1,2,\ldots,n\}$  of indices such that  $$ \sum_{\begin{smallmatrix}i\in\mathcal Jj\notin\mathcal J\end{smallmatrix}}a_{i,j}+\sum_{\begin{smallmatrix}i\notin\mathcal Jj\in\mathcal J\end{smallmatrix}}a_{i,j}\ge\frac12\sum_{i,j=1}^na_{i,j}. $$
solution_md:
[quote name=jasperE3 url=https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/user/261984]Let $n\in\mathbb{N}^*$ and $\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}$ be a real matrix such that $a_{i,i}=0$ for all integers $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$ . Prove that there exists a set $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}$ of indices such that: \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}a_{i,j}\] [rule] $\text{See the post at the following address:}$ [**jasperE3's question**](https://artofproblemsolving.com/community/c7h2606117p22499693) [rule]
SolutionFirst, notice that the inequality \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}a_{i,j}\] can be re-written to an equivalent form i.e. \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\left(\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{i,j\not\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)\] by cutting the right-hand sum over $\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}$ in four sums, each corresponding to a part of the disjoint union \[\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}^2=\left(\mathcal{J}\times\overline{\mathcal{J}}\right)\cup\left(\mathcal{J}\times\mathcal{J}\right)\cup\left(\overline{\mathcal{J}}\times\mathcal{J}\right)\cup\left(\overline{\mathcal{J}}\times\overline{\mathcal{J}}\right)\] [rule] The idea is to build $\mathcal{J}$ recursively. Let $n\in\mathbb{N}^*$ be a positive integer, we note: \[\mathcal{M}_n=\left\{\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}\big/\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}\in\mathcal{M}_n\left(\mathbb{R}\right)\text{ and }a_{i,i}=0\text{ for all integers }1\leqslant i\leqslant n\right\}\] a set of matrices. Now, we define a proposition $\mathcal{P}$ , depending on $n$ , as: \[\mathcal{P}\left(n\right):"\emph{For any matrix }\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}\in\mathcal{M}_n\emph{ there exists }\mathcal{J}\subseteq\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}\emph{ satisfying }\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}a_{i,j}"\] We'll prove the property $\mathcal{P}$ being true for every positive integers using simple induction: $\textbf{Initialization:}$ for $n=1$ , $\mathcal{M}_1=\left\{\begin{pmatrix}0\end{pmatrix}\right\}$ so, setting $\mathcal{J}=\left\{1\right\}$ gives that both members (in our inequality) are equal to $0$ . Hence, $\mathcal{P}\left(0\right)$ is true. $\textbf{Heredity:}$ suppose the property $\mathcal{P}$ is true for a positive integer $n$ , then let $A=\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n+1}\in\mathcal{M}_{n+1}$ . We have: \[A=\begin{pmatrix}0&a_{1,2}&a_{1,3}&\ldots&a_{1,n}&a_{1,n+1}a_{2,1}&0&a_{2,3}&\ldots&a_{2,n}&a_{2,n+1}\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots&\vdots&\vdotsa_{n,1}&a_{n,2}&\ldots&\ldots&0&a_{n,n+1}a_{n+1,1}&a_{n+1,2}&\ldots&\ldots&a_{n+1,n}&0\end{pmatrix}\] Now, consider its sub-matrix $B=\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}$ (we just remove ending row and column). As $B\in\mathcal{M}_n$ (it's still a real matrix having a principal diagonal of zeros) then, according to our induction hypothesis $\mathcal{P}\left(n\right)$ , there exists a set $\mathcal{I}\subseteq\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}$ such that: \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{I}j\not\in\mathcal{I}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{I}j\in\mathcal{I}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\left(\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{i,j\not\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,j}\right)\] Then, we distinguish two cases (below, we'll note $\overline{\mathcal{I}}=\left\{1,2,\ldots,n+1\right\}\setminus\mathcal{I}$ . Also, keep in mind that $a_{n+1,n+1}=0$ and $\left(n+1\right)\not\in\mathcal{I}$ ): $\textbf{Case }1\textbf{:}$ if $\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,n+1}\right)+\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}a_{n+1,j}\right)\geqslant\left(\sum_{i\not\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,n+1}\right)+\left(\sum_{j\not\in\mathcal{I}}a_{n+1,j}\right)$ , that's say, if the sum of the coeffients in the lasts row and column whose indices are in $\left(\mathcal{I}\times\overline{\mathcal{I}}\right)\cup\left(\overline{\mathcal{I}}\times\mathcal{I}\right)$ is bigger (or equals to) the sum of the other coefficients (in the same row and column) then, we set $\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{I}$ . This gives: \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\left(\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{i,j\not\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)\] $\textbf{Case }2\textbf{:}$ otherwise, i.e. if $\left(\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,n+1}\right)+\left(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}a_{n+1,j}\right)<\left(\sum_{i\not\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i,n+1}\right)+\left(\sum_{j\not\in\mathcal{I}}a_{n+1,j}\right)$ , we set $\mathcal{J}=\mathcal{I}\cup\left\{n+1\right\}$ . Hence, we obtain, now, that the sum of the coeffients in the lasts row and column whose indices are in $\left(\mathcal{J}\times\overline{\mathcal{J}}\right)\cup\left(\overline{\mathcal{J}}\times\mathcal{J}\right)$ is bigger than the sum of the other coefficients (in the same row and column). Actually, as $a_{n+1,n+1}=0$ , we can replace $\mathcal{I}$ by $\mathcal{J}$ in the above strict inequality. From where we get, again, the following inequality: \[\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\left(\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{i,j\not\in\mathcal{J}}a_{i,j}\right)\] Thus, in both cases, we built a set $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\left\{1,2,\ldots,n+1\right\}$ such that the required inequality holds. This proves that the property $\mathcal{P}$ is hereditary. $\textbf{Conclusion:}$ the property $\mathcal{P}$ have been initialized and it's hereditary. We conclude, by simple induction, that $\left(\forall n\in\mathbb{N}^*\right)$ , $\mathcal{P}\left(n\right)$ is true. [rule] To conclude, for any $\boxed{n\in\mathbb{N}^*}$ and any $\boxed{\text{real matrix }\left(a_{i,j}\right)_{1\leqslant i, j\leqslant n}}$ such that $\boxed{a_{i,i}=0\text{ for all integers }1\leqslant i\leqslant n}$ , there exists a set $\mathcal{J}\subseteq\left\{1,2,\ldots,n\right\}$ of indices such that: \[\boxed{\left(\sum_{\substack{i\in\mathcal{J}j\not\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)+\left(\sum_{\substack{i\not\in\mathcal{J}j\in\mathcal{J}}}a_{i,j}\right)\geqslant\frac{1}{2}\sum_{1\leqslant i,j\leqslant n}a_{i,j}}\] [rule]
Remark(s)Here is a Python program that implements the above procedure in order to build such a set $\mathcal{J}$ : [pywindow] from random import uniform def build_a_matrix(n, m, M, _type = lambda x: x): '''Build a real n*n square matrix with a principal diagonal of zeros. Its coefficients are randomly taken in the segment [n, M]. The function '_type' may be used to convert the random reals produced to integers.''' '''Returns: a such matrix as a 2-D Python array.''' mat = [[0] * n for _ in range(n)] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if j != i: mat[i][j] = _type(uniform(m, M)) return mat def print_mat(mat): '''Prints, in a prettier way, a square matrix with its coefficents.''' n = len(mat) lengths_per_column = [max([len(str(mat[i][j])) for i in range(n)]) for j in range(n)] for i in range(n): string = ['['] for j in range(n): coefficient = str(mat[i][j]) shift = ' ' * (lengths_per_column[j] - len(coefficient)) string.append(coefficient + ', ' * (j < n - 1) + shift) print(''.join(string) + ']') def find_a_J(mat): '''Given a n*n square matrix, build a set J following the above algorithm.''' '''Returns: a set J c {1, 2, ..., n}.''' J = [1] n = len(mat) for k in range(1, n): lhs, rhs = 0, 0 for i in range(k): if (i + 1 in J): lhs += mat[i][k] + mat[k][i] else: rhs += mat[i][k] + mat[k][i] if lhs < rhs: J.append(k + 1) return J def check_the_J(mat, J): '''Given a square matrix of size n*n and a set J c {1, 2, ..., n}, test if the required inequality holds.''' '''Returns: a boolean, 'True' if the required inequality holds, 'False' otherwise.''' lhs, rhs = 0, 0 n = len(mat) for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if ((i + 1 in J) and (j + 1 not in J)) or ((i + 1 not in J) and (j + 1 in J)): lhs += mat[i][j] # If a_{i,j} is part of the LHS (a.k.a. left-hand-side). rhs += mat[i][j] return lhs >= rhs/2 # An example: mat = build_a_matrix(15, 1, 20, int) J = find_a_J(mat) print('The matrix:') print_mat(mat) print('A solution: J =', J) print('Checking...', check_the_J(mat, J)) [/pywindow]

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\times[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be a continuous function. Find the limit  $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}\left(\frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2}\right)^2\int^1_0\int^1_0(xy(1-x)(1-y))^nf(x,y)\text dx\text dy. $$
solution_md: Official Solution **Answer:** $f \left (\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right)$ **Proof:** Set \begin{align*} L_n(f) = \left( \frac{(2n+1)!}{(n!)^2} \right)^2 \int \int_{Q} (xy(1-x)(1-y))^n f(x,y) \text{dx dy} \end{align*}**Step 1:** $\lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} L_n (x^k y^l) = \frac{1}{2^{k+l}} = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^k \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^l$ . This is a straightforward calculation : \begin{align*} \int \int_{Q} (xy(1-x)(1-y))^n x^k y^l \text{dx dy} = \int_{0}^{1} x^{n+k} (1-x)^n \text{dx} \int_{0}^{1} y^{n+l} (1-y)^n \text{dy} = = \frac{(n+k)! n!}{(2n + k +1)!} \cdot \frac{(n+l)! n!}{(2n + l +1)!} \end{align*} Thus \begin{align*} \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} L_n (x^k y^l) = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{(n+1)(n+2) \dots (n+k)}{(2n+2)(2n+3) \dots (2n+k+1)} \frac{(n+1)(n+2) \dots (n+l)}{(2n+2)(2n+3) \dots (2n+l+1)} = \frac{1}{2^{k+l}} \end{align*} **Step 2:** The desired result is satisfied for every polynomial $P(x,y)$ . Indeed , the limit and $L_n$ are linear operators **Step 3:** Fix an arbitrary $\varepsilon > 0$ . A polynomial $P(x,y)$ can be chosen such that $|f(x,y) - P(x,y)| < \varepsilon$ for every $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Q}$ . Then \begin{align*} |L_n(f) - L_n(P)| \leq L_n (|f - P|) < L_n(\varepsilon \cdot \mathbb{I}) = \varepsilon \end{align*} where $\mathbb{I}(x,y) = 1$ for every $(x,y) \in \mathbb{Q}$ According step 2 there exists $n_0$ such that $|L_n(P) - P \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right)| < \varepsilon$ for $n > n_0$ . For these integers \begin{align*} \left |L_n(f) - f \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right)\right | \leq |L_n(f) - L_n(P)| + |L_n(P) - P \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right)| + |f \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right) - P \left(\frac{1}{2} , \frac{1}{2} \right)| < 3 \varepsilon \end{align*} $\blacksquare$

Yes, polynomial approximation is a good and maybe even the natural way to solve the problem. But there's a more elementary way to solve the problem. The general idea in my solution is to divide the unit square into two parts: a small square around the point  $(1/2,1/2),$  and the rest of the unit square. You'll see why the point  $(1/2,1/2)$  is significant in this problem, something that the polynomial approximation approach doesn't quite show. 

I'm going to give the solution into several steps. Let  $$ c_n:= \frac{(2n+1)!}{n!^2}, \ \ \ \ \ \ g(x):=x(1-x), \ \ \  x \in [0,1]. $$  <u>Claim 1</u>. If  $|x| < 1/4,$  then  $\lim_{n\to\infty}c_nx^n=0.$ <u>Proof</u>. By the ratio test, the power series  $\sum_{n \ge 0}c_nx^n$  converges if  $|x| < 1/4.$ <u>Claim 2</u>.  $c_n^2\int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^ndx \ dy=1.$ <u>Proof</u>. We have    $$ \int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^ndx \ dy=\int_0^1 (g(x))^ndx \int_0^1(g(y))^ndy=\left(\int_0^1(g(x))^ndx\right)^2=\left(\int_0^1x^n(1-x)^ndx\right)^2=\frac{1}{c_n^2}. $$  <u>Claim 3</u>. Let  $A \subset [0,1]^2$  be a square such that the point  $(1/2,1/2)$  is inside  $A.$  Then   $$ \lim_{n\to\infty}c_n^2 \int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A}(g(x)g(y))^n \ dx \ dy =0. $$  <u>Proof</u>. Since  $\max_{x \in [0,1]} g(x)=g(1/2)=\frac{1}{4}$  and  $(1/2,1/2)$  is insider  $A,$  we have  $g(x)g(y) \le \alpha^2$  for some  $0 < \alpha < 1/4$  and all  $(x,y) \in [0,1]^2 \setminus A.$  Thus   $$ 0 \le c_n^2 \int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A}(g(x)g(y))^n \ dx \ dy \le c_n^2\alpha^{2n}=(c_n\alpha^n)^2 $$  and the result follows from Claim 1 and the squeeze theorem.

Now, we're ready to complete the solution. Let   $$ I_n:=c_n^2\int^1_0\int^1_0(g(x)g(y))^nf(x,y) \ dx \ dy. $$  Then  $$ I_n=c_n^2\int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^n(f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)) \ dx \ dy + f(1/2,1/2)c_n^2\int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^ndx \ dy $$    $$ =c_n^2\int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^n(f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2))\ dx \ dy + f(1/2,1/2), \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \text{by Claim 2}, $$  and so, to complete the solution, we only need to prove that  $\lim_{n\to\infty} J_n=0,$  where   $$ J_n:=c_n^2\int_0^1\int_0^1(g(x)g(y))^n(f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)) \ dx \ dy. $$  **Proof of**  $\lim_{n\to\infty}J_n=0.$  Let  $\epsilon > 0$  be given. Since  $f$  is continuous at  $(1/2,1/2),$  there exists  $0 < \delta \le 1/2$  such that  $|f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)| < \epsilon$  whenever  $|x-1/2| \le \delta$  and  $|y-1/2| \le \delta.$  Let   $$ A_{\delta}=[1/2-\delta,1/2+\delta]^2, \ \ \ \ \ \ M:=\max_{(x,y) \in [0,1]^2}|f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)|. $$  Then  $$ 0 \le |J_n| \le c_n^2\int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A_{\delta}}(g(x)g(y))^n|f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)| \ dx \ dy+c_n^2\int \int_A (g(x)g(y))^n|f(x,y)-f(1/2,1/2)| \ dx \ dy $$    $$ \le Mc_n^2\int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A_{\delta}}(g(x)g(y))^n \ dx \ dy+ \epsilon c_n^2 \int \int_A (g(x)g(y))^n dx \ dy $$    $$  \le Mc_n^2\int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A_{\delta}}(g(x)g(y))^n \ dx \ dy+ \epsilon c_n^2 \int_0^1 \int_0^1 (g(x)g(y))^n dx \ dy $$    $$ =Mc_n^2\int \int_{[0,1]^2 \setminus A_{\delta}}(g(x)g(y))^n \ dx \ dy+ \epsilon, \ \ \ \ \ \text{by Claim 2}, $$  and hence, by Claim 3,  $0 \le \limsup_n |J_n| \le \epsilon,$  implying that  $\lim_{n\to\infty}J_n=0.$

Let  $R$  ba a finite ring with the following property: for any  $a,b\in R$  there exists an element  $c\in R$  (depending on  $a$  and  $b$ ) such that  $a^2+b^2=c^2$ .
Prove that for any  $a,b,c\in R$  there exists  $d\in R$  such that  $2abc=d^2$ .
(Here  $2abc$  denotes  $abc+abc$ . The ring  $R$  is assumed to be associative, but not necessarily commutative and not necessarily containing a unit.
solution_md:
Let $R$ ba a finite ring with the following property: for any $a,b\in R$ there exists an element $c\in R$ (depending on $a$ and $b$ ) such that $a^2+b^2=c^2$ . Prove that for any $a,b,c\in R$ there exists $d\in R$ such that $2abc=d^2$ . (Here $2abc$ denotes $abc+abc$ . The ring $R$ is assumed to be associative, but not necessarily commutative and not necessarily containing a unit.
Let $a\in R$ . Since $R$ is finite there is a minimal positive integer $n$ such that $na^2=0$ . So $-a^2=(n-1)a^2$ is as a sum of squares itself a sqaure for $n>1$ . For $a^2=0$ we have $-a^2=0=0^2$ . We have \begin{align*} 2abc=(ab+c)^2+(a+bc)^2-(ca+b)^2-a^2+b^2-c^2-(ab)^2-(bc)^2+(ca)^2. \end{align*} So $2abc$ is as a sum of squares itself a square.

stem_md: Suppose that  $(a_n)$  is a sequence of real numbers such that the series  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_n}n $$  is convergent. Show that the sequence  $$ b_n=\frac1n\sum^n_{j=1}a_j $$  is convergent and find its limit.
solution_md:
Suppose that $(a_n)$ is a sequence of real numbers such that the series $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{a_n}n $$ is convergent. Show that the sequence $$ b_n=\frac1n\sum^n_{j=1}a_j $$ is convergent and find its limit.
Define $s_n:=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{a_i}{i}$ for $n\geq0$ and let $s:=\lim_{n\to\infty}s_n$ . We have \[ b_n=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^ni(s_i-s_{i-1})=s_n-\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}s_i \] But $s_n$ and $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}s_i$ converge to $s$ for $n\to\infty$ . So $b_n$ converges to $0$ for $n\to\infty$ .

Let  $A=[a_{ij}]_{n\times n}$  be a matrix with nonnegative entries such that  $$ \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^na_{ij}=n. $$  (a) Prove that  $|\det A|\le1$ .

solution_md:
Let $A=[a_{ij}]_{n\times n}$ be a matrix with nonnegative entries such that $$ \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{j=1}^na_{ij}=n. $$ (a) Prove that $|\det A|\le1$ . (b) If $|\det A|=1$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb C$ is an arbitrary eigenvalue of $A$ , show that $|\lambda|=1$ .
Lemma: The determinant of a matrix is at most the product of the length of the coloum vectors.Project the second, third, ..., $n$ -th coloum vector onto the orthogonal space of the first one. The determinant does not change and the vectors get shorter. Continue inductivly until all vectors are pairwise orthogonal. In this case the determinant is the product of the lenght of the coloum vectors.
\begin{align*} \det(A)^2\leq\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{i=1}^na_{ij}^2\right)\leq\prod_{j=1}^n\left(\sum_{i=1}^na_{ij}\right)^2\leq\left(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{i=1}^na_{ij}}{n}\right)^{2n}=1 \end{align*} If equality holds we have equality in every step. So the coloum vectors are pairwise equal, all entries are 0 or 1 and all the sum of the entries in every coloum vector is 1. So there is exacty one 1 in every row and coloum and all other entries are 0. So $A$ permutes the standard basis vectors. If w.l.o.g. $e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_k$ is a cycle of standard basis vectors under $A$ we have $k$ eigenvectors $\sum_{i=1}^ke^{2\pi ia/k}e_i$ with eigenvalue $e^{2\pi a/k}$ for 0\leq a

stem_md:
(a) Let  $u$  and  $v$  be two nilpotent elements in a commutative ring (with or without unity). Prove that  $u+v$  is also nilpotent.
(b) Show an example of a (non-commutative) ring  $R$  and nilpotent elements  $u,v\in R$  such that  $u+v$  is not nilpotent.
solution_md:
a) Choose  $p>0$  such that  $u^p=v^p=0$ . Then  $(u+v)^{2p}=\sum_{k+l=2p} {{2p}\choose k} u^k v^l=0$  since for each term we have  $k\ge p \vee l\ge p$ .
b) Take  $R=M(2,{\bf R})$  and  $u=\begin{pmatrix} 0&10&0\end{pmatrix}, v=\begin{pmatrix} 0&01&0\end{pmatrix}$ . Then  $u+v$  has order 2.

stem_md: Two players play the following game: Let  $n$  be a fixed integer greater than  $1$ . Starting from number  $k=2$ , each player has two possible moves: either replace the number  $k$  by  $k+1$  or by  $2k$ . The player who is forced to write a number greater than  $n$  loses the game. Which player has a winning strategy for which  $n$ ?
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution?</summary>We claim that player 2 has the winning strategy if n is a number of the form  $2^{2k+1} + 2c$ , where  $k$  is a nonnegative integer and  $c$  is a nonnegative integer such that  $c < 2^{k}$ , and player 1 has the winning strategy otherwise. 

First, suppose that n is odd. Note that player 1 can force player 2 to always land on an even integer by adding 1 to the number each time. So player 1 will first make k 3, which is odd, and regardless of whether or not player 2 makes the number k+1 or 2k, it will be even, so player 1 can add 1 to that number to make it odd. Eventually, either player 2 will either go above n, in which case they lose, or player 1 is guaranteed to land on exactly the number n, forcing player 2 to make the number go above n and lose.

Now suppose n is even. We will show that if a player has a winning strategy for n, they also have one for 4n and 4n+2. First, suppose that the player uses the winning strategy of n to get to n. Then there are two cases for the moves of the second player:

Case 1: The other player makes the number n+1. The player with the winning strategy doubles it to make it 2n+2. Since any player loses if they double again, all of the numbers will be added linearly. So the player with the winning strategy hits all of the even numbers while the other player hits all the odd ones, guaranteeing that the player with the winning strategy hits 4n or 4n+2, causing the other player to lose.
Case 2: The other player makes the number 2n. The player with the winning strategy doubles it to make it 4n. In the 4n case, they win, while in the 4n+2 case, they force the other player to make the number 4n+1, in which case they make it 4n+2 and win as well.

Finally, we can consider the "base" cases of  $n=2, n=4,$  and  $n=6.$  For  $n=2,$  player 1 automatically loses, so player 2 wins. For  $n=4,$  player 1 can double 2 to get 4, forcing player 2 to lose. For  $n=6,$  player 1 can double 2 to get 4, forcing player 2 to make the number 5, and then player 1 making the number 6 winning. By using induction we can prove that player 2 wins if and only if n is of the form  $2^{2k+1} + 2c$ , where  $k$  is any nonnegative integer and  $c$  is a corresponding nonnnegative integer such that  $c<2^{k}.$</details>
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/Vojtěch Jarník IMC/2006 VJIMC/2603953.json

stem_md: Let  $(G,\cdot)$  be a finite group of order  $n$ . Show that each element of  $G$  is a square if and only if  $n$  is odd.
solution_md:
Note that each element of  $G$  is a square if and only if  $x \mapsto x^2$  is surjective on  $G$ . Since  $G$  is finite, this is equivalent to  $x \mapsto x^2$  being injective.
Now if  $|G|$  is even, by Cauchy's theorem there exists a nontrivial element  $a \in G$  with  $a^2=e=e^2$ , and hence the square map is not injective.
If  $|G|$  is odd, assume that  $x,y \in G$  satisfy  $x^2 = y^2$ . Since  $|G|$  is odd, we know that both  $\operatorname{ord} x$  and  $\operatorname{ord} y$  are odd. Hence,  $\operatorname{lcm} (\operatorname{ord} x, \operatorname{ord} y ) + 1 := m$  is even. Now   $$ x ^2 = y^2 \Longrightarrow x^m = y^m \Longrightarrow x=y, $$  which proves injectivity.

stem_md: Alice has got a circular key ring with  $n$  keys,  $n\ge3$ . When she takes it out of her pocket, she does not know whether it got rotated and/or flipped. The only way she can distinguish the keys is by coloring them (a color is assigned to each key). What is the minimum number of colors needed?
solution_md:
I'm not 100% sure I understand the question, but I'll give it a go.

The objective is to come up with sequences  $X=x_1x_2\ldots x_n$   such that  $X$  is distinct from its  $n-1$  cyclic rotations and its  $n$  rotations after reversal.  A sequence is no good if it is fixed some non-identity composition of shifts and reversals.

For  $n\ge 6$ , two colours suffice.  The colouring  $X=100101(1)_{n-6}$  is easily seen to work, where  $(1)_{n-6}$  is  $n-6$  consecutive  $1$ 's.

For  $n=3,4,5$ , two colours aren't enough.  Up to rotation, reversal and relabelling, the patterns are

- $11111$ , trivially useless.
- $01111$ , fixed by  $\tau_1$ .
- $00111$ , fixed by  $\tau_4$ .
- $01011$ , fixed by  $\tau_2$ .[/list][list]
- $1111$ , trivially useless.
- $0111$ , fixed by  $\tau_1$ .
- $0011$ , fixed by  $\sigma\tau_2$ .
- $0101$ , fixed by  $\tau_1$ .[/list][list]
- $111$ , trivially useless.
- $011$ , fixed by  $\tau_1$ .

where  $\tau_k$  reverses  $X$  around  $x_k$ ,  $\sigma$  is circular left shift by one, and  $\sigma\tau$  means reverse then shift.

In those cases,  $01(2)_{n-2}$  is obviously sufficient.**Summary:**  $2$  colours suffice for  $n\ge 6$ , but you need  $3$  colours for  $n=3,4,5$ .

stem_md: Can the set of positive rationals be split into two nonempty disjoint subsets  $\mathbb Q_1$  and  $\mathbb Q_2$ , such that both are closed under addition, i.e.  $p+q\in\mathbb Q_k$  for every  $p,q\in\mathbb Q_k$ ,  $k=1,2$ ? Can it be done when addition is exchanged for multiplication, i.e.  $p\cdot q\in\mathbb Q_k$  for every  $p,q\in\mathbb Q_k$ ,  $k=1,2$ ?
solution_md: The answer to the first part is negative because suppose that  $1 \in Q_1.$  Then  $n \in Q_1$  for all positive integers  $n$  because  $Q_1$  is closed under addition. Now let  $x:=n/m \in Q_2,$  where  $m,n$  are positive integers. Then since  $Q_2$  is closed under addition,  $mx=n \in Q_2 \cap Q_1=\emptyset.$ The answer to the second part is positive; in fact there are infinity many ways to do that. For example, given any prime number  $p,$  choose  $Q_1$  to be the set of all positive rational numbers in the form  $n/p^m$  where  $m \ge 1, \ p \nmid n,$  and  $Q_2$  to be the rest of the positive rational numbers.

stem_md: A function  $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$  is called *slowly changing* if for any  $t>1$  the limit  $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f(tx)}{f(x)}$  exists and is equal to  $1$ . Is it true that every slowly changing function has for sufficiently large  $x$  a constant sign (i.e., is it true that for every slowly changing  $f$  there exists an  $N$  such that for every  $x,y>N$  we have  $f(x)f(y)>0$ ?)
solution_md:
A function $f:[0,\infty)\to\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$ is called *slowly changing* if for any $t>1$ the limit $\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{f(tx)}{f(x)}$ exists and is equal to $1$ . Is it true that every slowly changing function has for sufficiently large $x$ a constant sign (i.e., is it true that for every slowly changing $f$ there exists an $N$ such that for every $x,y>N$ we have $f(x)f(y)>0$ ?)
Yes. Assume not. Let $C$ be large enough such that $\frac{f(2x)}{f(x)}>0$ . There are $x,y>C$ so that $f(x)>0,f(y)<0$ . We have $f\left(2^nx\right)>0,f\left(2^ny\right)<0$ . So $\frac{f\left(2^nx\right)}{f\left(2^ny\right)}<0$ contradicting that $f$ ist slowly changing $\left(t=\frac{x}{y}\right)$ .

stem_md: Let  $A$  be a real  $n\times n$  matrix satisfying  $$ A+A^{\text T}=I, $$  where  $A^{\text T}$  denotes the transpose of  $A$  and  $I$  the  $n\times n$  identity matrix. Show that  $\det A>0$ .
solution_md:
Let  $A=[a_{ij}].$  Then from  $A^T+A=I$  we get that  $a_{ii}=\frac{1}{2}$  and  $a_{ij}=-a_{ji}$  for all  $i$  and all  $j \ne i.$  So   $$ A=\frac{1}{2}I +B $$   
for some real skew-symmetric matrix  $B.$  Let  $p_M(x):=\det(xI-M)$  be the characteristic polynomial of  $M \in M_n(\mathbb{R}).$  Then   $$ p_A(x)=\det(xI-A)=\det\left(\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)I-B\right)=p_B\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right). \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ (*) $$  Now, since  $B$  is real skew-symmetric, the eigenvalue of  $B$  are in the form  $ci$  for some  $c \in \mathbb{R}.$  So, since  $B$  is real, the eigenvalues of  $B$  are either  $0$  or are paired as  $ci,-ci$  for some non-zero real number  $c.$  Thus, by  $(*),$  the eigenvalues of  $A$  are either  $\frac{1}{2}$  or are paired as  $\frac{1}{2}+ci, \ \frac{1}{2}-ci$  for some non-zero real number  $c.$  Hence   $$ \det A=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{2}+c_1i\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}-c_1i\right) \cdots \left(\frac{1}{2}+c_mi\right)\left(\frac{1}{2}-c_mi\right)=\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^k\left(\frac{1}{4}+c_1^2\right) \cdots \left(\frac{1}{4}+c_m^2\right) > 0, $$   
for some integers  $k,m$  and some non-zero real numbers  $c_1, \cdots , c_m.$

stem_md: Let  $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R$  be a continuous function such that  $f(0)=f(1)=0$ . Prove that the set  $$ A:=\{h\in[0,1]:f(x+h)=f(x)\text{ for some }x\in[0,1]\} $$  is Lebesgue measureable and has Lebesgue measure at least  $\frac12$ .
solution_md:
Let's see I still remember some stuff from my mesure theory course few years ago  :laugh: :  $A$  is clearly mesurable because of the continuity of  $f$ .    Notice that if  $h\in A$  then  $x_{h}+h \leq 1$  and so   $0\leq x_{h} \leq 1-h$ .  



Let  $B=\{ h \in [0,1],~~ 1-h \in A\}$ .   $B$  has the same mesure of  $A$ . 

It suffice to prove that :  $A \cup B = [0,1]$   

Indeed for  $h\in [0,1]$  let   $r(x)= f(x+h)-f(x),~\text{if}~ x+h \leq 1$  and  $r(x)=f(x+1-h)-f(x),~ \text{if}~~ x+h > 1$ . 


Since  $f(1)=f(0)$  we have that  $r$  is continuous. Let  $f(a)=\max f$  and  $f(b)=\min f$  then :  $r(a) \times r(b) \leq 0$  and so there is  $c$   between  $a$  and  $b$  such that  $r(c)=0$ .  

Hence  $A\cap B=[0,1]$ . Finally :  $ 1=\mu( A\cup B) = 2\mu(A) -\mu(A\cap B)$  and so  $\mu(A) \geq \frac{1}{2}$  .

stem_md: Find all  $c\in\mathbb R$  for which there exists an infinitely differentiable function  $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$  such that for all  $n\in\mathbb N$  and  $x\in\mathbb R$  we have  $$ f^{(n+1)}(x)>f^{(n)}(x)+c. $$
solution_md:
The answer is  $c\leq 0$ .

For  $c\leq 0$ , f exists, in particular  $xe^x$  works. For c>0, suppose f exists and consider  $g=f'-f$ . It is strictly greater than c,  but has derivative strictly greater than c, which implies (by the middle value theorem) that lim f(x) = -inf as x tends to -inf. Contradiction, thus no function exists for c>0.

stem_md: Find all continuously differentiable functions  $f:[0,1]\to(0,\infty)$  such that  $\frac{f(1)}{f(0)}=e$  and  $$ \int^1_0\frac{\text dx}{f(x)^2}+\int^1_0f'(x)^2\text dx\le2. $$
solution_md: Note that   $$ 0\leq\int_0^1\bigg(f'(x)-\frac{1}{f(x)}\bigg)^2dx=\int_0^1\frac{dx}{f(x)^2}+\int_0^1f'(x)^2dx-2\int_0^1\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}dx\leq2-2\ln\frac{f(1)}{f(0)}=2-2=0 $$   Hence   $$ \int_0^1\bigg(f'(x)-\frac{1}{f(x)}\bigg)^2dx=0 $$   Since  $f$  is continuously differentiable on  $[0,1]$  , we have   $$ f(x)f'(x)=1 \ \forall \ x\in[0,1] $$   Solving which we get  $f(x)=\sqrt{2x+C}$  which together with the initial condition  $\frac{f(1)}{f(0)}=e$  gives  $C=\frac{2}{e^2-1}$  . Hence the only possible such  $f$  is   $$ \boxed{\color{blue}f(x)=\sqrt{2x+\frac{2}{e^2-1}}} $$   for  $x\in[0,1]$  .

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$  such that  $$ f(f(f(x)))+4f(f(x))+f(x)=6x. $$
solution_md:
The only solution to this is  $f(x)=x$ .First,the function is injective.Suppose  $f(x)=f(y)$  for  $x \neq y$ .Let  $f(x)=f(y)=t$ .Then  $f(f(t))+4f(t)+t=6x=6y$ ,which is false.Now,we have from this that the functional graph is composed out of cycles and infinite chains,with or without start.
Lemma  $1$ :Suppose there exist a minimal  $k$  such that  $f^k(x)=x$ .Then  $k=1$ .Suppose opposite.Consider the sequence  $x,f(x),f^2(x),...f^k(x)$ .Take the largest element.Let it be  $m$ .Then consider  $f(m)+4f(f(m))+f(f(f(m)))$ .It is less than or equal to  $6m$ ,but it is also strictly less than  $6m$  since  $f(m)$  is strictly less than  $m$ ,so we conclude the minimal period must be  $1$ .Now,what is happening is that we have an infinite chain of  $f^n(x)$  which is determined by its first  $3$  terms, $x,f(x),f(f(x))$ .We will prove that if  $f(x) \neq x$  we have that some term of the sequence  $f^n(x)$  will be negative.If we write the sequence as  $f^n(x)=a_n$ ,we have a recurrence relation  $a_{n+3}=6a_n-a_{n+1}-4a_{n+2}$  and its solution is  $a_n=c_1(-3)^n+c_2(-2)^n+c_3$ .Now we prove that  $c_1=c_2=0$ .Now we prove that if they are not both zero,there will exist a term of the sequence which is negative,which will be a contradiction.
Case  $1$ : $c_1 \neq 0$ .
Then, $c_1(-3)^n$  will eventually become much larger than both  $c_2(-2)^n$  and  $c_3$  and it will switch signs between positive and negative,so we pick when it is negative and then we will get a negative term of the sequence,which is a contradiction.
Case  $2$ : $c_1=0$  but  $c_2 \neq 0$ .Then, $c_2(-2)^n$  will eventually become larger than  $c_3$  by absolute value and it will switch signs between positive and negative,we pick when it's negative and get a negative term,which is a contradiction.
Now we proved that the sequence  $x,f(x),f^2(x),
...f^n(x)$  is constant which means that  $f(x)=x$  for all  $x$ .

stem_md: Find all functions  $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$  such that  $$ 19f(x)-17f(f(x))=2x $$  for all  $x\in\mathbb Z$ .
solution_md:
Find all functions $f:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ such that $$ 19f(x)-17f(f(x))=2x $$ for all $x\in\mathbb Z$ .
Looking $\pmod{17}$ , we get $f(x)\equiv x\pmod{17}$ and so $f(x)=x+17g(x)$ for some $g(x)$ from $\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z$ Equation becomes then $17g(f(x))=2g(x)$ and simple infinite descent mod $17$ implies $g\equiv 0$ And so $\boxed{f(x)=x\quad\forall x\in\mathbb Z}$

stem_md: We consider the following game for one person. The aim of the player is to reach a fixed capital  $C>2$ . The player begins with capital  $0<x_0<C$ . In each turn let  $x$  be the player’s current capital. Define  $s(x)$  as follows:  $$ s(x):=\begin{cases}x&\text{if }x<1C-x&\text{if }C-x<11&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$  Then a fair coin is tossed and the player’s capital either increases or decreases by  $s(x)$ , each with probability  $\frac12$ . Find the probability that in a finite number of turns the player wins by reaching the capital  $C$ .
solution_md: We consider the following game for one person. The aim of the player is to reach a fixed capital $C>2$ . The player begins with capital $0 Prodded by a friend to share the martingale solution, here it is. We shall use the [optional stopping theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optional_stopping_theorem). Let $X_t$ be the fortune of the gambler at time $t,$ for every $t \in \mathbb{N}_{0}.$ Then as commented above $(X_t)$ is a martingale. Let $\tau$ be the random time when the fortune of the gambler drops to $0$ or rises to $C.$ Then we have $0 \le X_{\tau \wedge t} \le C$ for all $t,$ and also $\mathbf{E} [ \tau ] < \infty.$ So by the optional stopping theorem $\mathbf{E} [ X_{\tau} ] = \mathbf{E} [ X_0 ] = x_0,$ now we condition on whether the fortune at time $\tau$ is $C$ or $0$ to get $0 \mathbf{P} \{ X_\tau = 0 \} + C \mathbf{P} \{ X_{\tau} = C \} = x_0,$ and clearly $\mathbf{P} \{ X_{\tau} = C \}$ is the probability we are looking for. $\square$

stem_md:
Let  $E$  be the set of all continuously differentiable real valued functions  $f$  on  $[0,1]$  such that  $f(0)=0$  and  $f(1)=1$ . Define  $$ J(f)=\int^1_0(1+x^2)f'(x)^2\text dx. $$  a) Show that  $J$  achieves its minimum value at some element of  $E$ .
b) Calculate  $\min_{f\in E}J(f)$ .
solution_md:
Let's use cauchy-schwartz inequality with  $g(x)=\sqrt{(1+x^2)}f'(x)$  and  $h(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ , so: $|\int_0^1 g(x)h(x)dx|^2 \leq \int_0^1 g(x)^2dx \times \int_0^1 h(x)^2dx$  $|\int_0^1 f'(x)dx|^2 \leq \int_0^1 (1+x^2)f'(x)^2 \times \int_0^1 \frac{1}{1+x^2}$  $|f(1)-f(0)|\leq J(f) \times \arctan(1)-\arctan(0)$  $1\leq \frac{\pi}{4}J(f)$ .

Therefore  $J(f)\geq \frac{4}{\pi}$ . Equality holds if  $g=\lambda h$ ,, for some  $\lambda$  so  $f$  has to satisfy  $\sqrt{1+x^2}f'(x)=\frac{\lambda}{\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ , that implies  $f'(x)=\frac{\lambda}{1+x^2}$ , proving (a).

Integrating we have: $f(1)-f(0)=1=\int_0^1\frac{\lambda}{1+x^2}dx=\lambda \pi/4$ , so  $\lambda=\frac{4}{\pi}$ .

So for a):  $f(x)=\frac{4}{\pi}\arctan(x)\in E$  minimizes  $J(f)$ , and b) his minimum value is  $\frac{4}{\pi}$ .

Regards
Claudio.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/Vojtěch Jarník IMC/2009 VJIMC/2588749.json

stem_md: Let  $A$  be an  $n\times n$  square matrix with integer entries. Suppose that  $p^2A^{p^2}=q^2A^{q^2}+r^2I_n$  for some positive integers  $p,q,r$  where  $r$  is odd and  $p^2=q^2+r^2$ . Prove that  $|\det A|=1$ . (Here  $I_n$  means the  $n\times n$  identity matrix.)
solution_md: Let  $\Pi(x)=p^2x^{p^2}-q^2A^{q^2}-r^2$  such that  $\Pi(A)=0$ . Therefore,  $\forall\lambda\in\mathrm{Sp(A)}=\{\lambda_1,...,\lambda_n\}$ ,  $\Pi(\lambda)=0$ . Therefore,  $p^2\lambda^{p^2}=q^2\lambda^{q^2}+r^2\implies p^2|\lambda|^{p^2}\le q^2|\lambda|^{q^2}+r^2$  by the triangle inequality, which thus yields  $\Pi(|\lambda|)\le0$ . Furthermore, we have  $\Pi'(x)=p^4x^{p^2-1}-q^4x^{q^2-1}=p^4x^{q^2-1}\left(x^{p^2-q^2}-\left(\frac qp\right)^4\right)=p^4x^{q^2-1}\left(x^{r^2}-\left(\frac qp\right)^4\right)$  hence  $\Pi'(x)=0\iff x=0$  or  $x=\left(\frac qp\right)^\frac{4}{r^2}=C$ . Indeed,  $r$  odd  $\implies r>0$  and since there are no consecutive square of integers greater than  $1$ ,  $q\ne1$ . We also have  $p^2> q^2\implies C\in[0,1)$ . We also notice that  $\Pi(0)=-r^2<0$  and  $\Pi(1)=0$ . Since  $\lim_{x\rightarrow+\infty}\Pi(x)=+\infty$ , then  $\Pi$  is increasing on  $[C,+\infty)$ . Since  $\Pi$  has a root on  $[C,+\infty)$ , we deduce by the Intermediate Value Theorem that  $\Pi(C)<0$ , which also means that  $\Pi$  has no roots on  $(0,1)$ . Finally,  $r$  odd  $\implies r^2\equiv1\pmod 4\implies p^2\equiv q^2+1\pmod 4$ . This forces  $p$  to be odd and  $q$  to be even, which means that  $\lim_{x\to-\infty}\Pi(x)=-\infty$  because  $\mathrm{deg}\Pi=p^2$ . Therefore,  $\Pi$  is increasing on  $(-\infty,0)$  and so  $1$  is the only real root of  $\Pi$  and we have  $\Pi(x)\le0\iff x\le1$  and since  $0$  isn't a root of  $\Pi$ , we have  $\forall\lambda\in\mathrm{Sp(A)},0<|\lambda|\le1$ . We thus have :  $$ |\det A|=\prod_{i=1}^n|\lambda_i|\in(0,1] $$  Finally since  $A\in\mathcal M_n(\mathbb Z)$ , we have  $\det A\in\mathbb Z$  which finally gives us  $|\det A|=1$  as wanted

stem_md: Prove that the number  $$ 2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1 $$  is composite (not prime) for all positive integers  $k>2$ .
solution_md:
Note that if  $k$  is even, then  $2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1 \equiv -1-1-1 \equiv 0 \pmod{3}$ , and  $2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1 > 3$  for all  $k > 2$ , so it is composite.
If  $k$  is odd, then  $2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1 = \frac{1}{2}(2^{2^k}-2^{k+1}-2) = \frac{1}{2}((2^{2^k}-1)-(2^{k+1}+1)) =\frac{1}{2}((2+1)(2^2 + 1)\ldots(2^{2^{k-1}}+1) - (2^{k+1} + 1)).$ Since  $k+1$  is even,  $k+1 = 2^ab$  for some odd positive integer  $b$  and integer  $a \geq 1$ . Since  $x + y \mid x^n + y^n$  if  $n$  is odd,  $2^{2^a} + 1 \mid 2^{k+1} + 1$ .
If  $a \geq k$ , then  $a + 1 \geq k + 1 = 2^ab \geq 2^a$ , which is only true if  $a = k = 1$ , but  $k > 2$ , contradiction. 
Thus,  $a \leq k - 1$  and  $2^{2^a} + 1 \mid (2+1)(2^2 + 1)\ldots(2^{2^{k-1}}+1)$ . 
Therefore, since  $2^{2^a} + 1$  is odd,  $2^{2^a} + 1 \mid 2^{2^k-1}-2^k-1$ , making it composite.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/Vojtěch Jarník IMC/2009 VJIMC/2588752.json

stem_md:
a) Is it true that for every bijection  $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$  the series  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{nf(n)} $$  is convergent?
b) Prove that there exists a bijection  $f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$  such that the series  $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac1{n+f(n)} $$  is convergent.
( $\mathbb N$  is the set of all positive integers.)
solution_md:
b) The idea is that we would like to choose  $f(n)$  really large most of the time. But of course to get a bijection, we also need to attach the small numbers to some  $n$ . But if we choose these  $n$  to be a very rapidly growing subsequence, we will still win.
To be more precise, let  $A \subset \mathbb{N}$  be any infinite set such that  $\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n}$  converges (e.g. the set of perfect squares or of powers of  $2$ ,...). This will be our rapidly growing subsequence on which  $f$  can be arbitrary.
For  $n \not \in A$ , we define  $f(n)=n^2$ . We then just choose an arbitrary bijection  $f:A \to \mathbb{N} \{n^2: n \not \in A\}$  (e.g. just match the smallest element with the smallest one etc.). We claim that this function does the job.
Indeed,
\[\sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n+f(n)} \le \sum_{n \in A} \frac{1}{n}\]
is convergent by construction of  $A$ , regardless the values of  $f(n)$  for  $n\in A$ . On the other hand,
\[\sum_{n \not \in A} \frac{1}{n+f(n)} \le \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n+n^2}\]
is of course also convergent and we win.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/Undergraduate Contests/Vojtěch Jarník IMC/2010 VJIMC/2579854.json

\[\sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{nf(n)} \le \sum_{n=1}^N \frac{1}{n^2}\]
for all  $N$  whenever  $f$  is injective. Since the series  $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^2}$  is convergent, this will show that the series in the problem is also convergent.
Indeed, by decreasing  $f$  if necessary we may assume that  $f:\{1,2,\dots,n\} \to \{1,2,\dots,n\}$  is a bijection. But then the claim follows directly from the rearrangement inequality.
